text: Did the major axes of color pattern variation in my family originate early in its history and then slow down, or have color patterns continued to diversify at a steady pace all the way to the present?

title: Recipe 19: Disparity Through Time
text: Did the major axes of color pattern variation in my family originate early in its history and then slow down, or have color patterns continued to diversify at a steady pace all the way to the present?

title: Recipe 19: Disparity Through Time
text:
This Is an Instance Of…






Macroevolutionary tempo analysis



Disparity-through-time (DTT) analysis asks how morphological (or color) diversity was distributed across the tree at each moment in evolutionary history. It works by computing, for each internal node, the average pairwise disparity within subclades descending from that node, then watching how that subclade disparity changes as you move from the root toward the tips. If subclades partition color space early — each major lineage staking out its own region — disparity within subclades will be low relative to total disparity, and you get a negative MDI. If subclades overlap in color space and diversification is ongoing, disparity within subclades stays high relative to total disparity, and you get a positive MDI. This is one of the few macroevolutionary methods that directly tests whether an adaptive radiation “front-loaded” its diversity.

title: Recipe 19: Disparity Through Time
section: Why This Matters for Your Clade
text:
Why This Matters for Your Clade
Reef fish families differ enormously in whether their color diversity looks early-burst or gradual. Some families, like angelfishes, have iconic deep-clade differences in color pattern (adults vs. juveniles, planktivores vs. cleaners) that were established millions of years ago. Others, like wrasses, show more recent explosions of color in sexual signals. DTT analysis gives you a visual and quantitative answer to which pattern dominates in your family. It also connects directly to lectures on macroevolutionary rates (Lec 18) — you are putting your family’s color evolution on the same framework used to study entire adaptive radiations.






Clade-specific tips




Pomacanthidae (angelfishes): The juvenile–adult color difference is a developmental, not evolutionary, pattern — make sure your pavo metrics all come from adult photographs. If early diverging genera (e.g., Pomacanthus) have very different color from derived genera (e.g., Centropyge), expect a negative MDI: early lineages staked out very different color space.
Cirrhilabrini (fairy wrasses): The extreme color diversity in this tribe is largely concentrated in Cirrhilabrus and Paracheilinus. Whether this shows as early or late on the DTT curve depends on where the tribe-level split falls relative to the species-level diversification within these genera.
Hypsigenyinae (hogfishes and allies): With only ~38 species, your DTT null envelope will be wide. A non-significant MDI does not mean the pattern is absent — report MDI and interpret it qualitatively even if the p-value is borderline.
Balistoidea (triggerfishes + filefishes): The two families (Balistidae and Monacanthidae) diverged early and have quite different color strategies. If your bundle spans both, expect early-burst signal from that deep split.

title: Recipe 19: Disparity Through Time
text:
The Method
DTT uses your pavo trait matrix and your time-calibrated phylogeny to compute subclade disparity at each internal node. The dtt() function in the geiger package does the heavy lifting. It then compares the observed DTT curve against a Brownian motion null, generated by simulating 1,000 random datasets on the same tree. The morphological disparity index (MDI) is the signed area between the observed DTT curve and the Brownian motion median. Positive MDI means your observed disparity stays higher than expected under drift (subclades overlap — late-filling color space); negative MDI means your observed disparity falls below expected (subclades are partitioned — early-burst pattern).
The input should be a matrix where rows are species and columns are your pavo variables (m, A, Jc, Jt, m_dS, m_dL). Using all six variables jointly captures overall color pattern disparity rather than any single axis.
This analysis requires the geiger package. If it is not installed, run install.packages("geiger") once before sourcing helpers.

title: Recipe 19: Disparity Through Time
text:
How to Interpret Results








MDI
Meaning
What to say on your poster




MDI > 0 (p < 0.05)
Subclades overlap in color space — ongoing diversification, clades have not partitioned color axes
“Color pattern diversity accumulated gradually and continuously; major clades have not converged on distinct color strategies.”


MDI < 0 (p < 0.05)
Subclades partitioned — early niche partitioning, each major clade occupies distinct color space
“Color pattern diversity shows an early-burst signature: major color axes were established early in the family’s history and subsequent diversification filled within-clade space.”


MDI ~ 0 (p > 0.05)
Observed trajectory matches Brownian motion expectation
“Color pattern disparity accumulates at a rate consistent with neutral evolutionary drift, without strong evidence for either early burst or recent acceleration.”


p-value marginally significant (0.05–0.10)
Borderline
Report MDI and direction; note that your sample size may limit power.









Common pitfalls




DTT requires a time-calibrated (ultrametric) tree. Check that your tree is ultrametric before running: ape::is.ultrametric(tree). If it returns FALSE, small numerical errors from tree-building may be to blame; try phytools::force.ultrametric(tree) to correct them, and report that you did so.
Interpret the MDI in light of your tree shape. A heavily pectinate (ladder-shaped) tree will produce different null expectations than a balanced tree. The Brownian motion simulation envelope accounts for this, but if your tree is very asymmetric, the envelope will be wide and power will be lower.
Missing data affects disparity estimates. If some species lack values for one or more pavo variables, remove them before building the trait matrix. Do not impute missing values for this analysis.
DTT is a whole-tree summary. It does not tell you which node drove the early burst. If you want to identify the responsible clade, compare DTT curves for subclades separately (run dtt() on pruned subtrees).

title: Recipe 19: Disparity Through Time
text:
The Code

# ── Recipe 19: Disparity Through Time ───────────────────────────
# Requires the geiger package.
# If not installed: install.packages("geiger")

source("https://michaelalfaro.github.io/eeb187-demos/recipes/code/helpers.R")   # loads ape, phytools, ggplot2, theme_poster
library(geiger)

# ── 1. Load your tree and pavo data ─────────────────────────────
bundle   <- load_bundle("path/to/your-family-mini-bundle")
pavo_csv <- read.csv("path/to/your-pavo-metrics.csv",
                      stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# ── 2. Match tree to data ───────────────────────────────────────
matched <- match_tree_data(bundle$tree, pavo_csv, species_col = "species")
tree    <- matched$tree
dat     <- matched$data

cat("Working with", length(tree$tip.label), "species\n")

# ── 3. Check that tree is ultrametric ───────────────────────────
if (!ape::is.ultrametric(tree)) {
  cat("Tree is not ultrametric — forcing ultrametric (small numerical fix)\n")
  tree <- phytools::force.ultrametric(tree, method = "extend")
}

# ── 4. Build trait matrix ───────────────────────────────────────
pavo_vars <- c("m", "A", "Jc", "Jt", "m_dS", "m_dL")
complete  <- complete.cases(dat[, pavo_vars])
if (any(!complete)) {
  cat("Dropping", sum(!complete), "species with missing pavo values\n")
}
dat_complete <- dat[complete, ]
tree         <- ape::drop.tip(tree,
                              setdiff(tree$tip.label, dat_complete$species))

trait_mat            <- as.matrix(dat_complete[, pavo_vars])
rownames(trait_mat)  <- dat_complete$species
trait_mat            <- trait_mat[tree$tip.label, ]   # align row order

cat("Final sample for DTT:", nrow(trait_mat), "species\n")

# ── 5. DTT analysis with 1000 simulations ───────────────────────
set.seed(42)   # for reproducibility
dtt_result <- dtt(tree, trait_mat, nsim = 1000, plot = FALSE)

# ── 6. Compute p-value and report MDI ─────────────────────────────
# geiger's dtt() returns MDI but not always a p-value (depends on
# package version). We compute it from the simulation matrix:
# for each BM simulation, compute its MDI, then ask what fraction
# of simulated MDIs are >= the observed MDI.
bm_median <- apply(dtt_result$sim, 1, median, na.rm = TRUE)
sim_mdis  <- apply(dtt_result$sim, 2, function(s) mean(s - bm_median))
obs_mdi   <- as.numeric(dtt_result$MDI)
mdi_pval  <- mean(sim_mdis >= obs_mdi)

cat("\n── Disparity-Through-Time results ──\n")
cat("MDI (morphological disparity index):", round(obs_mdi, 3), "\n")
cat("p-value (proportion of BM sims with MDI >= observed):",
    round(mdi_pval, 3), "\n")

if (obs_mdi > 0) {
  cat("Interpretation: subclades OVERLAP in color space (MDI > 0)\n")
  cat("  Color diversity has accumulated continuously; no early partitioning.\n")
} else {
  cat("Interpretation: subclades are PARTITIONED in color space (MDI < 0)\n")
  cat("  Early-burst signature: major color axes established early.\n")
}

# ── 7. Helper function to plot a DTT result ───────────────────────
# geiger 2.0.11 does not provide a plot method for dtt objects,
# so we draw the DTT envelope manually.
plot_dtt <- function(dtt_obj, main = "Disparity Through Time", ...) {
  times     <- dtt_obj$times
  obs_curve <- dtt_obj$dtt
  sim_lower <- apply(dtt_obj$sim, 1, quantile, probs = 0.025, na.rm = TRUE)
  sim_upper <- apply(dtt_obj$sim, 1, quantile, probs = 0.975, na.rm = TRUE)
  sim_med   <- apply(dtt_obj$sim, 1, median, na.rm = TRUE)

  plot(times, obs_curve, type = "n",
       ylim = range(c(obs_curve, sim_lower, sim_upper), na.rm = TRUE),
       main = main,
       xlab = "Relative time (root = 0, tips = 1)",
       ylab = "Average subclade disparity", ...)
  polygon(c(times, rev(times)), c(sim_lower, rev(sim_upper)),
          col = rgb(0, 0, 0, 0.1), border = NA)
  lines(times, sim_med, col = "grey50", lty = 2)
  lines(times, obs_curve, col = "black", lwd = 2)
}

# ── 7b. Save DTT plot as PDF ─────────────────────────────────────
pdf("results/recipe19-dtt.pdf", width = 8, height = 6)
plot_dtt(dtt_result,
         main = "Disparity Through Time — Color Pattern")
mtext(paste0("MDI = ", round(obs_mdi, 3),
             "  (p = ", round(mdi_pval, 3), ")"),
      side = 1, line = -2, adj = 0.05, cex = 0.9)
dev.off()
cat("Saved: results/recipe19-dtt.pdf\n")

# ── 8. Optional: DTT for individual pavo variables ──────────────
# Run DTT separately for each variable to see which drives the pattern.
pdf("results/recipe19-dtt-by-variable.pdf", width = 12, height = 8)
par(mfrow = c(2, 3))
for (v in pavo_vars) {
  x_vec            <- setNames(dat_complete[[v]], dat_complete$species)
  x_vec            <- x_vec[tree$tip.label]
  x_mat            <- matrix(x_vec, ncol = 1,
                             dimnames = list(names(x_vec), v))
  dtt_v <- tryCatch(
    dtt(tree, x_mat, nsim = 200, plot = FALSE),
    error = function(e) NULL
  )
  if (!is.null(dtt_v)) {
    bm_med_v   <- apply(dtt_v$sim, 1, median, na.rm = TRUE)
    sim_mdis_v <- apply(dtt_v$sim, 2, function(s) mean(s - bm_med_v))
    mdi_v      <- as.numeric(dtt_v$MDI)
    pval_v     <- mean(sim_mdis_v >= mdi_v)

    plot_dtt(dtt_v, main = v)
    mtext(paste0("MDI=", round(mdi_v, 2), " p=", round(pval_v, 2)),
          side = 1, line = -1.5, adj = 0.05, cex = 0.75)
  }
}
dev.off()
cat("Saved: results/recipe19-dtt-by-variable.pdf\n")

title: Recipe 19: Disparity Through Time
text:
From the Literature

Harmon, L. J., Schulte, J. A., II, Larson, A., & Losos, J. B. (2003) — Introduced the disparity-through-time framework and the MDI statistic by applying it to iguanian lizard radiations. Showed that Anolis lizards show a classic adaptive radiation pattern (early partitioning of ecomorphs) while other iguanians do not. This paper is the primary reference for the DTT method. Science, 301(5635), 961–964. DOI


Slater, G. J., Price, S. A., Santini, F., & Alfaro, M. E. (2010) — Applied DTT analysis to body size evolution in elopomorph fishes, showing that this diverse lineage does not show an early-burst pattern despite being an ancient radiation. A good example of how to report and interpret a non-significant or positive MDI result. Proceedings of the Royal Society B, 277(1687), 1563–1569. DOI


Melville, J., Harmon, L. J., & Losos, J. B. (2006) — Used DTT to compare color and morphological disparity in Ctenotus skinks, demonstrating that color and body shape can show different macroevolutionary tempos within the same clade — a useful precedent for interpreting divergent results across your six pavo variables. Evolution, 60(8), 1577–1587. DOI

title: Recipe 22: Expanded Evolutionary Model Comparison
text: Beyond drift, constraint, and early burst — does color evolve punctuationally, with a directional trend, or under an alternative mode?

title: Recipe 22: Expanded Evolutionary Model Comparison
text: Beyond drift, constraint, and early burst — does color evolve punctuationally, with a directional trend, or under an alternative mode?

title: Recipe 22: Expanded Evolutionary Model Comparison
text:
This Is an Instance Of…






Extended model selection for trait evolution



Recipe 20 tests three evolutionary models (BM, OU, EB). This recipe extends that comparison to eight models by adding Pagel’s branch-length transformations (lambda, kappa, delta), a directional trend model, and a white noise null. Each additional model captures a distinct evolutionary scenario that BM/OU/EB cannot distinguish. Together, the eight models cover nearly every major hypothesis about how a continuous trait might evolve on a phylogeny.

title: Recipe 22: Expanded Evolutionary Model Comparison
section: Why This Matters for Your Clade
text:
Why This Matters for Your Clade
Recipe 20 may tell you that BM wins — but what if the real process is punctuational change concentrated at speciation events (kappa), or a directional trend toward increasing color complexity over time? These alternatives are invisible to a BM/OU/EB comparison. By fitting all eight models, you cast a wider net and reduce the chance of missing the true evolutionary mode. If kappa wins, your story becomes about speciation-associated change. If delta wins, you learn whether evolution was front-loaded or back-loaded. If lambda wins with a low value, phylogeny may not predict color at all.






Clade-specific tips




Pomacanthidae (angelfishes): If kappa < 1 wins, color changes at speciation events rather than along branches — consistent with the dramatic genus-level color differences in angelfishes.
Cirrhilabrini (fairy wrasses): A trend model might capture directional evolution toward increasing male display color complexity, driven by persistent sexual selection.
Balistoidea (triggerfishes + filefishes): Delta < 1 (early change) would be consistent with the deep split between the two families establishing distinct color strategies early.
Scarinae (parrotfishes): The lambda model might reveal that phylogenetic signal in color is weaker than the tree topology suggests, because phase changes scramble the phylogenetic pattern.

title: Recipe 22: Expanded Evolutionary Model Comparison
text:
The Method
The fitContinuous() function in the geiger package fits all eight models to a named trait vector and a phylogeny. Each model transforms the tree’s branch lengths or variance-covariance structure in a different way to best fit the observed trait data.
Here is what each model captures:

BM (Brownian motion): Random drift at a constant rate. The null model.
OU (Ornstein-Uhlenbeck): Drift with a “rubber band” pulling toward an optimum. Stabilizing selection.
EB (Early Burst): Rate of evolution decays exponentially from root to tips. Adaptive radiation signature.
Lambda: Scales the internal branch lengths (0 = star tree, 1 = original tree). Tests phylogenetic signal strength directly.
Kappa: Raises branch lengths to a power. Kappa < 1 = punctuational (change concentrated at nodes). Kappa > 1 = gradual (change proportional to time).
Delta: Raises path lengths to a power. Delta < 1 = early change. Delta > 1 = late change.
Trend: Brownian motion with a directional drift — the trait mean shifts systematically over time.
White noise: No phylogenetic structure at all. Every species is drawn independently from a single distribution.

We compare all eight using AICc (corrected Akaike Information Criterion, which penalizes extra parameters more strongly with small sample sizes). The model with the lowest AICc is preferred, and Akaike weights quantify the relative support for each model.

title: Recipe 22: Expanded Evolutionary Model Comparison
text:
How to Interpret Results








Winning model
Biological interpretation
What to say on your poster




BM
Neutral drift at constant rate
“Color evolves as a random walk with no detectable directional or selective pressure.”


OU
Stabilizing selection toward an optimum
“Color is constrained by stabilizing selection — lineages that stray too far are pulled back toward a family-level optimum.”


EB
Early burst, rates slow down
“Color diversified rapidly early in the family’s history and has since slowed, consistent with early niche filling.”


Lambda (low)
Weak phylogenetic signal
“Phylogeny is a poor predictor of color — closely related species are no more similar than expected by chance.”


Kappa (< 1)
Punctuational evolution
“Color changes are concentrated at speciation events rather than accumulating gradually along branches.”


Delta (< 1)
Early change dominates
“Most color evolution occurred early in the family’s history, with little change in recent branches.”


Delta (> 1)
Late change dominates
“Color evolution has accelerated toward the present, with most change in recent lineages.”


Trend
Directional evolution
“Color has evolved directionally over time — there is a systematic trend toward [higher/lower] values.”


White noise
No phylogenetic structure
“Color variation shows no phylogenetic structure at all — the tree contains no information about color similarity.”









Common pitfalls




Overfitting with 8 models and small trees: With < 40 species, AICc differences among models may be too small to be meaningful. Focus on the top 2–3 models and whether they tell a consistent story.
Lambda and OU can mimic each other. Both capture “less phylogenetic signal than expected.” If both rank near the top, the key result is that signal is reduced — the specific mechanism (branch scaling vs. rubber band) may be indistinguishable.
Trend requires a root-to-tip direction. The trend model assumes time flows from root to tips. It is only meaningful for ultrametric (time-calibrated) trees.
Do not interpret winning model parameters in isolation. A kappa of 0.8 that wins by 1 AICc unit over BM is a weak result. Always report the deltaAICc and Akaike weights alongside the winning model.
This extends Recipe 20. If you have already run Recipe 20, you can report the extended comparison as a sensitivity analysis that confirms or refines your earlier result.

title: Recipe 22: Expanded Evolutionary Model Comparison
text:
The Code

# ── Recipe 22: Expanded Evolutionary Model Comparison ─────────────
# Requires the geiger package.
# If not installed: install.packages("geiger")

source("https://michaelalfaro.github.io/eeb187-demos/recipes/code/helpers.R")   # loads ape, phytools, ggplot2, theme_poster
library(geiger)

# ── 1. Load your tree and pavo data ───────────────────────────────
bundle   <- load_bundle("path/to/your-family-mini-bundle")
pavo_csv <- read.csv("path/to/your-pavo-metrics.csv",
                      stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# ── 2. Match tree to data ─────────────────────────────────────────
matched <- match_tree_data(bundle$tree, pavo_csv, species_col = "species")
tree    <- matched$tree
dat     <- matched$data

cat("Working with", length(tree$tip.label), "species\n")

# ── 3. Check ultrametric ──────────────────────────────────────────
if (!ape::is.ultrametric(tree)) {
  cat("Forcing ultrametric tree (small numerical correction)\n")
  tree <- phytools::force.ultrametric(tree, method = "extend")
}

# ── 4. Build PC1 as focal trait ───────────────────────────────────
pavo_vars <- c("m", "A", "Jc", "Jt", "m_dS", "m_dL")

complete <- complete.cases(dat[, pavo_vars])
if (any(!complete)) {
  cat("Dropping", sum(!complete), "species with missing values\n")
}
dat_complete <- dat[complete, ]
tree         <- ape::drop.tip(tree,
                              setdiff(tree$tip.label, dat_complete$species))

trait_mat           <- dat_complete[, pavo_vars]
rownames(trait_mat) <- dat_complete$species
trait_mat           <- trait_mat[tree$tip.label, ]

pca <- prcomp(trait_mat, scale. = TRUE)
pc1 <- setNames(pca$x[, 1], rownames(pca$x))

var_explained <- round(summary(pca)$importance[2, 1] * 100, 1)
cat("PC1 explains", var_explained, "% of color pattern variance\n")

# ── 5. Fit all 8 evolutionary models ─────────────────────────────
models <- c("BM", "OU", "EB", "lambda", "kappa", "delta", "trend", "white")

fits <- lapply(setNames(models, models), function(m) {
  tryCatch(
    fitContinuous(tree, pc1, model = m),
    error = function(e) {
      message("Model '", m, "' failed: ", e$message)
      NULL
    }
  )
})

# Remove any models that failed
fits <- fits[!sapply(fits, is.null)]
cat("Successfully fit", length(fits), "of", length(models), "models\n")

# ── 6. Build AICc comparison table ───────────────────────────────
aic_table <- data.frame(
  Model    = names(fits),
  AICc     = sapply(fits, function(f) f$opt$aicc),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
aic_table$deltaAICc <- round(aic_table$AICc - min(aic_table$AICc), 2)
aic_table$weight    <- round(
  exp(-0.5 * aic_table$deltaAICc) /
  sum(exp(-0.5 * aic_table$deltaAICc)), 3
)
aic_table$AICc      <- round(aic_table$AICc, 2)
aic_table           <- aic_table[order(aic_table$deltaAICc), ]

cat("\n── Extended Model Comparison (PC1) ─────────────────────────\n")
print(aic_table, row.names = FALSE)

best <- aic_table$Model[1]
cat("\nBest model:", best, "(Akaike weight =", aic_table$weight[1], ")\n")

# ── 7. Report key parameters for the best model ──────────────────
cat("\n── Best model parameters ──────────────────────────────────\n")
best_fit <- fits[[best]]
if (best == "lambda") {
  cat("  lambda:", round(best_fit$opt$lambda, 3), "\n")
  if (best_fit$opt$lambda < 0.3) cat("  → Weak phylogenetic signal\n")
} else if (best == "kappa") {
  cat("  kappa:", round(best_fit$opt$kappa, 3), "\n")
  if (best_fit$opt$kappa < 1) cat("  → Punctuational evolution\n")
  if (best_fit$opt$kappa > 1) cat("  → Gradual evolution\n")
} else if (best == "delta") {
  cat("  delta:", round(best_fit$opt$delta, 3), "\n")
  if (best_fit$opt$delta < 1) cat("  → Early change dominates\n")
  if (best_fit$opt$delta > 1) cat("  → Late change dominates\n")
} else if (best == "trend") {
  cat("  slope:", round(best_fit$opt$slope, 4), "\n")
  cat("  → Directional trend in color over time\n")
} else if (best == "OU") {
  cat("  alpha:", round(best_fit$opt$alpha, 4), "\n")
  if (best_fit$opt$alpha < 0.01) cat("  → alpha near zero: OU ≈ BM\n")
} else if (best == "EB") {
  cat("  a (rate decay):", round(best_fit$opt$a, 4), "\n")
  if (abs(best_fit$opt$a) < 0.001) cat("  → a near zero: EB ≈ BM\n")
}

# ── 8. Bar chart of Akaike weights ───────────────────────────────
aic_table$Model <- factor(aic_table$Model, levels = aic_table$Model)

ggplot(aic_table, aes(x = Model, y = weight, fill = Model)) +
  geom_col(alpha = 0.85, width = 0.7) +
  labs(title = "Akaike weights across 8 evolutionary models (PC1)",
       x = "", y = "Akaike weight") +
  theme_poster +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))

ggsave("results/recipe22-model-weights-pc1.pdf", width = 9, height = 6)
cat("Saved: results/recipe22-model-weights-pc1.pdf\n")

# ── 9. Heatmap: all traits x all models ──────────────────────────
# Run model comparison for each pavo variable + PC1
all_traits <- c(pavo_vars, "PC1")
heatmap_data <- data.frame()

for (v in all_traits) {
  if (v == "PC1") {
    x <- pc1
  } else {
    x <- setNames(dat_complete[[v]], dat_complete$species)
    x <- x[tree$tip.label]
  }

  for (m in models) {
    fit <- tryCatch(
      fitContinuous(tree, x, model = m),
      error = function(e) NULL
    )
    if (!is.null(fit)) {
      heatmap_data <- rbind(heatmap_data, data.frame(
        trait = v, model = m, aicc = fit$opt$aicc,
        stringsAsFactors = FALSE
      ))
    }
  }
}

# Compute weights within each trait
library(dplyr)
heatmap_data <- heatmap_data %>%
  group_by(trait) %>%
  mutate(
    delta_aicc = aicc - min(aicc),
    weight = exp(-0.5 * delta_aicc) / sum(exp(-0.5 * delta_aicc))
  ) %>%
  ungroup()

# Plot heatmap
heatmap_data$trait <- factor(heatmap_data$trait, levels = rev(all_traits))
heatmap_data$model <- factor(heatmap_data$model, levels = models)

ggplot(heatmap_data, aes(x = model, y = trait, fill = weight)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(weight, 2)), size = 3.5) +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = "#2a9d8f",
                      name = "Akaike\nweight") +
  labs(title = "Model support across color variables",
       x = "Evolutionary model", y = "Color variable") +
  theme_poster +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1))

ggsave("results/recipe22-model-heatmap.pdf", width = 10, height = 7)
cat("Saved: results/recipe22-model-heatmap.pdf\n")

title: Recipe 22: Expanded Evolutionary Model Comparison
text:
From the Literature

Pagel, M. (1999) — Introduced the lambda, kappa, and delta branch-length transformations for testing the tempo and mode of trait evolution on phylogenies. Lambda tests phylogenetic signal, kappa tests punctuational vs. gradual change, and delta tests early vs. late change. These three transformations remain the standard tools for exploring how trait evolution departs from Brownian motion. Nature, 401(6756), 877–884. DOI


Harmon, L. J., Losos, J. B., Davies, T. J., Gillespie, R. G., Gittleman, J. L., Jennings, W. B., … & Mooers, A. O. (2010) — Systematically evaluated BM, OU, and EB models across hundreds of comparative datasets using fitContinuous(), finding that early burst is surprisingly rare. This paper provides the analytical framework and the geiger implementation used in this recipe. Evolution, 64(8), 2385–2396. DOI

title: Balistoidea — Triggerfishes and Filefishes
text:
Taxonomy and Phylogenetics
Balistoidea is a superfamily within the order Tetraodontiformes, the morphologically extreme clade of acanthomorph fishes that also contains pufferfishes, porcupinefishes, boxfishes, and the giant sunfishes (Molidae). Modern molecular and morphological analyses agree that Balistoidea is composed of two reciprocally monophyletic sister families: Balistidae (triggerfishes) and Monacanthidae (filefishes) (Holcroft, 2005; Santini, Alfaro & Brock, 2007; Alfaro, Sorenson & Santini, 2013). Some older classifications used “Balistoidea” more inclusively to encompass boxfishes (Ostraciidae) and other lineages, but recent multi-locus phylogenies recover a narrower Balistoidea = Balistidae + Monacanthidae, with Ostraciidae and the gymnodont families (Tetraodontidae, Diodontidae, Molidae) outside it (Alfaro et al., 2013; Holcroft, 2005).
Within Tetraodontiformes, Balistoidea sits in the suborder Balistoidei, sister to the more derived Tetraodontoidei (pufferfishes and allies). Crown Tetraodontiformes is estimated to have originated near the K-Pg boundary, with much of the morphological disparity that defines the order accumulating rapidly in the Paleocene and Eocene (Santini et al., 2007; Alfaro et al., 2013). Within Balistoidea itself, Santini, Sorenson and Alfaro (2013) used a multi-locus time-calibrated phylogeny to show that triggerfishes and filefishes diverged in the Middle Eocene, roughly 45 million years ago. Crucially, crown-group Monacanthidae is substantially older than crown-group Balistidae: the filefish radiation began in the Eocene-Oligocene, while modern triggerfish diversity originated in the Late Miocene. This asymmetry helps explain why Monacanthidae contains more than twice as many extant species as Balistidae despite similar per-lineage rates of speciation and body-size evolution (Santini, Sorenson & Alfaro, 2013). Bayesian phylogenetic work by Dornburg, Santini and Alfaro (2008) also illustrated — using triggerfishes as the empirical example — how model averaging substantially changes posterior support values within Balistidae, a methodological lesson with broad applicability to small-to-medium-sized reef-fish clades.
Generic relationships within Balistidae have been moderately stable across studies, with Balistes, Balistoides, Pseudobalistes, Sufflamen, Rhinecanthus, Xanthichthys, Melichthys, Odonus, Abalistes, and Canthidermis recovered as well-supported genera. Within Monacanthidae, generic boundaries are less stable; Cantherhines, Aluterus, Acreichthys, Stephanolepis, Chaetodermis, Paraluteres, Oxymonacanthus, and Monacanthus are well-supported, but several smaller genera nest awkwardly inside larger ones. Sorenson, Santini and Alfaro (2015) examined the evolution of the developmental gene BMP4 across Balistoidea and found rapid sequence evolution coincident with the diversification of triggerfish jaw morphology — an early hint that color and pattern diversity in this clade may have developmental-genetic correlates that are still under-explored.

title: Balistoidea — Triggerfishes and Filefishes
text:
Natural History
Balistoideans are predominantly tropical and subtropical, with their greatest diversity on Indo-Pacific coral reefs but with notable temperate-water lineages (e.g., Cantherhines in subtropical Australian waters, Stephanolepis in the Mediterranean and temperate Atlantic). Triggerfishes are conspicuous, mid-water and benthic reef occupants; filefishes are more ecologically diverse, ranging from cryptic reef-rubble dwellers (Acreichthys, Pervagor) to seagrass and algal-bed specialists (Monacanthus, Stephanolepis) to the long-bodied, near-pelagic Aluterus (Marshall, Cortesi & de Busserolles, 2018).
Diet spans an extraordinary range. Many triggerfishes are powerful durophages: Balistapus undulatus, Pseudobalistes species, and Balistoides viridescens use strongly fused jaws and stout incisor-like teeth to crush sea urchins, gastropods, and crustaceans. Mechanistic and developmental work on the tetraodontiform jaw apparatus shows that the balistoid feeding system represents a derived configuration in which the autopalatine has lost bony contact with the suspensorium, increasing jaw mobility and bite strength relative to the percomorph ancestral condition (Konstantinidis & Johnson, 2012). Other triggerfishes are planktivorous (Melichthys niger, Odonus niger, Xanthichthys), feeding well above the substrate in current-swept areas. Among filefishes, Oxymonacanthus longirostris is an obligate corallivore that feeds almost exclusively on Acropora polyps and uses chemical as well as visual cues from its prey for crypsis (Brooker, Munday, Jones & Chivers, 2015; Brooker, Munday & Jones, 2011). Other monacanthids are generalist browsers on sponges, hydroids, ascidians, and macroalgae.
A defining behavioral feature of Balistidae is site-attached, biparental or female-tended benthic nesting. Unlike the broadcast spawners that dominate most reef fish families, triggerfishes excavate a nest in sand or rubble, deposit demersal eggs in the depression, and aggressively defend the clutch until hatching. Gladstone (1994) provided a foundational description for Pseudobalistes flavimarginatus on the Great Barrier Reef, documenting lek-like mating grounds, semi-lunar spawning, and strict division of labor between sexes during egg care. Seki, Kohda and Takamoto (2008) experimentally demonstrated female-defense polygyny in Sufflamen chrysopterum, showing that males defend females rather than fixed territories. Rivera Hernández and Shervette (2024) recently quantified age-structured demography and reproductive seasonality for Balistes vetula in the Caribbean, confirming that prolonged nest-tending behavior is conserved across genera and ocean basins. Nest defense in triggerfishes is famously vigorous — nesting Balistoides viridescens and Pseudobalistes fuscus will attack divers — and this behavioral context is essential for interpreting the bold facial and body patterns seen in many balistids.
Filefishes show generally weaker territoriality, but many species are also pair-bonded, demersal spawners. Oxymonacanthus longirostris is unusual among reef fishes in being predominantly socially monogamous, with active female-female aggression maintaining the pair bond (Kokita, 2002).

title: Balistoidea — Triggerfishes and Filefishes
text:
Visual Ecology and Signaling
The visual ecology of Balistoidea is less studied than in butterflyfishes, damselfishes, or labrids, but available data and broad comparative work suggest that triggerfishes and filefishes have visual systems typical of diurnal shallow-reef teleosts. Marshall, Cortesi and de Busserolles (2018) reviewed reef-fish colors and color vision and noted that most balistoid reef-dwelling species are expected to possess the standard reef-fish complement of cone visual pigments tuned to the blue-green wavelengths that dominate shallow water, with at least some species having UV sensitivity. Direct microspectrophotometry and opsin expression data exist for very few balistoid species, however, and this is a notable gap in the literature. Inferences about visual signaling in this clade therefore rest largely on reef-fish-general work and on close relatives within Tetraodontiformes.
Three signaling axes appear important. First, conspicuous facial and body patterns in many triggerfishes (the geometric stripes of Rhinecanthus, the polka dots of Balistoides conspicillum, the orange-and-green pattern of Balistapus undulatus) likely function in species recognition and individual identification in diverse multispecies reef assemblages, similar to the functions documented for related patterns in butterflyfishes (Frédérich, Salis, Lorin & Salzburger, 2019). Second, transient color signaling is documented in nesting triggerfishes: females tending nests have been photographed displaying white blotches and intensified chin darkening, suggesting that brood-defense state is signaled through rapid (likely sympathetic-nervous) chromatophore changes (Rivera Hernández & Shervette, 2024). Third, in filefishes, changeable camouflage dominates over conspicuous signaling. Allen, Akkaynak, Sugden, Schomaker, Driscoll and Hanlon (2015) documented in Monacanthus tuckeri on Caribbean reefs that filefishes can change body pattern in 1-3 seconds across an ethogram of components (small and large spots, stripes, bars), producing both background-matching and disruptive camouflage on the same individual.
A clade-wide synthesis of opsin expression, cone abundance, and perceived color contrasts in Balistoidea remains to be written — a genuine opportunity for student projects.

title: Balistoidea — Triggerfishes and Filefishes
text:
Color Pattern Diversity
Balistoid color patterns span the full reef-fish gamut. Triggerfishes include some of the most graphically patterned of all reef fishes: the Picasso triggerfish Rhinecanthus aculeatus with its black-and-yellow facial stripes set against a pale flank; the clown triggerfish Balistoides conspicillum with bold white spots on a black ventral half and yellow-and-black saddle dorsally; the orange-lined triggerfish Balistapus undulatus with its dense diagonal lines on a green background; and the redtoothed triggerfish Odonus niger with its near-uniform blue-black body and contrasting red teeth. Several triggerfishes (e.g., Sufflamen verres, Xanthichthys ringens) are more muted but still display species-diagnostic facial striping and fin coloration.
Filefishes tend toward cryptic and changeable coloration. Many Cantherhines and Acreichthys species are mottled brown, gray, or olive, with skin tassels or papillae that increase the three-dimensional complexity of the body outline. Genuine masquerade is documented in Oxymonacanthus longirostris, which resembles a branch of Acropora coral in body shape, color, and resting orientation, and is also chemically cryptic via dietary sequestration of coral metabolites (Brooker et al., 2011, 2015). The slender filefish Monacanthus tuckeri combines background matching, disruptive coloration on the body interior, and three-dimensional dermal flaps that disguise the body outline; Allen et al. (2015) showed quantitatively that the species more closely matches the color of nearby visual stimuli than that of the surrounding background — a fine-scale rather than gestalt camouflage strategy. The genus Aluterus contains some of the most dramatic rapid color changers among reef fishes, capable of shifting between near-uniform white, mottled brown, and dark spotted phases within seconds.
One of the best-documented cases of interspecific color mimicry on coral reefs involves a balistoid: the blacksaddle filefish Paraluteres prionurus (Monacanthidae) is a Batesian mimic of the tetrodotoxin-bearing pufferfish Canthigaster valentini (Tetraodontidae). Caley and Schluter (2003) used graded plastic replicas to show that the umbrella of protection conferred by resembling the toxic model is broad: piscivores approach replicas less often as similarity to C. valentini increases, and protection extends to imperfect mimics. The system has been a touchstone for Batesian-mimicry theory in vertebrates (Williams, 2010).
Convergences with other reef-fish families are striking. The bold facial stripes of Rhinecanthus parallel patterns in butterflyfishes; the uniform dark blue of Odonus niger is paralleled in several surgeonfishes; and the disruptive bars of some Balistes species resemble the patterning of unrelated piscivores. Recent comparative work on pigmentation pattern evolution across six iconic reef-fish families (Frédérich, Mittelheiser, Gillet et al., 2026) suggests that such convergences reflect a constrained set of pattern motifs (spots, stripes, bars, mottling, complex maze patterns) that re-evolve repeatedly across the reef-fish tree of life, with pattern disparity rising steeply early in clade history and remaining relatively constant thereafter.

title: Balistoidea — Triggerfishes and Filefishes
text:
Sexual Dimorphism, Ontogeny, and Polymorphism
Sexual dimorphism in Balistoidea is generally weak in static body coloration but more pronounced in body size and in transient signaling. Across triggerfishes, males are usually larger than females at age (Rivera Hernández & Shervette, 2024), and males of several species display ephemeral courtship coloration — darkened chin patches, intensified facial stripes, brightened pelvic-fin tabs — that lasts seconds to minutes during spawning interactions. Genuine permanent dichromatism is uncommon, although a few filefishes (Pervagor, some Cantherhines) show subtle but consistent male-female differences in caudal-fin coloration.
Ontogenetic color change is modest in most balistoids compared to the dramatic transformations seen in pomacanthids: juveniles typically resemble adults in overall pattern but with muted saturation or less-developed pattern elements. Notable exceptions occur in Aluterus species, where juveniles are often more conspicuously spotted than adults, and in some Balistapus and Balistoides species, where juvenile pattern elements may be more contrast-rich than the slightly faded adult expression. Recent work on the corallivorous filefish Oxymonacanthus has additionally shown that adults can shift their effective camouflage rapidly via diet-mediated odor changes, suggesting that “color polymorphism” in this clade includes chemical as well as visual dimensions (Brooker et al., 2015).
Rapid, behaviorally-controlled color polymorphism is the defining feature of Aluterus and Monacanthus filefishes. Allen et al. (2015) catalogued at least nine distinct pattern components in Monacanthus tuckeri that can be combined and recombined within seconds, producing a repertoire of camouflage states presumably tuned to specific background types. This kind of plastic, within-individual polymorphism is qualitatively different from genetic color polymorphism (e.g., Centropyge hybrids in pomacanthids) and requires care in image-based analyses because a single individual can be photographed in multiple “phenotypes.”

title: Balistoidea — Triggerfishes and Filefishes
section: Optional Deep Dive: Camouflage in Filefishes
text:
Optional Deep Dive: Camouflage in Filefishes
Filefishes (Monacanthidae) include some of the most accomplished vertebrate camouflage practitioners outside the cephalopods, and their camouflage biology has emerged as one of the strongest research themes in balistoid visual ecology. The work of Justine Allen, Roger Hanlon and colleagues on the slender filefish Monacanthus tuckeri in the Caribbean (Allen et al., 2015) extended to teleosts the cephalopod-inspired framework that Hanlon and colleagues developed for cuttlefish: an animal’s camouflage is best understood as a finite repertoire of body-pattern components that are combined into a smaller number of functional pattern categories (uniform, mottle, disruptive), with rapid neural control over which category is expressed.
In M. tuckeri, Allen et al. documented (i) component-level body patterns (large and small spots, stripes, bars) deployable in 1-3 seconds; (ii) three-dimensional dermal flaps that disrupt body outline independently of pigment patterning; (iii) postural and orientation behaviors (head-down stalking among gorgonians, vertical alignment with seagrass blades) that amplify the effectiveness of pigment-level camouflage; and (iv) measurable color matching of the fish to nearby visual stimuli (specific corals, sponges, algal patches) rather than to the gross background. The combined result is camouflage that exploits both background matching — well-established as effective in uniform habitats (Price, Green, Troscianko et al., 2019) — and disruptive coloration on the body outline, which provides protection across a wider range of backgrounds (Schaefer & Stobbe, 2006).
A parallel and complementary story is told by Oxymonacanthus longirostris, which has converged on a different camouflage solution: masquerade as an Acropora coral branch (Brooker et al., 2011), reinforced by diet-induced chemical crypsis that masks the fish’s odor from olfactorily-hunting predators (Brooker et al., 2015). Filefishes therefore exemplify three distinct camouflage strategies — rapid background matching, disruptive coloration, and masquerade with chemical crypsis — often within a single species’ lifetime. Triggerfishes, by contrast, are largely conspicuous and territorial; their visual ecology pivots on signaling and species recognition rather than concealment. This camouflage-versus-signaling contrast between the two balistoid families maps cleanly onto their differing life histories (cryptic, schooling or pair-bonded filefishes vs. conspicuous, nest-defending triggerfishes) and is one of the most pedagogically rich comparisons available in reef-fish color biology.

title: Balistoidea — Triggerfishes and Filefishes
text:
Data Quality Warnings






Data quality: what to watch for



Post-mortem color fading is severe in Balistoidea. Triggerfishes and filefishes lose color saturation within minutes of death; the deep blues, oranges, and greens characteristic of Balistapus, Odonus, Rhinecanthus, and many filefishes wash out to muddy browns and grays. Do not use museum-specimen photographs as color data for this clade. Restrict your image set to in-situ underwater photographs of living fishes (FishBase live-image galleries, iNaturalist research-grade observations, dive-photo databases). Aquarium photographs are acceptable but flag them if lighting differs strongly from reef conditions.
Rapid color change confounds image curation in filefishes. Aluterus, Monacanthus, Cantherhines, and Acreichthys can switch between multiple pattern states in seconds (Allen et al., 2015). A single individual photographed in two different camouflage states could appear as two different “species” to an automated analysis. When multiple images of a species are available, document the pattern category (uniform vs. mottled vs. disruptive) and either choose a representative state or quantify variation explicitly.
Transient nesting and courtship coloration in triggerfishes. Female triggerfishes tending nests may display brood-state white blotches or chin darkening (Rivera Hernández & Shervette, 2024); courting males may show ephemeral pelvic-fin and facial intensification. These are not the “default” color state of the species. Prefer non-reproductive-context images for cross-species comparison.
Ontogeny: Juvenile balistoids are usually similar in pattern to adults but more muted; gradual transformation rather than discrete metamorphosis. Verify body size when possible; treat fish under ~50% of species maximum total length as sub-adult.
Taxonomy: Several genera in your tree may appear under older synonyms in FishBase (e.g., Cantherhines / Cantheschenia, Paramonacanthus / Monacanthus). Cross-check current accepted names in the Catalog of Fishes (California Academy of Sciences) before merging data sources.
The Paraluteres mimicry system crosses family boundaries (Monacanthidae mimicking Tetraodontidae). If your tree includes both Paraluteres prionurus and Canthigaster valentini, treat the mimic-model resemblance as biologically meaningful color convergence, not as a phylogenetic signal.

title: Balistoidea — Triggerfishes and Filefishes
text:
Promising Questions for This Clade

Functional Hypothesis Testing — Triggerfishes have a locked first dorsal spine that genuinely deters extraction by gape-limited predators. Does the presence and effectiveness of this spine correlate with bolder, more conspicuous coloration (as predicted by aposematism theory)? Compare conspicuousness between strongly-spined triggerfishes and less-strongly-spined filefishes.
Biogeographic Color Comparison — Balistoids include tropical reef specialists, temperate-water species (e.g., Mediterranean Stephanolepis, southern-Australia Cantherhines), and near-pelagic Aluterus. Do tropical reef species show greater pattern complexity or saturation than temperate or pelagic relatives?
Discrete Trait Mapping — Map “conspicuous-signaling” vs. “cryptic / changeable” color strategy onto the phylogeny. Is the cryptic-camouflage syndrome of filefishes monophyletic, or has it evolved repeatedly? Where on the tree do the Paraluteres mimics and the Oxymonacanthus corallivore lineage fall?
Diet and Conspicuousness — With diets ranging from open-water planktivory (Melichthys, Odonus) to durophagy (Balistapus, Pseudobalistes) to obligate corallivory (Oxymonacanthus), balistoids offer one of the strongest dietary gradients available for testing diet-color hypotheses in a single clade.

title: Scarinae — Parrotfishes
text:
Taxonomy and Phylogenetics
Parrotfishes have one of the most unsettled taxonomic histories of any reef fish group. Traditionally treated as the family Scaridae, molecular phylogenetic work over the past two decades has shown unambiguously that parrotfishes are nested deep inside the wrasse family Labridae (Streelman & Karl, 1997; Westneat & Alfaro, 2005). The modern convention is to treat them as the subfamily Scarinae within Labridae, although many ecological and fisheries papers still use Scaridae. Whatever the rank, the clade comprises roughly 100 living species in ten genera: Scarus (~52 species), Chlorurus (~18), Sparisoma (~15), and the smaller genera Cetoscarus, Bolbometopon, Hipposcarus, Cryptotomus, Calotomus, Leptoscarus, and Nicholsina (Choat et al., 2012). Your tree includes 78 of these.
Molecular work by Streelman, Alfaro & Westneat (2002) overturned the morphology-based phylogeny of Bellwood (1994) and recovered a deep split between a “seagrass clade” (Cryptotomus, Nicholsina, Leptoscarus, Calotomus, and most Sparisoma) and a “reef clade” (Bolbometopon, Cetoscarus, Hipposcarus, Chlorurus, and Scarus) that contains roughly 80 percent of described species. The expanded multilocus analysis of Streelman, Smith & Fessler (2008) confirmed this two-clade topology and, using fossil-calibrated codon-rate models, dated the parrotfish crown to ~22 Ma in the Miocene with most species-level divergence in Scarus and Chlorurus concentrated in the last 5 Ma. The most comprehensive species-level treatment to date is Choat et al. (2012), who reconstructed relationships among 61 of the ~70 Scarus + Chlorurus species and recovered 15 well-supported clades whose origins fell in the mid-Pliocene to Pleistocene. They found that sympatric sister-species pairs were more divergent in morphology, ecology, and dichromatic color pattern than allopatric pairs — suggesting that ecological and signal divergence have actively driven speciation in this clade rather than simply being passive byproducts of allopatry.

title: Scarinae — Parrotfishes
text:
Natural History
Parrotfishes are circumtropical and occupy nearly every shallow tropical hard-bottom and seagrass habitat between roughly 1 and 40 m depth. Their biogeography is structured by a deep Atlantic vs. Indo-Pacific split: Sparisoma (and the seagrass-associated Cryptotomus and Nicholsina) dominates Caribbean and tropical Atlantic reefs, while Scarus and Chlorurus dominate the Indo-Pacific, where they are among the most abundant non-cryptic fishes on any given reef (Choat et al., 2019). A few species (most notably Scarus ghobban and S. rubroviolaceus) range broadly across the Indo-Pacific, and the Tropical Eastern Pacific holds an interesting four-species Scarus assemblage that includes the hybrid-origin S. compressus (Robertson, Carlon & Barron, 2021).
Almost all parrotfishes are herbivores or detritivores, but their feeding ecology subdivides into functional groups that map onto jaw morphology and body size. Scrapers (most Scarus, small Sparisoma) use their fused beak-like oral jaws to remove a thin layer of algal turf, sediment, and the microbial epilithic and endolithic film from coral and rock surfaces. Excavators (large Chlorurus, Bolbometopon muricatum) take much deeper bites, gouging chunks of carbonate framework with each pass. Browsers (several Sparisoma, Calotomus, Leptoscarus) preferentially target fleshy macroalgae and seagrasses. Recent isotopic and microscopy work (e.g., Bellwood et al., 2012) suggests that even scraping and excavating species are largely targeting protein-rich endolithic cyanobacteria rather than the algal turf per se — a reinterpretation that has reshaped how we think about parrotfish “herbivory.” Whatever the precise food, the ecological consequence is dramatic: parrotfishes are the dominant external bioeroders on most coral reefs worldwide, accounting for 60 to >90 percent of all measured bioerosion in cross-shelf and global comparisons, and contributing several tons of carbonate sediment per hectare per year (Bellwood et al., 2012; Mumby, Bozec & O’Farrell, 2016). The bumphead parrotfish Bolbometopon muricatum, the largest scarine at ~130 cm and 46 kg, alone can ingest more than five tonnes of structural carbonate per year per individual.
Social organization is dominated by protogynous hermaphroditism, almost always in a diandric form: most individuals begin life as females (or as drab “initial phase,” IP, primary males) and the largest fish ultimately transition into vivid “terminal phase” (TP) males that defend territories or harems and dominate spawning (Robertson & Warner, 1978). Mating systems range from haremic with site-attached TP males (typical of many Scarus) to group spawning and lek-like aggregations (typical of some Caribbean Sparisoma), and these social systems strongly influence both body-size distributions and the size at sex change (Choat & Taylor, 2014). One of the most distinctive natural-history traits in the clade is the nocturnal mucous cocoon that parrotfishes (and some wrasses) spin around themselves before sleeping in reef crevices: Grutter et al. (2010) showed experimentally that these cocoons are not principally an antipredator barrier but rather a “mosquito net” that blocks bloodfeeding gnathiid isopods, at a cost of about 2.5 percent of the fish’s daily energy budget.

title: Scarinae — Parrotfishes
text:
Visual Ecology and Signaling
Parrotfishes live in the brightest, most spectrally rich light environment available to any reef fish: shallow (1–15 m) reef flats and crests bathed in broadband downwelling sunlight that retains substantial energy from ultraviolet through far-red. This light environment imposes very different selective pressures on visual systems than the deeper, blue-shifted habitats of pomacentrids or anthiines, and it permits color signals across the full visible spectrum. Direct visual-pigment data are sparse for parrotfishes themselves, but the broader labrid visual literature provides strong context. Stieb, Cortesi et al. (2017) showed that damselfishes — which share parrotfish habitats — retain all five major teleost cone opsin classes (SWS1 in the UV, SWS2 in the blue, two RH2 paralogs in the green, and LWS in the red) and that opsin sequence and expression evolve under strong positive selection associated with feeding ecology and body color. A follow-up multi-family study by Stieb, Cortesi et al. (2023) included the parrotfish Chlorurus sordidus and found that herbivorous reef fishes upregulate the long-wavelength-sensitive (LWS) opsin relative to zooplanktivores, and that high LWS expression correlates with possession of orange/red body coloration — exactly the trait state typical of many parrotfish IP individuals and several Caribbean Sparisoma. This pattern is consistent with the “sensory bias” prediction that long-wavelength sensitivity evolved first for detecting algae against the reef substrate and was subsequently co-opted for intraspecific signaling.
For your group’s purposes, the practical implication is that parrotfishes very likely have access to the full reef color gamut and can in principle discriminate the subtle hue and saturation differences that distinguish closely related TP males. Visual modeling against a labrid or damselfish receiver should be defensible.

title: Scarinae — Parrotfishes
text:
Color Pattern Diversity
Few reef fish clades approach the parrotfishes in raw color-pattern diversity, and almost none match them in within-species polymorphism. Indo-Pacific TP Scarus and Chlorurus males display some of the most saturated greens, teals, and electric blues found in any vertebrate: Scarus quoyi TP males have a deep blue-green body and a magenta lower jaw; Chlorurus microrhinos TP males are bright emerald with a prominent cephalic hump and pink facial bars; S. ghobban TP males have an iridescent yellow-and-blue scale pattern. Caribbean Sparisoma tend toward a different color space dominated by red-browns, oranges, and dark greens, with crescent-shaped tail markings (e.g., S. viride) and bicolored tails (S. aurofrenatum). Across the family there is a strong axis of variation between species with high-contrast, intricately patterned TP faces (Scarus, Chlorurus) and species with more uniform body coloration (Bolbometopon, Cetoscarus).
Streelman, Smith & Fessler (2008) attempted to map color characters onto a molecular phylogeny of Scarus and Chlorurus and found that color patterns evolve rapidly and recurrently, with little phylogenetic conservatism at the level of specific facial markings. This is one of the reasons that morphology-based parrotfish taxonomy proved so unreliable: color characters that appear diagnostically distinct turn out to have evolved independently many times, and species that look very similar can be only distantly related within Scarus. Choat et al. (2012) further showed that sympatric sister species are more divergent in color than allopatric ones, consistent with a role for visual signaling in reinforcing reproductive isolation where parrotfishes overlap.

title: Scarinae — Parrotfishes
text:
Sexual Dimorphism, Ontogeny, and Polymorphism
The Scarinae are the textbook example of extreme sexual dichromatism in reef fishes. In most species, IP individuals (juveniles, females, and primary males) and TP individuals (terminal-phase, sex-changed or large primary males) differ so drastically in coloration that nineteenth- and early twentieth-century ichthyologists routinely described them as separate species (Robertson & Warner, 1978; Choat et al., 2012). Robertson and Warner’s (1978) monograph on ten Caribbean parrotfishes remains the foundational treatment: they documented that protogynous sex change in the Scaridae is typically diandric — some males develop directly from juveniles as drab primary males (IP males) while others develop first as females and later transform into vivid TP males — and that the IP and TP color phases correspond to fundamentally different mating tactics (sneaking and group spawning by IP males vs. territorial defense and pair spawning by TP males).
Ontogeny adds a third pattern layer: juveniles of many Scarus are uniformly dark with a pale lateral stripe, becoming IP-like only after several months. Cetoscarus bicolor juveniles are white with a black-edged orange spot and look nothing like either adult phase. Some species also harbor intraspecific color polymorphism within a single sex-and-phase class: Sparisoma rubripinne has both gonochoristic and protogynous populations and IP males with multiple distinct color morphs; Scarus iseri juveniles include both a “striped” and a “bicolored” morph. Hybridization adds yet more variation in regions of sympatry: Robertson et al. (2021) showed that nearly 90 percent of Scarus compressus individuals in the Tropical Eastern Pacific are F1 hybrids between S. perrico and either S. ghobban or S. rubroviolaceus, producing intermediate IP and TP phenotypes that have confused taxonomists since the species was first described.

title: Scarinae — Parrotfishes
text:
Initial-Phase / Terminal-Phase Color Evolution
If your group wants to anchor its project around a single big question, IP/TP color evolution is the obvious choice for Scarinae. The system has several features that make it analytically tractable. First, the trait is genuinely binary at the level of an individual photograph: in nearly every species, a fish either bears the IP color pattern or the TP color pattern, with relatively few transitional individuals (Robertson & Warner, 1978). Second, the IP-to-TP transformation is repeatable: it happens during a discrete sex-change event in protogynous hermaphrodites, and the corresponding color change is hormonally regulated and runs to completion over days to weeks. Third, the magnitude of IP-TP color difference is itself a quantitative trait that varies dramatically across species — from the radical difference in Scarus vetula or S. quoyi to the relatively subtle difference in Cryptotomus roseus or Bolbometopon muricatum — and that variation can be mapped onto the Choat et al. (2012) phylogeny.
Several biologically interesting predictions follow. Larger TP-male territories and more intense male-male competition should select for more extreme TP coloration (Choat & Taylor, 2014, who showed that size at sex change varies systematically with reef exposure and mating-system intensity). Species with diandric mating systems — where IP males also spawn and benefit from female mimicry — should retain more drab and female-like IP coloration to support sneak-spawning, while species with strictly protogynous (monandric) systems can let IP color drift more freely (Robertson & Warner, 1978). Recent molecular and visual-modeling work in damselfishes (Stieb et al., 2023) suggests that the evolution of long-wavelength visual sensitivity may have preceded and enabled the elaboration of red/orange social signals — a hypothesis that could be tested directly in parrotfishes given the strong red/orange component of many Sparisoma TP patterns and the basal position of Sparisoma in the broader scarine phylogeny.

title: Scarinae — Parrotfishes
text:
Data Quality Warnings






Data quality: read this section before you start



The IP/TP problem is the single largest data-quality risk in this entire course. Initial-phase and terminal-phase parrotfishes look like entirely different species in nearly every member of your tree. If you mix IP and TP photographs even casually — one IP Scarus vetula alongside a TP Scarus iseri, for example — your color metrics will be dominated by phase variation rather than species variation and your phylogenetic comparative analyses will be uninterpretable. Pick one phase and stick with it for every species. We recommend TP males because (a) they are the most photographed phase in field guides and online image repositories, (b) they show the greatest interspecific color variation (giving you signal to work with), and (c) they represent the reproductively mature, fully-developed adult phenotype that comparative methods are usually trying to capture.
How to identify TP males in photographs:

Vivid blues, greens, and teals, with complex facial markings (lines, swirls, spots around the eye and jaw).
Often larger than IP individuals; sometimes with a developed cephalic hump (Chlorurus, Bolbometopon, Cetoscarus).
Often photographed solo or patrolling, rather than in mixed groups.

How to identify IP individuals to exclude:

Drab red-brown, olive, gray, or muted maroon. Often blotchy or uniformly washed-out.
Smaller, more streamlined, no cephalic hump.
Often in loose feeding groups.

Juveniles: Many Scarus juveniles are uniformly dark with a pale stripe; Cetoscarus bicolor juveniles are white with a black-edged orange spot. Exclude juveniles entirely.
Species with weak or unusual dichromatism (handle with care):

Cryptotomus roseus: both phases translucent pink; will be a color-space outlier.
Bolbometopon muricatum: both phases relatively uniform olive-gray; TP identified by size and forehead bump rather than color.
Sparisoma generally: IP/TP difference is real but more muted than in Indo-Pacific Scarus.

Historical taxonomic confusion: Robertson & Warner (1978) documented that many nineteenth-century parrotfish “species” turned out to be IP or juvenile phases of already-named species. Older field guides and museum lots may still carry these misidentifications. If a name in your image set returns very few hits or images that look inconsistent, cross-check against FishBase synonymy before including it.
Hybrids: Scarus compressus in the Tropical Eastern Pacific is largely a hybrid population (Robertson et al., 2021) with intermediate IP and TP phenotypes. If your tree includes S. compressus, treat it cautiously or exclude it.
Consistency rule: For every species, verify that you are using a TP male image. If you cannot find a confirmed TP male photograph for a given species, drop that species rather than substitute an IP image.

title: Scarinae — Parrotfishes
text:
Promising Questions for This Clade

Sexual System and Color Complexity — Scarinae is arguably the best clade in the entire student tree for testing whether protogynous hermaphroditism drives the evolution of extreme dichromatism. Compare TP-male color complexity across species and ask whether the magnitude of IP–TP color difference correlates with mating-system intensity (haremic territoriality vs. group spawning).
Body Size and Color Complexity — With a >10-fold size range from Cryptotomus (~12 cm) to Bolbometopon (~130 cm), parrotfishes offer a strong gradient for testing whether larger species can “afford” more complex color patterns (greater visual target area, reduced predation risk).
Biogeographic Color Comparison — The Atlantic (Sparisoma) vs. Indo-Pacific (Scarus, Chlorurus) split is one of the cleanest biogeographic contrasts in any reef fish family. Do Indo-Pacific parrotfishes occupy a broader region of color space? Has the Atlantic lineage been more constrained?
Diet and Conspicuousness — Scrapers, excavators, and browsers differ in feeding posture, reef-surface exposure time, and the chromatic background against which they feed. Do excavators (which spend more time head-down on bright carbonate) differ in TP color or contrast from scrapers (more often in motion against algal turf)?
