title: Acanthuridae — Surgeonfishes, Tangs, and Unicornfishes
text:
Taxonomy and Phylogenetics
The Acanthuridae comprise approximately 86 extant species in six genera, traditionally arranged in three subfamilies: Acanthurinae (Acanthurus, Ctenochaetus, Zebrasoma, Paracanthurus), Nasinae (Naso), and Prionurinae (Prionurus). The earliest comprehensive molecular phylogeny of the family (Sorenson et al., 2013) used multi-locus nuclear and mitochondrial data to produce a time-calibrated tree, recovering Nasinae and Prionurinae as successively basal to a well-supported Acanthurinae crown clade. Within Acanthurinae, Ctenochaetus nests inside a paraphyletic Acanthurus, and Zebrasoma plus Paracanthurus form a distinct lineage. More recent phylogenomic analyses of acanthuriform fishes (Brownstein et al., 2025) place the origin of crown Acanthuridae in the Early Miocene, with most extant generic diversity arising during a burst of cladogenesis between approximately 20 and 10 Mya that coincides with the expansion of modern Indo-Pacific reef habitat. Ludt et al. (2019) used mitogenomic data to resolve the temperate Prionurus clade, confirming its early divergence from the tropical acanthurine lineages.
Your pruned tree contains 63 species drawn from across all three subfamilies. The outgroup taxa Zanclus cornutus (Moorish idol) and Luvarus imperialis (luvar) — both sister or near-sister to crown Acanthuridae in most analyses (Sorenson et al., 2013) — have been removed for this exercise, so every tip in your tree represents a true acanthurid. Acanthurus and Naso together account for roughly two-thirds of the family’s species richness and dominate the tree.

title: Acanthuridae — Surgeonfishes, Tangs, and Unicornfishes
text:
Natural History
Acanthurids are circumglobally distributed across tropical and subtropical reefs, with their highest species richness in the Indo-Australian Archipelago and progressively reduced diversity across the Pacific and into the Atlantic (Bellwood et al., 2019). The family’s signature morphological feature is the caudal peduncle spine (“scalpel”) — a sharp, blade-like structure that can inflict deep lacerations on competitors and predators. In Acanthurus, Ctenochaetus, Zebrasoma, and Paracanthurus the spine is single and retractable into a sheath; in Naso it is replaced by one or two fixed keeled plates on each side of the peduncle; in Prionurus a row of fixed bony plates lines the peduncle.
Surgeonfishes are central to coral-reef ecosystem function. Most species are herbivores or detritivores that crop algal turfs, remove sediment from reef substrate, and graze on detrital aggregates (Choat et al., 2012). This grazing pressure regulates benthic community composition and helps maintain coral-dominated rather than macroalgae-dominated reef states. Recent comparative work (Mihalitsis et al., 2025) shows that acanthurid feeding morphology has diversified repeatedly along axes of substrate scraping, water-column planktivory, and selective browsing, with each axis associated with characteristic head and jaw shapes. Ctenochaetus uses comb-like teeth to sweep fine detrital particles from coral rubble, and these particles are processed by a specialized gut microbiome that ferments algal polysaccharides (Ngugi et al., 2017). Naso includes both benthic grazers (e.g., N. unicornis) and large midwater planktivores (e.g., N. hexacanthus, N. vlamingii) that form aggregations off reef edges.
Reproduction is broadcast spawning in pairs or groups, typically at reef edges during outgoing tides. Unlike labrids and pomacanthids, acanthurids are gonochoristic and do not change sex. Larvae pass through a distinctive transparent, disc-shaped pelagic “acronurus” stage before settling onto reefs. Phylogeographic studies of Acanthurus species have documented strong genetic connectivity across the Indo-Pacific, consistent with a long pelagic larval duration and frequent long-distance dispersal (Gaither et al., 2015).

title: Acanthuridae — Surgeonfishes, Tangs, and Unicornfishes
text:
Visual Ecology and Signaling
Acanthurids inhabit shallow, well-lit reef environments where the full visible spectrum is available, and several lines of evidence indicate that they exploit this broad spectral range. Losey et al. (2003) measured ocular media transmittance in 195 species of Hawaiian reef fishes and showed that many acanthurids transmit substantial ultraviolet (UV) light to the retina — a prerequisite for UV vision. Marshall (2000) reviewed the visual ecology of coral reef fishes and argued that the steep spectral gradient of shallow water creates conditions in which both long-wavelength (orange, red) and short-wavelength (blue, violet, UV) signals can convey information over short distances, even though they attenuate rapidly with depth. Siebeck et al. (2014) used behavioral assays and microspectrophotometry to demonstrate that reef fishes can extract luminance and chromatic information across at least four spectral channels, supporting a tetrachromatic interpretation of visual ecology in many shallow reef taxa. A subsequent comparative review (Siebeck et al., 2018) placed surgeonfishes among the reef-fish families with the broadest spectral sensitivities documented to date.
The functional significance of UV sensitivity in acanthurids remains an active research area, but two non-exclusive hypotheses dominate the literature. First, UV reflectance from body markings and from the caudal-peduncle region may function as a private signaling channel that is highly visible to conspecifics at close range but invisible to many large predators whose ocular media block UV (Siebeck & Marshall, 2000; Siebeck et al., 2018). Second, UV signals attenuate rapidly with distance, making them effective for short-range species recognition during the dense aggregating and schooling behavior that characterizes many surgeonfish species. The combination of UV-transmitting ocular media, conspicuous body markings, and tight social aggregations places acanthurids among the most promising clades for testing private-channel hypotheses in reef fishes.

title: Acanthuridae — Surgeonfishes, Tangs, and Unicornfishes
text:
Color Pattern Diversity
Acanthurid color patterns span a remarkable range. At one extreme, Ctenochaetus strigosus is uniformly drab brown with fine dark streaks; at the other, Acanthurus lineatus displays brilliant alternating blue and orange horizontal stripes. Zebrasoma flavescens is uniformly bright yellow — one of the most recognizable fishes in the world — while its congener Z. veliferum shows complex brown-and-yellow vertical barring set off by extended median fins. Paracanthurus hepatus (palette surgeonfish) carries a bold “palette” of cobalt blue, black, and yellow that has become iconic in the popular imagination. Naso species generally show muted blue-gray or olive body coloration set against vividly colored caudal-peduncle keels (yellow, orange, or electric blue) and, in some species, ornate facial markings or rostral horns.
Frédérich et al. (2026) coded 30 discrete pattern categories across 918 species in six reef-fish families, including Acanthuridae, and found that pattern diversity scales positively with species richness and shows pronounced lability across the family. Their analyses recover repeated independent origins of stripes, bars, spots, and large color blocks within Acanthuridae, with no single pattern type strongly conserved at the subfamily level. Hemingson et al. (2018) similarly documented rapid color-pattern divergence among sympatric reef fishes and identified surgeonfishes as a group with above-average pattern turnover relative to phylogenetic age. The earlier review by Frédérich et al. (2019) frames these patterns within the broader “magic trait” literature, arguing that reef-fish color patterns can simultaneously mediate species recognition, mate choice, and ecological signaling — a combination that may accelerate diversification.
Pattern convergences across families are notable. The bold vertical barring of Zebrasoma veliferum parallels patterns in pomacanthids and chaetodontids that share its reef-edge habitat. Conversely, the uniform bright yellow of Z. flavescens converges on the lemonpeel angelfish (Centropyge flavissima) at similar depths and latitudes — a convergence that may reflect shared signaling environments rather than common ancestry (Floeter et al., 2018).

title: Acanthuridae — Surgeonfishes, Tangs, and Unicornfishes
text:
Sexual Dimorphism, Ontogeny, and Polymorphism
Sexual dichromatism is weak or absent in most acanthurid species, and males and females typically appear essentially identical in static photographs. This contrasts sharply with labrids and pomacanthids and simplifies data curation for comparative analysis. Several species do show transient context-dependent color change, however. Males of Acanthurus nigricans pale dramatically during spawning rushes, and territorial A. lineatus males intensify the contrast of their facial stripes during agonistic displays. Paracanthurus hepatus can fade its blue coloration when stressed or at night. These transient states are not stable diagnostic traits but can introduce noise into pavo-derived metrics if a substantial fraction of images captured fish in atypical condition.
Ontogenetic color change in Acanthuridae is generally subtle compared with the extreme juvenile-to-adult transformations seen in Pomacanthus, with one striking exception: juvenile Acanthurus pyroferus exhibit geographic mimicry of locally abundant Centropyge pygmy angelfishes, adopting yellow (C. flavissima-like), brown (C. vrolikii-like), or pale-yellow (C. heraldi-like) coloration depending on which model species predominates in their habitat (Eagle & Jones, 2004; Rainey, 2009). Adults transition to a uniform chocolate-brown body with a yellow eye patch, losing all resemblance to the angelfish models. This system is one of the best-documented cases of ontogenetic, geographically variable mimicry in vertebrates and remains an active area of research on the developmental basis of color-pattern lability. Juvenile Naso species lack the rostral horn and elaborated caudal armature of adults but generally share body coloration with conspecific adults.

title: Acanthuridae — Surgeonfishes, Tangs, and Unicornfishes
section: Caudal-Spine Aposematism: A Clade-Specific Deep Dive
text:
Caudal-Spine Aposematism: A Clade-Specific Deep Dive
The caudal scalpel of Acanthuridae is a genuine weapon, and its often-conspicuous coloration has long invited interpretation as an aposematic signal. In Acanthurus achilles and several other Acanthurus species the spine sheath is outlined in bright orange or red against a dark body; in Naso the keeled peduncle plates are frequently bordered with yellow or orange; in Prionurus the row of bony plates is darker than the surrounding skin and bordered by a pale margin. These color-on-weapon combinations satisfy the basic structural prediction of aposematism: a conspicuous signal placed directly on a defensive structure (Marshall, 2000).
Formal tests of aposematism in acanthurids remain limited, but the comparative ingredients are now in place. Frédérich et al. (2026) provide pattern-coded data for the family; visual-ecology studies (Losey et al., 2003; Siebeck et al., 2018) document the spectral sensitivity of likely receivers; and phylogenetic comparative methods can readily map caudal-region conspicuousness against measures of overall body conspicuousness, body size, depth, and group living. Hemingson et al. (2018) and Frédérich et al. (2019) emphasize that color signals in reef fishes can carry multiple non-exclusive functions (species recognition, social signaling, defense), so single-function explanations should be tested rather than assumed. A pavo-based analysis of contrast between the caudal-spine region and the adjacent flank — mapped onto the Sorenson et al. (2013) phylogeny — would constitute a tractable and publishable test of the aposematism hypothesis.

title: Acanthuridae — Surgeonfishes, Tangs, and Unicornfishes
text:
Data Quality Warnings






Data quality: what to watch for



Weak dichromatism — simpler data curation. Most acanthurids show little or no sexual dimorphism in coloration, so a single representative image per species is generally adequate and you do not need to track initial-phase vs. terminal-phase morphs as you would in labrids.
Context-dependent color change. Some species can temporarily alter body color in response to stress, social context, or cleaning interactions. Images of recently netted, captive, or stressed fish may show washed-out or “fright pattern” coloration that does not represent the species’ typical reef appearance. When curating images:

Prefer photographs of undisturbed fish in natural reef settings.
Avoid images where the fish appears unusually pale, mottled, or blotchy.
If multiple images are available, select the one that best represents typical daytime reef coloration.

Juvenile mimicry in A. pyroferus. Juveniles of this species mimic Centropyge pygmy angelfishes and will look nothing like adult A. pyroferus. Use only adult images (uniform chocolate-brown body with a yellow eye-patch). The same precaution applies to any locally documented mimic morphs.
Outgroup taxa already removed. Your tree has been pruned so that Zanclus cornutus and Luvarus imperialis do not appear. If you encounter any non-acanthurid tips during your analysis, flag them and check the tree before proceeding.
Species identification. Several Acanthurus species are superficially similar (e.g., A. nigricans, A. achilles, A. japonicus). Pay close attention to caudal-spine coloration and facial markings when identifying images. Misidentification at the species level will propagate directly into your pavo metrics.
UV reflectance is invisible to standard cameras. Any UV-mediated signals discussed in the literature will not be captured by your RGB images. Treat conclusions about overall conspicuousness as conservative: a species that looks drab to humans may carry strong UV signals that are highly visible to conspecifics.

title: Acanthuridae — Surgeonfishes, Tangs, and Unicornfishes
text:
Promising Questions for This Clade

Functional Hypothesis Testing — Surgeonfishes have a genuine weapon (the caudal scalpel) that makes aposematism biologically plausible. Test whether species with more conspicuously colored scalpel regions show higher overall body conspicuousness, as predicted by honest signaling of defensive capability.
Diet and Conspicuousness — With three distinct feeding guilds (grazing, detritivory, planktivory), acanthurids offer a clean test of the prediction that feeding ecology shapes color evolution. Are planktivorous species (which are exposed in the water column) more or less conspicuous than benthic grazers?
Cross-Family Comparison — As the walkthrough dataset, your pavo metrics can be directly compared to other clades. How does the overall color diversity (morphospace volume) of Acanthuridae compare to similarly sized labrid or pomacanthid clades?
Discrete Trait Mapping — Map mimicry (juvenile A. pyroferus mimicking Centropyge), scalpel coloration (bright vs. cryptic), and the presence of horizontal striping across the phylogeny to test how many times each trait has evolved.
Latitude Gradient — Several acanthurid species, especially in Prionurus and some Naso, extend into subtropical or warm-temperate waters. Test whether higher-latitude species show reduced conspicuousness compared to tropical congeners.

title: Pomacanthidae — Marine Angelfishes
text:
Note










Field
Content




Species in tree
47 (outgroups pruned — pomacanthids only)


Family size
~88 species in 8 genera (Baraf et al., 2019)


Sexual system
Protogynous hermaphrodites; predominantly haremic


Dichromatism
Subtle to moderate in most genera; pronounced in Genicanthus


Primary diet
Spongivory (large genera) to omnivory and algal grazing (Centropyge, Paracentropyge) (Konow & Bellwood, 2011)


Depth range
~1–70 m; some Paracentropyge and Centropyge extend into the mesophotic zone


Key references
Bellwood et al. (2004); Gaither et al. (2014); Baraf et al. (2019, 2024); Tea et al. (2020)







Pomacanthidae are placed in the order Acanthuriformes (or, under older classifications, Perciformes), and have long been considered sister to butterflyfishes (Chaetodontidae), with which they share many ecological and morphological features (Bellwood et al., 2004). Family-level monophyly is well supported, but generic boundaries have been turbulent. The first molecular phylogeny of the family, based on mitochondrial 12S and 16S rRNA, recovered all but one genus as monophyletic: Centropyge was paraphyletic, with the swallowtail genus Genicanthus and the smoke-angelfish genus Apolemichthys nested within it (Bellwood et al., 2004). Subsequent multi-locus work confirmed and refined this picture, additionally elevating Paracentropyge and Xiphypops to genus rank to restore monophyly (Gaither et al., 2014).
The Atlantic and tropical eastern Pacific genus Holacanthus is itself a small, well-supported clade whose internal phylogeny tracks the closure of the Isthmus of Panama (Alva-Campbell et al., 2010). Pomacanthid biogeography is dominated by an Indo-Australian centre of origin and diversity, from which lineages have repeatedly dispersed into the Indian Ocean, the Red Sea, and (less often) the Atlantic (Baraf et al., 2019). The most recent target-capture phylogenomic analysis, using ~1,000 ultraconserved elements from 45 species, recovers a well-resolved family backbone but flags persistent discordance around the Centropyge radiation and the monotypic Pygoplites lineage, consistent with ancient introgression and incomplete lineage sorting (Baraf et al., 2024). For this lab, the key practical point is that close phylogenetic relatives can look dramatically different (e.g., flame Centropyge loricula vs. lemonpeel C. flavissima) and distantly related species can look remarkably similar (cross-genus convergence on vertical-bar patterns) — meaning color, although taxonomically informative, is not a clean proxy for phylogenetic distance in this family (Gaither et al., 2014).



Pomacanthidae are obligate coral-reef inhabitants of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific oceans, with species richness peaking in the Coral Triangle (Baraf et al., 2019). Adults occupy fore-reef slopes, walls, lagoon patch reefs, and (for many Centropyge and Paracentropyge) mesophotic reef habitats below 50 m. Most species are diurnal and strongly site-attached, defending feeding and mating territories within structurally complex substrate.
Diet varies substantially across the family. Large-bodied genera (Pomacanthus, Holacanthus, Pomacanthops, Chaetodontoplus) are best known as spongivores — one of the few vertebrate groups that exploits sponges in quantity — and supplement sponges with tunicates, hydroids, filamentous algae, and small benthic invertebrates. The pygmy and dwarf genera (Centropyge, Paracentropyge, Xiphypops) graze algal turf and detritus, and Genicanthus is unusual within the family for being a midwater zooplanktivore. Despite this broad trophic range, the underlying feeding apparatus is morphologically and kinematically conservative: high trophic diversity has evolved with surprisingly limited functional disparity in jaw morphology and feeding kinematics (Konow & Bellwood, 2011).
Mating systems are predominantly haremic, with a dominant male defending a territory containing one to several females. All pomacanthids studied to date are protogynous hermaphrodites: females change sex to male upon loss of the dominant individual, and the transition is typically accompanied by behavioural change and, in some genera, conspicuous color change (Pyle & Randall, 1994). Spawning is pelagic and pair-based, with planktonic larval durations on the order of weeks, which contributes to the broad distributions and apparent panmixia of many species (Schultz et al., 2007).
A defining natural-history feature of the family is the extraordinarily high frequency of interspecific hybridization. A recent genomic survey detected putative hybrids involving 42 of 88 species (~48% of the family), distributed across every extant genus except the monotypic Pygoplites (Tea et al., 2020). Field studies at hybrid hotspots such as Christmas Island show that hybridization tends to be promoted by a combination of low local abundance of one parent species and broad niche overlap between parents — conditions easily met as Indo-Pacific lineages contact one another along suture zones (Hodge et al., 2019).



Primary measurements of pomacanthid visual systems — microspectrophotometry of cone visual pigments, opsin gene expression, behavioural psychophysics — are essentially absent from the literature. Almost everything we know about how angelfishes perceive their reef is inferred from the broader reef-fish literature (Marshall et al., 2019). It is worth stating this gap explicitly: despite the family’s status as a charismatic, visually conspicuous group, no published study has directly characterised the cone complement of any pomacanthid.
What is known generalises across most acanthuriforms and percomorphs (Marshall et al., 2019). Reef fishes typically possess a duplex retina with one rod opsin (RH1) and up to five cone opsin classes (SWS1, SWS2, RH2 paralogues, LWS), arranged as single cones (expressing short-wavelength opsins) and pairs of double cones (expressing medium- and long-wavelength opsins). Several reef-fish lineages, including some butterflyfishes and damselfishes, are UV-sensitive via SWS1 in single cones, and a parsimonious assumption is that at least some pomacanthids retain UV sensitivity, especially those species (e.g., Genicanthus, Centropyge) whose body colours include UV-reflective whites or yellows that would otherwise be invisible to ecologically relevant viewers. This remains an open empirical question.
Light environments occupied by pomacanthids span the near-surface blue-green spectrum of shallow lagoons through the increasingly monochromatic blue light of mesophotic reefs (Marshall et al., 2019). The most likely functional contexts for color signalling in the family are species recognition (especially in sympatric Centropyge species where hybridization is rampant), sex recognition (in Genicanthus, where dichromatism is strong), and territorial advertisement. Color also functions as a developmental signal: juveniles of large Pomacanthus species use radically different patterns from adults, which is widely interpreted as a mechanism for avoiding aggression from territorial conspecifics (Pyle & Randall, 1994).



Within the standardised pattern survey of Frédérich et al. (2026), Pomacanthidae stand out among the six reef-fish families analysed for the diversity and lability of their patterns. Pomacanthid evolution has produced near-monochromatic body plans (e.g., Centropyge flavissima in uniform yellow with a blue eye-ring), bold vertical-bar patterns (Pygoplites diacanthus, several Pomacanthus), striking concentric-arc juveniles (Pomacanthus spp.; see below), and intricate face-and-fin masks (Apolemichthys, Chaetodontoplus). Frédérich et al. (2026) further show that pigmentation patterns have evolved rapidly and repeatedly across reef-fish families, with multiple independent origins of the same visual motifs — a result consistent with convergence on a limited set of “designs” that work in reef light environments.
Convergence with other families is striking. Vertical-bar patterns broadly resembling those of butterflyfishes have evolved at least twice in pomacanthids (in Pygoplites and in juvenile Pomacanthus), and the bar/stripe axis is one of the most labile features of reef-fish colouration generally (Hemingson et al., 2019). Hemingson and colleagues showed in butterflyfishes that pattern divergence is most rapid when closely related species have overlapping geographic ranges of similar size — a prediction worth testing explicitly in pomacanthids, where many sister-pair contact zones are sites of both pattern divergence and hybridization (Tea et al., 2020).
Within-genus disparities are also instructive. The Holacanthus radiation occupies a relatively narrow morphological space but a wide chromatic one, from the cool blues of H. ciliaris to the bold yellow/black contrast of H. tricolor (Alva-Campbell et al., 2010). Centropyge spans the most colourful range of any genus in the family but is also the most paraphyletic, the most hybridised, and the most taxonomically unstable — a reminder that bright, distinctive colours need not reflect deep evolutionary distinctiveness (Gaither et al., 2014).



Sexual dichromatism in Pomacanthidae ranges from negligible (most Centropyge, Holacanthus, Pomacanthus) to extreme. The clearest case is Genicanthus, where males and females differ in body pattern so dramatically that they were originally described as separate species: male G. lamarck has bold horizontal black stripes on a white body whereas females are darker dorsally and whitish below. Because sex change is protogynous, all Genicanthus individuals begin life with female colouration and acquire male pattern upon ascending to the dominant breeding position (Pyle & Randall, 1994).
Geographic colour polymorphism is also well documented. The flame angelfish Centropyge loricula expresses three regional colour morphs across the Pacific — red (Hawai‘i), reduced-black (Marquesas), and orange (broader Oceania) — yet population genetic markers reveal little differentiation among morphs, indicating that morph variation is not tracking deep population structure (Schultz et al., 2007). Similar morph complexes have been described in C. flavissima and C. heraldi, which appear to comprise cryptic sibling species pairs (Gaither et al., 2014). For comparative colour analyses, these examples emphasise that within-species chromatic variation in pomacanthids can be substantial and ecologically meaningful, not noise.
Hybrid individuals typically show intermediate or mosaic colour patterns relative to parental species, and these intermediates form a near-continuous chromatic spectrum at sympatric contact zones (Pyle & Randall, 1994; Tea et al., 2020). Because hybrids are frequent (~48% of species; Tea et al., 2020) and because they bias quantitative colour summaries toward parental averages, hybrids must be flagged or excluded from comparative analyses rather than coerced into one parental category.



The most spectacular ontogenetic colour change in any reef-fish family occurs in Pomacanthus and its close relatives. Juveniles of P. imperator, P. semicirculatus, P. annularis, P. navarchus, and P. paru display dark bodies marked with electric-blue and white concentric arcs or rings centred near the caudal peduncle. As individuals reach roughly 8–12 cm standard length, the arcs progressively elongate and flatten over a period of weeks to months, ultimately resolving into the species-specific adult pattern — which in P. imperator and P. semicirculatus takes the form of horizontal blue-and-yellow stripes (Pyle & Randall, 1994).
Two adaptive hypotheses are commonly invoked for this developmental shift. First, the disruptive concentric pattern is thought to enhance crypsis among coral rubble and rocky substrate where juveniles shelter. Second, the radically different juvenile pattern may reduce intraspecific aggression by signalling to territorial adults that the juvenile is not a competitor for the local territory or mate (Pyle & Randall, 1994). These hypotheses have rarely been tested experimentally in Pomacanthus, and the developmental and genetic basis of the transformation — how the arcs reorganise into stripes, what regulatory changes underlie the shift — remains essentially unknown. Pomacanthids are therefore an attractive but underexploited model for the evo-devo of pattern formation, complementing better-studied systems like cichlids and damselfishes.
The macroevolutionary distribution of extreme ontogenetic colour change within the family has not been formally mapped, though it appears largely restricted to large-bodied genera (Pomacanthus, Holacanthus, some Chaetodontoplus) and is muted or absent in the dwarf genera. This pattern offers a natural opportunity for ancestral-state reconstruction across the family phylogeny (Baraf et al., 2019, 2024).









Data quality: what to watch for



Ontogenetic colour change is the single largest risk for this group. Juvenile and adult Pomacanthus and Holacanthus look like entirely different species, and a few mislabelled juvenile images can swamp the chromatic signal of an entire genus. When curating images:

Verify that each image is an adult (or sub-adult expressing predominantly adult pattern).
Juveniles of large Pomacanthus species are typically dark-bodied with concentric blue-and-white arcs or rings centred near the tail.
If a fish appears to be less than ~half the species’ maximum total length, treat it as a juvenile until you have evidence otherwise.

Sexual dimorphism in Genicanthus. Males and females differ dramatically. Be consistent in which sex you use for a species, and record the choice in your metadata. For all other genera, a single adult representative per species is generally adequate.
Hybridisation. Pomacanthidae have the highest documented hybrid frequency of any reef-fish family (Tea et al., 2020); Centropyge, Pomacanthus, Genicanthus, and Chaetodontoplus all contain hybrids that look intermediate to or unlike either parent. If a specimen looks “off” relative to a standard field guide, suspect a hybrid and flag it for review rather than forcing it into a species category.
Geographic colour morphs. Several Centropyge species (notably C. loricula, C. flavissima, C. heraldi) include regional colour morphs that may be genetically nearly identical but visually distinct (Schultz et al., 2007). Decide a priori whether you are analysing species means, morph-specific values, or both.






Discrete Trait Mapping — Map the juvenile-to-adult pattern transformation across the pomacanthid phylogeny. Is extreme ontogenetic colour change ancestral to the family, or has it evolved independently in large-bodied lineages? Do pygmy angelfishes (Centropyge, Paracentropyge, Xiphypops), which show less dramatic ontogenetic change, represent the derived condition — or simply a body-size-correlated loss of the juvenile pattern?
Depth and Color — Pomacanthids range from shallow lagoons to mesophotic reef slopes, with some Centropyge and Paracentropyge occurring well below 50 m. Do deeper-dwelling species show reduced spectral conspicuousness or shifts toward longer-wavelength reflectance, as predicted by the depth-and-light-environment hypothesis?
Evolutionary Model Comparison — Given the paraphyly of Centropyge, the prevalence of ancient introgression, and the high frequency of contemporary hybridisation, pomacanthids likely violate the assumptions of standard Brownian motion models. Compare BM, OU (single and multi-optima), and early-burst models on continuous colour traits, and consider whether reticulate-network-aware comparative methods would change the inference.
Cross-Family Comparison — Angelfishes are frequently mistaken for butterflyfishes by casual observers, and Frédérich et al. (2026) and Hemingson et al. (2019) provide quantitative frameworks for testing whether vertical-bar and eyespot motifs in Pomacanthidae and Chaetodontidae represent statistically detectable convergence on the same chromatic phenotype.

title: Pomacanthidae — Marine Angelfishes
text:
Pomacanthidae are placed in the order Acanthuriformes (or, under older classifications, Perciformes), and have long been considered sister to butterflyfishes (Chaetodontidae), with which they share many ecological and morphological features (Bellwood et al., 2004). Family-level monophyly is well supported, but generic boundaries have been turbulent. The first molecular phylogeny of the family, based on mitochondrial 12S and 16S rRNA, recovered all but one genus as monophyletic: Centropyge was paraphyletic, with the swallowtail genus Genicanthus and the smoke-angelfish genus Apolemichthys nested within it (Bellwood et al., 2004). Subsequent multi-locus work confirmed and refined this picture, additionally elevating Paracentropyge and Xiphypops to genus rank to restore monophyly (Gaither et al., 2014).
The Atlantic and tropical eastern Pacific genus Holacanthus is itself a small, well-supported clade whose internal phylogeny tracks the closure of the Isthmus of Panama (Alva-Campbell et al., 2010). Pomacanthid biogeography is dominated by an Indo-Australian centre of origin and diversity, from which lineages have repeatedly dispersed into the Indian Ocean, the Red Sea, and (less often) the Atlantic (Baraf et al., 2019). The most recent target-capture phylogenomic analysis, using ~1,000 ultraconserved elements from 45 species, recovers a well-resolved family backbone but flags persistent discordance around the Centropyge radiation and the monotypic Pygoplites lineage, consistent with ancient introgression and incomplete lineage sorting (Baraf et al., 2024). For this lab, the key practical point is that close phylogenetic relatives can look dramatically different (e.g., flame Centropyge loricula vs. lemonpeel C. flavissima) and distantly related species can look remarkably similar (cross-genus convergence on vertical-bar patterns) — meaning color, although taxonomically informative, is not a clean proxy for phylogenetic distance in this family (Gaither et al., 2014).

title: Pomacanthidae — Marine Angelfishes
text:
Pomacanthidae are obligate coral-reef inhabitants of the Atlantic, Indian, and Pacific oceans, with species richness peaking in the Coral Triangle (Baraf et al., 2019). Adults occupy fore-reef slopes, walls, lagoon patch reefs, and (for many Centropyge and Paracentropyge) mesophotic reef habitats below 50 m. Most species are diurnal and strongly site-attached, defending feeding and mating territories within structurally complex substrate.
Diet varies substantially across the family. Large-bodied genera (Pomacanthus, Holacanthus, Pomacanthops, Chaetodontoplus) are best known as spongivores — one of the few vertebrate groups that exploits sponges in quantity — and supplement sponges with tunicates, hydroids, filamentous algae, and small benthic invertebrates. The pygmy and dwarf genera (Centropyge, Paracentropyge, Xiphypops) graze algal turf and detritus, and Genicanthus is unusual within the family for being a midwater zooplanktivore. Despite this broad trophic range, the underlying feeding apparatus is morphologically and kinematically conservative: high trophic diversity has evolved with surprisingly limited functional disparity in jaw morphology and feeding kinematics (Konow & Bellwood, 2011).
Mating systems are predominantly haremic, with a dominant male defending a territory containing one to several females. All pomacanthids studied to date are protogynous hermaphrodites: females change sex to male upon loss of the dominant individual, and the transition is typically accompanied by behavioural change and, in some genera, conspicuous color change (Pyle & Randall, 1994). Spawning is pelagic and pair-based, with planktonic larval durations on the order of weeks, which contributes to the broad distributions and apparent panmixia of many species (Schultz et al., 2007).
A defining natural-history feature of the family is the extraordinarily high frequency of interspecific hybridization. A recent genomic survey detected putative hybrids involving 42 of 88 species (~48% of the family), distributed across every extant genus except the monotypic Pygoplites (Tea et al., 2020). Field studies at hybrid hotspots such as Christmas Island show that hybridization tends to be promoted by a combination of low local abundance of one parent species and broad niche overlap between parents — conditions easily met as Indo-Pacific lineages contact one another along suture zones (Hodge et al., 2019).

title: Pomacanthidae — Marine Angelfishes
text:
Primary measurements of pomacanthid visual systems — microspectrophotometry of cone visual pigments, opsin gene expression, behavioural psychophysics — are essentially absent from the literature. Almost everything we know about how angelfishes perceive their reef is inferred from the broader reef-fish literature (Marshall et al., 2019). It is worth stating this gap explicitly: despite the family’s status as a charismatic, visually conspicuous group, no published study has directly characterised the cone complement of any pomacanthid.
What is known generalises across most acanthuriforms and percomorphs (Marshall et al., 2019). Reef fishes typically possess a duplex retina with one rod opsin (RH1) and up to five cone opsin classes (SWS1, SWS2, RH2 paralogues, LWS), arranged as single cones (expressing short-wavelength opsins) and pairs of double cones (expressing medium- and long-wavelength opsins). Several reef-fish lineages, including some butterflyfishes and damselfishes, are UV-sensitive via SWS1 in single cones, and a parsimonious assumption is that at least some pomacanthids retain UV sensitivity, especially those species (e.g., Genicanthus, Centropyge) whose body colours include UV-reflective whites or yellows that would otherwise be invisible to ecologically relevant viewers. This remains an open empirical question.
Light environments occupied by pomacanthids span the near-surface blue-green spectrum of shallow lagoons through the increasingly monochromatic blue light of mesophotic reefs (Marshall et al., 2019). The most likely functional contexts for color signalling in the family are species recognition (especially in sympatric Centropyge species where hybridization is rampant), sex recognition (in Genicanthus, where dichromatism is strong), and territorial advertisement. Color also functions as a developmental signal: juveniles of large Pomacanthus species use radically different patterns from adults, which is widely interpreted as a mechanism for avoiding aggression from territorial conspecifics (Pyle & Randall, 1994).

title: Pomacanthidae — Marine Angelfishes
text:
Within the standardised pattern survey of Frédérich et al. (2026), Pomacanthidae stand out among the six reef-fish families analysed for the diversity and lability of their patterns. Pomacanthid evolution has produced near-monochromatic body plans (e.g., Centropyge flavissima in uniform yellow with a blue eye-ring), bold vertical-bar patterns (Pygoplites diacanthus, several Pomacanthus), striking concentric-arc juveniles (Pomacanthus spp.; see below), and intricate face-and-fin masks (Apolemichthys, Chaetodontoplus). Frédérich et al. (2026) further show that pigmentation patterns have evolved rapidly and repeatedly across reef-fish families, with multiple independent origins of the same visual motifs — a result consistent with convergence on a limited set of “designs” that work in reef light environments.
Convergence with other families is striking. Vertical-bar patterns broadly resembling those of butterflyfishes have evolved at least twice in pomacanthids (in Pygoplites and in juvenile Pomacanthus), and the bar/stripe axis is one of the most labile features of reef-fish colouration generally (Hemingson et al., 2019). Hemingson and colleagues showed in butterflyfishes that pattern divergence is most rapid when closely related species have overlapping geographic ranges of similar size — a prediction worth testing explicitly in pomacanthids, where many sister-pair contact zones are sites of both pattern divergence and hybridization (Tea et al., 2020).
Within-genus disparities are also instructive. The Holacanthus radiation occupies a relatively narrow morphological space but a wide chromatic one, from the cool blues of H. ciliaris to the bold yellow/black contrast of H. tricolor (Alva-Campbell et al., 2010). Centropyge spans the most colourful range of any genus in the family but is also the most paraphyletic, the most hybridised, and the most taxonomically unstable — a reminder that bright, distinctive colours need not reflect deep evolutionary distinctiveness (Gaither et al., 2014).

title: Pomacanthidae — Marine Angelfishes
text:
Sexual dichromatism in Pomacanthidae ranges from negligible (most Centropyge, Holacanthus, Pomacanthus) to extreme. The clearest case is Genicanthus, where males and females differ in body pattern so dramatically that they were originally described as separate species: male G. lamarck has bold horizontal black stripes on a white body whereas females are darker dorsally and whitish below. Because sex change is protogynous, all Genicanthus individuals begin life with female colouration and acquire male pattern upon ascending to the dominant breeding position (Pyle & Randall, 1994).
Geographic colour polymorphism is also well documented. The flame angelfish Centropyge loricula expresses three regional colour morphs across the Pacific — red (Hawai‘i), reduced-black (Marquesas), and orange (broader Oceania) — yet population genetic markers reveal little differentiation among morphs, indicating that morph variation is not tracking deep population structure (Schultz et al., 2007). Similar morph complexes have been described in C. flavissima and C. heraldi, which appear to comprise cryptic sibling species pairs (Gaither et al., 2014). For comparative colour analyses, these examples emphasise that within-species chromatic variation in pomacanthids can be substantial and ecologically meaningful, not noise.
Hybrid individuals typically show intermediate or mosaic colour patterns relative to parental species, and these intermediates form a near-continuous chromatic spectrum at sympatric contact zones (Pyle & Randall, 1994; Tea et al., 2020). Because hybrids are frequent (~48% of species; Tea et al., 2020) and because they bias quantitative colour summaries toward parental averages, hybrids must be flagged or excluded from comparative analyses rather than coerced into one parental category.

title: Pomacanthidae — Marine Angelfishes
text:
The most spectacular ontogenetic colour change in any reef-fish family occurs in Pomacanthus and its close relatives. Juveniles of P. imperator, P. semicirculatus, P. annularis, P. navarchus, and P. paru display dark bodies marked with electric-blue and white concentric arcs or rings centred near the caudal peduncle. As individuals reach roughly 8–12 cm standard length, the arcs progressively elongate and flatten over a period of weeks to months, ultimately resolving into the species-specific adult pattern — which in P. imperator and P. semicirculatus takes the form of horizontal blue-and-yellow stripes (Pyle & Randall, 1994).
Two adaptive hypotheses are commonly invoked for this developmental shift. First, the disruptive concentric pattern is thought to enhance crypsis among coral rubble and rocky substrate where juveniles shelter. Second, the radically different juvenile pattern may reduce intraspecific aggression by signalling to territorial adults that the juvenile is not a competitor for the local territory or mate (Pyle & Randall, 1994). These hypotheses have rarely been tested experimentally in Pomacanthus, and the developmental and genetic basis of the transformation — how the arcs reorganise into stripes, what regulatory changes underlie the shift — remains essentially unknown. Pomacanthids are therefore an attractive but underexploited model for the evo-devo of pattern formation, complementing better-studied systems like cichlids and damselfishes.
The macroevolutionary distribution of extreme ontogenetic colour change within the family has not been formally mapped, though it appears largely restricted to large-bodied genera (Pomacanthus, Holacanthus, some Chaetodontoplus) and is muted or absent in the dwarf genera. This pattern offers a natural opportunity for ancestral-state reconstruction across the family phylogeny (Baraf et al., 2019, 2024).

title: Pomacanthidae — Marine Angelfishes
text:
Data quality: what to watch for



Ontogenetic colour change is the single largest risk for this group. Juvenile and adult Pomacanthus and Holacanthus look like entirely different species, and a few mislabelled juvenile images can swamp the chromatic signal of an entire genus. When curating images:

Verify that each image is an adult (or sub-adult expressing predominantly adult pattern).
Juveniles of large Pomacanthus species are typically dark-bodied with concentric blue-and-white arcs or rings centred near the tail.
If a fish appears to be less than ~half the species’ maximum total length, treat it as a juvenile until you have evidence otherwise.

Sexual dimorphism in Genicanthus. Males and females differ dramatically. Be consistent in which sex you use for a species, and record the choice in your metadata. For all other genera, a single adult representative per species is generally adequate.
Hybridisation. Pomacanthidae have the highest documented hybrid frequency of any reef-fish family (Tea et al., 2020); Centropyge, Pomacanthus, Genicanthus, and Chaetodontoplus all contain hybrids that look intermediate to or unlike either parent. If a specimen looks “off” relative to a standard field guide, suspect a hybrid and flag it for review rather than forcing it into a species category.
Geographic colour morphs. Several Centropyge species (notably C. loricula, C. flavissima, C. heraldi) include regional colour morphs that may be genetically nearly identical but visually distinct (Schultz et al., 2007). Decide a priori whether you are analysing species means, morph-specific values, or both.

title: Cirrhilabrini — Fairy Wrasses and Flasher Wrasses
text:
Taxonomy and Phylogenetics
The Cirrhilabrini is a tribe within Labridae comprising the genera Cirrhilabrus (fairy wrasses) and Paracheilinus (flasher wrasses), together totaling roughly 86 currently recognized species. The monotypic Conniella was formally synonymized into Cirrhilabrus by Tea, Allen, and Goatley (2021), so contemporary analyses treat the tribe as effectively bigeneric. Westneat and Alfaro (2005) provided the first broad molecular phylogeny of Labridae and placed the cirrhilabrines within the Labrinae subfamily, establishing the framework that all subsequent UCE-based phylogenomic work has refined.
Tea, Xu, DiBattista, et al. (2021) sequenced 991 ultraconserved elements across most described Cirrhilabrus lineages and recovered a Late Miocene origin for the tribe, with the majority of extant species diverging during the Plio-Pleistocene (2–5 Ma). Their dated tree shows that Cirrhilabrus and Paracheilinus are reciprocally monophyletic sister genera, and that the Coral Triangle was both the geographic origin and the principal engine of subsequent diversification. Brownstein et al. (2025), using phylogenomic data spanning reef vertebrates, recovered similar tempo estimates and placed labrid radiation in the broader context of Early Miocene reef community assembly.
Cirrhilabrine taxonomy is among the most active frontiers in reef-fish systematics. Tea et al. (2019) described Cirrhilabrus wakanda from Tanzanian mesophotic reefs, and Tea et al. (2022) described C. finifenmaa from the Maldives based on a combination of morphology, color pattern, and molecular data. Tea and Walsh (2023) revised Paracheilinus, recognizing new species and reclassifying others on the basis of nuptial coloration and meristic characters. Students should expect that some tip labels in the 49-species tree may have been split, synonymized, or recombined since the source phylogeny was published.

title: Cirrhilabrini — Fairy Wrasses and Flasher Wrasses
text:
Natural History
Cirrhilabrines are obligate diurnal planktivores that hover in loose, mixed-sex aggregations a meter or two above reef substrate. They pick small crustaceans, copepods, and larvaceans from passing currents, and most species are tightly associated with reef slopes, rubble fields, or deepwater reef edges where current delivers reliable plankton. Aggregations typically consist of one to a few terminal-phase (TP) males defending overlapping female territories.
Several lineages have independently colonized mesophotic coral ecosystems (MCEs) at 40–150 m, where downwelling light is strongly blue-shifted and red wavelengths are nearly absent (Tea et al., 2019). Mesophotic specialists such as C. wakanda and C. finifenmaa tend to display reduced red and orange coloration and increased emphasis on violet, magenta, and blue patterns — shifts that align broadly with the spectral environment in which these signals are deployed. The repeated, independent colonization of mesophotic habitats by closely related cirrhilabrines provides a natural experiment for testing how the light environment shapes color evolution.
Reproduction is driven by intense sexual selection. Females are protogynous; the largest individual in a group transitions to terminal-phase male and defends a small harem. During courtship, TP males perform the nuptial “flash” display described in detail below. Spawning occurs in the water column at dusk, after which fertilized eggs are dispersed by currents and develop as pelagic larvae for several weeks before settling.

title: Cirrhilabrini — Fairy Wrasses and Flasher Wrasses
text:
Visual Ecology and Signaling
Labrid visual systems are among the best-characterized of any reef fish family. Marshall, Cortesi, and de Busserolles (2018) reviewed reef-fish color vision and emphasized that labrids generally possess a rich opsin gene complement spanning UV (SWS1), short-wave (SWS2), middle-wave (RH2), and long-wave (LWS) sensitivities, with substantial variation in opsin gene expression among species and life stages. Cortesi, Musilová, and Salzburger (2021) further showed that teleost opsin gene duplication and tuning are particularly elaborate in reef-associated lineages, and that expressed opsin repertoires can shift rapidly across environments.
The visual environment of cirrhilabrines is consequential. Many species spawn and display in the late afternoon or at dusk, when downwelling irradiance is reduced and red wavelengths are attenuated. Gerlach, Theobald, and Hart (2016) characterized visual pigments in a related dottyback-wrasse assemblage and emphasized that the spectral position of LWS opsins covaries with diet and depth across small reef fishes. For mesophotic cirrhilabrines specifically, conspicuous reds are paradoxical: red pigments appear dark or black against blue downwelling light, so red ornaments only function as effective signals at short viewing distances or when the male is silhouetted against bright backgrounds during a near-vertical display ascent.
A particularly elegant body of work focuses on red fluorescence as a possible private signaling channel. Gerlach, Sprenger, and Michiels (2014) experimentally demonstrated that the fairy wrasse Cirrhilabrus solorensis perceives and behaviorally responds to red fluorescent signals, indicating that fluorescence is biologically meaningful rather than incidental. The capacity to perceive long-wavelength fluorescence, combined with the abundance of red and orange ornaments in cirrhilabrine TP males, suggests that fluorescence may augment conventional reflectance-based signals in the spectrally restricted environments these fishes occupy.

title: Cirrhilabrini — Fairy Wrasses and Flasher Wrasses
text:
Color Pattern Diversity
Cirrhilabrine TP-male coloration spans an extraordinary spectrum of saturated reds, oranges, magentas, blues, violets, and yellows, often arranged in species-specific combinations of body bands, dorsal-fin spots, and caudal markings. Cirrhilabrus jordani (Hawaiian flame wrasse) displays brilliant orange-red during nuptial display; C. cyanopleura combines vivid blue and purple flanks with a yellow-green saddle; C. temminckii pairs magenta fins with a green-blue body. Paracheilinus flashers are named for the dramatic extension of elongated dorsal-fin filaments during display, as in P. nursalim, which contrasts electric-blue dorsal filaments against a red body.
Hodge, Santini, and Wainwright (2020) analyzed colour dimorphism across Labridae and found that cirrhilabrines occupy an extreme position in trait space: they show some of the highest male-female color disparity values in the family, comparable in magnitude to that observed in scarines (parrotfishes), but achieved through a fundamentally different mechanism. In scarines, both sexes are conspicuously colored and the dimorphism arises because IP and TP have diverged independently. In cirrhilabrines, the dimorphism arises because females have converged on a single, cryptic phenotype while males have diversified into many distinct, conspicuous ones.
A striking feature of the clade is the convergent drab coloration of females. Across almost all Cirrhilabrus and Paracheilinus species, females are small (4–6 cm), uniformly pinkish-tan to mauve, with at most a faint lateral stripe or subtle fin tinting. Females of different species are often indistinguishable in the field. This pattern is consistent with stabilizing selection on females (likely predator avoidance) acting in opposition to strong directional sexual selection on males (species recognition and mate choice), and it makes cirrhilabrines an unusually clean system for testing whether color evolution is decoupled between sexes.
crumbs: Cirrhilabrini --- Fairy Wrasses and Flasher Wrasses

title: Cirrhilabrini — Fairy Wrasses and Flasher Wrasses
text:
Sexual Dimorphism, Ontogeny, and Polymorphism
Cirrhilabrines exhibit one of the most extreme sex-by-stage color phenotypes among reef fishes. The relevant phases are juvenile, initial-phase (IP, functionally female), and terminal-phase (TP, functionally male). Juveniles and IP females share a near-identical cryptic phenotype — small body, pinkish-tan ground color, minimal fin ornamentation. TP males emerge through protogynous sex change driven by social dominance: when a harem-holding male dies or is removed, the largest female transitions to male over a period of weeks, with the new TP phenotype developing progressively as gonadal restructuring proceeds (Tea et al., 2021).
Geographic polymorphism within nominal species adds another layer of complexity. Many Cirrhilabrus species exhibit pronounced regional color variation across the Indo-Pacific that has historically led to taxonomic confusion. The C. rubrisquamis / C. wakanda / C. finifenmaa complex is a worked example: what was treated as one variable species for decades was, on detailed examination, resolved into three allopatric lineages distinguishable primarily by male coloration (Tea et al., 2019, 2022). Students working with image data from biodiversity portals should be alert to the possibility that some “species” represent geographic morphs whose status is still being worked out.

title: Cirrhilabrini — Fairy Wrasses and Flasher Wrasses
section: Nuptial Display Coloration and Rapid Color Change
text:
Nuptial Display Coloration and Rapid Color Change
The single defining feature of cirrhilabrine signaling, and the focus of this clade-specific deep dive, is the nuptial flash display. TP males perform brief, intense courtship dashes in which they ascend a meter or more above the reef substrate, extend all fins to maximum spread, and undergo a near-instantaneous intensification of body coloration. Reds become incandescent, blues and violets brighten, and pattern elements that are muted or invisible during resting coloration become boldly defined. A single flash lasts a few seconds at most, but a courtship bout may include dozens of repeated flashes targeted at one or more females. This is among the most extreme examples of rapid, hormonally and neurally controlled color change in any reef-fish lineage.
Several features make this display worth a careful look in the context of an undergraduate research project. First, the mechanism is dual: rapid translocation of pigment granules within chromatophores produces the fast component (sub-second to seconds), while structural color elements (iridophore-based blues and violets) become more visible when overlying melanophores contract and reveal underlying iridescence. Second, the display is unambiguously a sexually selected trait. Tea and Walsh (2023) emphasize that Paracheilinus taxonomy is built almost entirely on nuptial-male coloration because resting-state morphology is uninformative; this strongly implies that nuptial color elements are under direct mate-choice selection. Third, the signal interacts with the visual environment in nontrivial ways. Because the flash occurs during a near-vertical ascent at dusk, the male’s body is briefly silhouetted against bright surface waters — a viewing geometry that would maximize the contrast of dark melanin patterns and minimize the visibility of red ornaments. The display therefore likely targets females positioned below and to the side of the male, who view his flanks against a darker, downwelling-dim background where red and orange ornaments achieve maximum contrast.
The implications for image-based color analysis are direct. Most underwater photographs capture resting-state coloration, in which signals are deliberately muted. Aquarium and competition photographs sometimes capture full nuptial display. Mixing the two states across species will produce artifactual variation in any color metric. Gerlach et al. (2014) further showed that fluorescent components of fairy wrasse signals are imperceptible to standard RGB cameras tuned to human vision, meaning that a fraction of the actual signal is invisible in most available imagery. Students should treat conventional photographs as a lower-bound proxy for the true perceived signal.

title: Cirrhilabrini — Fairy Wrasses and Flasher Wrasses
text:
Data Quality Warnings






Data quality: what to watch for



Use TP males consistently. Like parrotfishes, cirrhilabrines have extreme dimorphism, but the diagnostic problem is reversed. In Scarinae, IP and TP males look like different species. In Cirrhilabrini, females of different species look nearly identical, while TP males are the diagnostic phase. Your analysis should use TP-male images throughout.
How to identify TP males:

Color: Vivid, species-specific patterns with saturated reds, blues, purples, greens, or combinations; complex fin markings, often with elongated or filamentous dorsal rays.
Size: Larger than females within a species (typically 6–10 cm for Cirrhilabrus).
Behavior (in photos): Males are often photographed displaying (fins spread, body angled upward in mid-water).

How to identify females (to exclude or flag):

Color: Uniform pinkish-tan, mauve, or light reddish-brown; minimal fin coloration; sometimes a faint lateral stripe.
Size: Smaller, more streamlined.
If you cannot tell whether an image is a male or female, it is almost certainly a female — TP males are unmistakable.

Nuptial vs. resting coloration. TP males show two distinct color states: muted resting coloration and intensified nuptial flash coloration. Most underwater photographs capture resting state; some aquarium and competition photographs capture nuptial display. For consistency, standardize on resting-state TP males across all species. Mixing nuptial-display images for some species with resting images for others will bias your color metrics in an unpredictable direction.
Identical-looking females are real biology, not a data problem. When you find that female images for 15 different species look essentially the same, do not assume you have misidentified species. The convergent female phenotype is a documented evolutionary pattern (Hodge et al., 2020) and is itself a finding worth discussing in your write-up.
Recent taxonomic changes. Cirrhilabrini taxonomy is unusually active. Cross-check unfamiliar tip labels against Tea et al. (2021) and current FishBase / Catalog of Fishes records. Conniella records, if present, should be treated as Cirrhilabrus.
Fluorescence is invisible to standard cameras. RGB imagery captured for human-visible color analysis will miss the long-wavelength fluorescent component of cirrhilabrine signals (Gerlach et al., 2014). Treat your color metrics as a conservative, lower-bound description of the true perceived signal.

title: Cirrhilabrini — Fairy Wrasses and Flasher Wrasses
text:
Promising Questions for This Clade

Sexual System and Color Complexity — Cirrhilabrini is the canonical test case for sexual selection driving color diversification. Is TP-male conspicuousness (e.g., pavo metrics Jc, Jt, or dS against natural backgrounds) correlated with proxies for mating-system intensity, such as harem size or elaboration of dorsal-fin filaments?
Disparity Through Time — Given the explosive Plio-Pleistocene radiation documented by Tea et al. (2021), cirrhilabrines are ideal for DTT analysis. Has TP-male color diversified faster than expected under Brownian motion? Has the rate of color evolution accelerated during the recent species radiation, or is variation partitioned mostly among older lineages?
Depth and Color — Multiple cirrhilabrine lineages have independently invaded mesophotic reefs. Do mesophotic specialists show predictable shifts in color metrics (reduced long-wavelength chroma, increased short-wavelength reflectance) compared with shallow-reef relatives? This is a clean repeated-evolution test using FishBase depth ranges as the predictor.
Phylogenetic Signal — If TP-male coloration is the primary species-recognition signal and sexual selection drives rapid divergence, you might expect weak phylogenetic signal in male color metrics despite the clade’s young age. Compare signal strength in male vs. female color traits to test the decoupled-evolution hypothesis directly.
Sexual Dichromatism — Quantify male-female color distance (e.g., dS in a tetrachromat visual model) across all 49 tip species and compare with the across-family pattern reported by Hodge et al. (2020). Do cirrhilabrines occupy the same extreme position in the 49-species tree as they do in family-wide analyses?

title: Halichoerine — Coris-Allies and Halichoeres Wrasses
text:
Taxonomy and Phylogenetics
The Halichoerinae (or “julidine” lineage sensu Westneat & Alfaro, 2005) is a large, monophyletic radiation within Labridae that includes the genera Halichoeres, Coris, Thalassoma, Macropharyngodon, Anampses, Pseudocheilinus, Pseudojuloides, Stethojulis, and several smaller allies. Westneat and Alfaro’s (2005) molecular phylogeny based on mitochondrial 12S, 16S, and nuclear tmo-4C4 sequences recovered this group as a well-supported clade nested within the broader labrid tree, sister to the cheiline + scarine clade. More recent phylogenomic work has both confirmed the monophyly of the broad julidine lineage and refined intergeneric relationships within it (Cowman & Bellwood, 2011; Hodge & Bellwood, 2016).
The most taxonomically important finding to keep in mind when interpreting your tree is that Halichoeres as currently circumscribed is not monophyletic. Barber and Bellwood (2005) used mitochondrial cytochrome b* and 16S to show that Atlantic, Eastern Pacific, and Indo-Pacific Halichoeres do not form a single exclusive clade; instead, several lineages are more closely related to other genera (e.g., Macropharyngodon, Anampses) than to other Halichoeres. Rocha et al. (2010) reinforced this conclusion for the New World species, recovering at least two independent Halichoeres radiations on either side of the Isthmus of Panama. For your analyses, this means that any “within-Halichoeres” comparison actually spans multiple deep evolutionary lineages, and apparent color disparity within the genus reflects ancient divergences, not a recent burst within a single tight clade.
Diversification rates within the halichoerine clade accelerated during the Miocene, coinciding with expansion of Indo-Australian Archipelago (IAA) reef habitat (Cowman & Bellwood, 2011; Hodge & Bellwood, 2016). Repeated dispersal out of the IAA “biodiversity hotspot” appears to have seeded peripheral reef regions, including the Caribbean, Eastern Pacific, and Hawaiian provinces. The result is a clade whose geographic structure is layered: deep biogeographic signal at the genus level is overlain by recent, often shallow species-level divergences across well-dated barriers.

title: Halichoerine — Coris-Allies and Halichoeres Wrasses
text:
Natural History
Halichoerine wrasses are small to medium-sized (typically 8–40 cm TL), elongate reef fishes that swim by labriform pectoral-fin propulsion, a locomotor mode shared across Labridae and tied to maneuverable foraging in structurally complex habitat (Westneat & Alfaro, 2005). They are among the most conspicuous diurnal predators on tropical reefs worldwide. Most species are benthic invertivores, feeding on small crustaceans, polychaetes, gastropods, and ophiuroids picked from rubble, sand, or live coral interstices. Coris species are specialized “sand-flippers,” using strong pharyngeal jaws to crush hard-shelled prey extracted by digging; Macropharyngodon leopard wrasses target small foraminiferans and ostracods; Thalassoma and Pseudocheilinus are more generalized water-column foragers that also take zooplankton.
A widespread behavior in the clade is sand-sleeping: many halichoerine species (essentially all Halichoeres, Coris, Anampses, Macropharyngodon, Pseudojuloides) bury themselves in sand at dusk or when alarmed. This habit constrains body shape (laterally compressed, elongate) and may exert selection on dorsal coloration visible to aerial or planktonic predators during the brief moments fish are exposed at the substrate surface.
A second defining ecological feature is biogeographic structure. The closure of the Central American Seaway ~3.1 Ma (Coates & Stallard, 2013) produced multiple geminate species pairs within New World Halichoeres (e.g., H. bivittatus/H. dispilus, H. maculipinna/H. chierchiae). Rocha et al. (2010), however, demonstrated that not all trans-Isthmian splits date to final closure; several are substantially older (up to ~20 Ma), reflecting earlier episodes of restriction. The clade therefore offers replicate natural experiments at varying time depths — an unusually powerful setting for asking how rapidly color and pattern diverge after vicariance.

title: Halichoerine — Coris-Allies and Halichoeres Wrasses
text:
Visual Ecology and Signaling
Wrasses possess among the most spectrally rich visual systems documented in teleosts. They retain functional copies of all four ancestral cone opsin classes (SWS1 UV-sensitive; SWS2 violet/blue; RH2 blue-green; LWS red), and several lineages have undergone tandem duplication of the RH2 and SWS2 genes (Cortesi et al., 2015; Musilová et al., 2021). Cortesi et al. (2015) showed in a comparative survey across damselfishes and wrasses that opsin gene expression is dynamically tuned during ontogeny and across photic environments: juveniles and shallow-water species typically express UV- and short-wavelength-sensitive opsins more strongly, while deeper-living individuals shift expression toward longer wavelengths. Stieb et al. (2023) demonstrated that this expression plasticity persists in adults and can shift on weeks-to-months timescales when ambient spectral conditions change.
Functionally, this visual repertoire means halichoerine wrasses can both produce and perceive signals in the UV and short-blue regions of the spectrum, where many of their conspecific facial patterns reflect strongly (Cortesi et al., 2016; Marshall et al., 2003 in the broader reef-fish context). UV-reflective face markings in Thalassoma and Halichoeres TP males, and the iridescent blue lines on Anampses and Macropharyngodon, are therefore not merely human-visible ornaments but private or semi-private channels visible to conspecifics under reef light. Because pavo’s sensmodel and vismodel workflows let you reweight reflectance spectra against any visual model, this clade is a strong target for asking whether IP/TP differences predicted to be “subtle” in human RGB are in fact dramatic under wrasse-relevant cone weightings.

title: Halichoerine — Coris-Allies and Halichoeres Wrasses
text:
Color Pattern Diversity
The halichoerine clade contains some of the broadest color disparity in any single labrid lineage. Macropharyngodon leopard wrasses display intricate reticulated patterns of teal, orange, and black rosettes against pale backgrounds, with each individual carrying an effectively unique pattern. Thalassoma species are characterized by bold facial bars and head shields: T. bifasciatum (bluehead wrasse) TP males display a brilliant blue head separated from a green body by black-and-white vertical bars and are among the most studied reef fishes globally (Warner & Swearer, 1991). T. lunare exhibits a green body with vivid magenta-to-yellow facial markings. Coris gaimard shows pronounced ontogenetic color change: juveniles are vermillion-orange with white-edged black dorsal spots, while adults develop a dark blue-green body with brilliant blue facial spots.
Halichoeres spans nearly the full possible range from cryptic to maximally conspicuous. Some sand-associated species (e.g., H. poeyi, H. bivittatus IP) are olive-green or brown with subtle stripes, while others (e.g., H. ornatissimus, H. iridis) display rainbow-like sequences of red, green, blue, and orange facial lines. Anampses wrasses present a different syndrome: intricate white-spotting or fine-line patterns on dark bodies, with extreme IP/TP divergence (A. meleagrides females are black with white spots, TP males are dark green with blue facial lines and an orange tail). Hodge et al. (2020a) showed in a phylogenetic comparative framework that pattern complexity and chromatic contrast vary independently across reef fishes, and the halichoerine clade is an excellent within-family example: Macropharyngodon is high-complexity, moderate-contrast; Thalassoma is low-complexity, high-contrast; Halichoeres spans both axes.

title: Halichoerine — Coris-Allies and Halichoeres Wrasses
text:
Sexual Dimorphism, Ontogeny, and Polymorphism
All halichoerine wrasses studied to date are protogynous hermaphrodites: individuals mature as females (Initial Phase, IP) and a subset later transition to functional males (Terminal Phase, TP) following sex change, typically triggered by loss of a dominant male from the social group (Warner & Robertson, 1978; Warner et al., 1985). In many species, IP individuals include both functional females and small “sneaker” males that retain female-like coloration — a third phenotypic class that is genetically male but visually indistinguishable from females (Warner & Swearer, 1991). Terminal Phase males are larger, brighter, and behave as territorial spawners.
The magnitude of IP/TP color divergence varies systematically across the clade:

Thalassoma: extreme. TP males (e.g., bluehead wrasse blue phase) are essentially unrecognizable as the same species as IP individuals (Warner & Swearer, 1991).
Halichoeres: moderate to strong. TP males show more saturated colors, more contrasting facial bands, and often a unique flank spot or bar absent in IPs.
Coris: moderate. TP males have sharper facial pattern boundaries and brighter blues.
Macropharyngodon: moderate. Both phases are intricately patterned, but TP males have more saturated reds/oranges.
Anampses: extreme. IP and TP look like different species.

Ontogenetic color change is layered on top of this dichromatism. Coris species undergo striking juvenile-to-adult transformations (the C. gaimard “clown” juvenile becoming an adult “yellowtail coris”). Thalassoma juveniles are typically uniformly colored and lack adult facial markings. These ontogenetic transitions reflect changing visual ecology — juveniles often occupy different microhabitats than adults and may experience different predator regimes (Cortesi et al., 2016).

title: Halichoerine — Coris-Allies and Halichoeres Wrasses
section: IP/TP Dichromatism — A Clade Deep Dive
text:
IP/TP Dichromatism — A Clade Deep Dive
Because IP/TP dichromatism is the single most important source of within-species color variation in this clade, it requires careful treatment in any color-evolution analysis. The phenomenon arises from the intersection of three biological systems:
1. Socially controlled sex change. Warner and Robertson (1978), in a foundational study of Caribbean labrids, showed that protogynous sex change is triggered by social cues — specifically, the disappearance of dominant males allows the largest female in a group to transition. Warner et al. (1985) and Warner and Swearer (1991) extended this to Thalassoma bifasciatum, demonstrating that sex change is fast (days to weeks), involves complete gonadal reorganization, and produces a behaviorally and chromatically distinct individual. The size-advantage model (Warner, 1975) predicts protogyny will evolve when male reproductive success increases steeply with size and when small individuals have higher female fitness — conditions met in most halichoerine mating systems.
2. Alternative reproductive tactics. In many halichoerine species, including T. bifasciatum and several Halichoeres, small males in IP coloration (“sneakers” or “streakers”) participate in group spawnings dominated by TP males (Warner & Swearer, 1991; Kuwamura et al., 2002). This means IP coloration is not strictly diagnostic of female sex — a fraction of IP individuals are male. For pavo analyses, this caveat is conceptually important: an “IP” photograph may represent a female or a sneaker male, and these may not differ chromatically.
3. Hormonal control of pigment cells. The TP transition involves coordinated changes in xanthophore, erythrophore, iridophore, and melanophore distribution under the control of gonadal steroids (Warner et al., 2006). Iridophore density increases in the head region of TP males, producing the characteristic structural blues and greens of Thalassoma, Halichoeres, and Anampses face patterns. Because iridophore-based colors are angle-dependent, photographic standardization (consistent lateral view, diffuse lighting) is essential.
Practical implication for color-evolution analyses. If you mix IPs and TPs within a species, you will inflate within-species variance and deflate between-species effect sizes. The correct strategy is to choose one phase consistently across all species (TP males are conventional, because they are the more conspicuous “advertised” phenotype) and document any species for which only the alternative phase was available. For questions specifically about dichromatism itself (e.g., “Is the magnitude of TP-vs-IP divergence correlated with mating-system intensity?”), you should sample both phases for each species and compute a per-species dichromatism index.

title: Halichoerine — Coris-Allies and Halichoeres Wrasses
text:
Data Quality Warnings






What to watch for in image selection



IP/TP dimorphism — present and important. Use TP male images consistently. If you cannot determine sex from a photograph, choose the most vivid, boldly patterned individual — in halichoerines this is almost certainly a TP male. Sneaker males are visually indistinguishable from females and need not be excluded separately from IPs.
Ontogenetic color change. Coris species (especially C. gaimard, C. aygula, C. julis) undergo dramatic juvenile-to-adult transformations. Thalassoma juveniles are typically plain-colored. Exclude obvious juveniles.
Polyphyly of Halichoeres. Your tree may show Halichoeres species scattered across multiple parts of the phylogeny (Barber & Bellwood, 2005; Rocha et al., 2010). This is real biology, not a tree error. Consider analyzing well-supported subclades separately rather than treating the genus as a single unit.
Iridophore-based colors are angle-dependent. Structural blues and greens on TP male faces will change apparent hue with lighting geometry. Prefer photographs taken in diffuse natural light with a clean lateral view. Avoid strobed images that exaggerate iridescence.
Dataset size management. With 140 species, this is the largest student dataset. Not all species will have high-quality photographs. Curate a well-sampled subset of 50–70 species with verified TP male identification rather than including poor or uncertain images for every species. Document exclusions explicitly — this is good scientific practice.
Sand-sleeping species. Several species (Halichoeres, Anampses, Macropharyngodon) may be photographed half-buried or with disturbed dorsal pigmentation. Exclude these and use clean, fully exposed individuals.

title: Halichoerine — Coris-Allies and Halichoeres Wrasses
text:
Promising Questions for This Clade

Biogeographic Color Comparison — The Isthmus of Panama geminate species pairs provide a well-dated natural experiment. Have Caribbean and Pacific sister species diverged in pavo color metrics since vicariant separation? Is divergence magnitude correlated with time since splitting? Note that Rocha et al. (2010) showed not all trans-Isthmian splits date to ~3 Ma — you can leverage this variation in divergence times.
Cross-Family Comparison — As the largest labrid clade in the course, halichoerine wrasses contribute the most species to the combined labrid mega-analysis. Compare the color morphospace occupied by your clade to Scarinae, Cirrhilabrini, and Hypsigenyinae. Does the largest clade occupy the broadest color space, or is disparity decoupled from species richness?
Phylogenetic Signal — With 140 species (or your curated subset of ~60), you have strong statistical power for Blomberg’s K and Pagel’s lambda. Is color more phylogenetically conserved in Macropharyngodon (distinctive spotted pattern) than in Halichoeres (highly variable)?
Axis of Diversification — With color spanning cryptic sand-dwellers to psychedelic leopard wrasses, which axis of pavo color space (brightness, saturation, hue, pattern complexity) shows greatest disparity? Hodge et al. (2020a) show pattern complexity and chromatic contrast vary independently across reef fishes — test this within your clade.
Swimming Mode and Pattern — Halichoerine wrasses are predominantly labriform swimmers but vary in body elongation and tail shape. Does fin-and-body morphology correlate with stripe orientation or pattern geometry?
Sexual Dichromatism Index — For species where both IP and TP photographs are available, compute a per-species dichromatism index (e.g., Euclidean distance in pavo color space between IP and TP). Does dichromatism correlate with mating-system intensity (group spawning vs pair spawning; estimated from literature)?
