title: Hypsigenyinae — Hogfishes, Tuskfishes, and Sheepheads
text:
Taxonomy and Phylogenetics
Hypsigenyinae is one of the early-branching subfamilies within Labridae, the wrasses and parrotfishes. Westneat and Alfaro (2005) produced the first comprehensive molecular phylogeny of Labridae using nuclear and mitochondrial markers, recovering Hypsigenyinae (including Bodianus, Choerodon, Lachnolaimus, Semicossyphus, and Clepticus) as a distinct clade near the base of the family. This basal position is biologically important: hypsigenyines retain several plesiomorphic features (large body size, robust jaws, generalist crushing morphology) that have been lost or modified in the more derived labrid subfamilies such as Cheilininae, Halichoerinae, and Scarinae.
The clade comprises roughly 90 described species. Bodianus is the most species-rich genus (~44 species), distributed in tropical and warm-temperate seas worldwide. Choerodon (~25 species, tuskfishes) is centered in the Indo-West Pacific. Lachnolaimus contains a single species, the Atlantic hogfish L. maximus. Semicossyphus (2 species) includes the California sheephead S. pulcher and the Asian sheephead S. reticulatus. Clepticus (2 species, Creole wrasses) are mid-water planktivores, and Decodon contains a handful of deep-reef species.
Phylogenetic analyses have repeatedly recovered Bodianus as paraphyletic with respect to Semicossyphus and Clepticus (Santini, Sorenson, & Alfaro, 2016). Gomon (2006) recognized ten subgenera of Bodianus based on morphology, and Santini et al. (2016) produced the first multi-locus, time-calibrated phylogeny for the hogfishes, dating the origin of the Bodianus radiation to the Early Miocene (~20 Ma). Brownstein et al. (2025) embedded hypsigenyines in a broader analysis of reef-fish diversification near the Miocene–Pliocene boundary, finding that several reef-fish clades — including labrids — underwent rate accelerations coincident with the modern expansion of coral reefs.

title: Hypsigenyinae — Hogfishes, Tuskfishes, and Sheepheads
text:
Natural History
Hypsigenyines are durophagous (hard-prey) predators. The clade is dominated by benthic foragers that use robust canine teeth and powerful pharyngeal jaws to subdue mollusks, crustaceans, sea urchins, and brittlestars (Westneat & Alfaro, 2005). Bodianus species typically forage by lifting rocks, biting prey, and crushing armored items in the pharyngeal mill. Choerodon tuskfishes have taken this strategy further: multiple species use rocks as anvils to break open bivalve shells, one of the best-documented examples of tool use in any fish (Jones, Brown, & Gardner, 2011; Bernardi, 2012). The behavior involves grasping a clam, swimming to a favored anvil rock, and delivering alternating blows by rapidly rotating the body until the shell cracks. Pryor and Milton (2019) reviewed the evidence for tool use across teleosts and concluded that anvil use in Choerodon meets the strictest behavioral definitions of the term, with implications for our understanding of fish cognition.
The clade is also notable for its extraordinary depth range. While most labrid clades concentrate in the upper 30 m, hypsigenyines span from the intertidal (juvenile Semicossyphus pulcher in California tidepools) to deep mesophotic reefs and seamounts beyond 200 m (some Bodianus and Decodon species). This depth range exceeds that of any other labrid subfamily and provides a powerful natural experiment for testing how the ambient light environment shapes color evolution (Stieb et al., 2023).
Reproduction follows the standard labrid pattern of protogynous hermaphroditism with an initial-phase (IP) / terminal-phase (TP) life-history transition. Females mature first, may spawn as IP fish, and then change sex to become TP males that defend territories and engage in pair spawning (Warner & Swearer, 1991). The size and social conditions that trigger sex change vary widely across the clade and remain an active area of research (Kuwamura et al., 2002). Many Bodianus species also exhibit a striking ontogenetic shift in feeding ecology: juveniles serve as cleaner fish, removing ectoparasites from larger reef fishes before transitioning to the adult crushing niche (Cote, 2000, in Harborne & Tholan, 2016).

title: Hypsigenyinae — Hogfishes, Tuskfishes, and Sheepheads
text:
Visual Ecology
The visual ecology of hypsigenyines is shaped by two strong selective pressures: their broad depth range and their reliance on visually mediated social signals during IP/TP transitions. Stieb et al. (2023) analyzed long-wavelength-sensitive (LWS) opsin expression across reef fishes, including labrids, and found that species occupying deeper or more turbid habitats tend to downregulate red-sensitive opsins — a pattern consistent with the spectral shift toward blue-green light at depth. Hypsigenyines, with members spanning 0–200+ m, are an ideal group for testing this prediction at fine taxonomic resolution.
Gerlach et al. (2016) characterized visual pigments and fluorescence in pseudocheilinid wrasses, providing a methodological template for studying opsin expression and reflectance in their hypsigenyine relatives. Although direct opsin characterization for Bodianus and Choerodon remains limited, the broader labrid literature suggests that wrasses generally possess multiple cone opsins (SWS1, SWS2, RH2, LWS) supporting tetra- or pentachromatic vision, with the relative expression of these opsins tunable to local light environments (Stieb et al., 2023).
The cleaning ecology of juvenile Bodianus adds a second layer of visual-ecological interest. Cleaner fish and their clients communicate visually using stereotyped color patterns — typically a bold horizontal stripe on a contrasting background — that advertise cleaning services across species boundaries (Harborne & Tholan, 2016). The convergent evolution of similar livery in unrelated cleaner lineages (e.g., juvenile Bodianus, Labroides cleaner wrasses, and gobies) is strong evidence that cleaning patterns are shaped by client-fish perception rather than phylogenetic inheritance.

title: Hypsigenyinae — Hogfishes, Tuskfishes, and Sheepheads
text:
Color Pattern Diversity
Hypsigenyine coloration is diverse and often spectacular. Bodianus rufus (Spanish hogfish, Caribbean) displays a bold bicolor pattern: deep purple-blue anterior grading to bright yellow posterior. B. pulchellus (spotfin hogfish) shows vivid red-orange with white banding. B. diana and related Indo-Pacific species combine red bodies with white spots and dark blotches. The Atlantic hogfish Lachnolaimus maximus is famously plastic, capable of changing color and pattern over seconds to minutes to match reef substrates — a capability tied directly to the dermal photoreception system discussed below.
Semicossyphus pulcher (California sheephead) undergoes one of the most extreme color transformations in the family: juveniles are bright orange-red with a white lateral stripe flanked by black spots; females are uniform pink with a white chin; terminal-phase males have a black head and tail with a broad red midbody band and a white chin. Choerodon tuskfishes display a different aesthetic: many species are green, blue-green, or olive with complex facial markings, prominent blue or yellow patches around the eyes, and variable trunk banding. Clepticus (Creole wrasse) is uniformly purple-blue, consistent with its mid-water planktivorous niche, where countershading and a blue-shifted background spectrum favor monochromatic blue livery (Floeter et al., 2018).
Temperate hypsigenyines (Semicossyphus, some deep-water Bodianus) tend toward muted pinks, reds, and reddish-browns. This temperate–tropical color contrast within a single clade is unusual among reef fishes and offers another tractable comparative test of how habitat shapes color.

title: Hypsigenyinae — Hogfishes, Tuskfishes, and Sheepheads
text:
Sexual Dimorphism, Ontogeny, and Polymorphism
Hypsigenyines are protogynous hermaphrodites, and most species exhibit IP/TP color differences (Warner & Swearer, 1991; Kuwamura et al., 2002). The magnitude of dimorphism varies widely:

Semicossyphus pulcher: TP males (black/red/black tricolor) are unmistakably different from IPs (uniform pink females). This is one of the most extreme IP/TP transitions in Labridae.
Bodianus spp.: TP males tend to be more intensely colored, with bolder markings and brighter background hues. IP females are often similar in pattern but with muted colors. Differences are subtle in some species (e.g., B. rufus) and pronounced in others (e.g., B. axillaris).
Choerodon spp.: Dimorphism is variable. Some species (e.g., C. fasciatus) show striking facial markings in TP males; others are nearly monomorphic.
Lachnolaimus maximus: Adult color is highly labile in both sexes due to chromatophore-mediated rapid color change; “dimorphism” in the conventional fixed-pattern sense is therefore difficult to characterize (Schweikert et al., 2018).

In addition to IP/TP differences, juvenile Bodianus species typically display cleaning livery that is dramatically different from the adult pattern — usually a dark dorsum and pale ventrum bisected by a conspicuous lateral stripe. This pattern is functional (it advertises cleaning services to client fish) rather than diagnostic of species identity (Harborne & Tholan, 2016; Estienne et al., 2024).

title: Hypsigenyinae — Hogfishes, Tuskfishes, and Sheepheads
section: Deep Dive: Dermal Photoreception in Lachnolaimus maximus
text:
Deep Dive: Dermal Photoreception in Lachnolaimus maximus
The most exciting recent discovery in hypsigenyine visual ecology — and arguably in fish visual biology generally — comes from work on the Atlantic hogfish Lachnolaimus maximus. Hogfish are renowned for rapid color change: an individual can shift from pale white to mottled brown to bold red within seconds, matching the appearance of nearby substrate even when the fish cannot see its own body. How does the animal coordinate this color change without visual feedback from its own skin?
Schweikert et al. (2018) first characterized opsin expression in L. maximus skin using transcriptomics, finding that the short-wavelength-sensitive opsin SWS1 — normally associated with cone photoreceptors in the retina — is expressed in the dermis as well. This was the first hint that hogfish skin might be light-sensitive. Schweikert, Grace, and colleagues (2023) followed up with a direct test of this hypothesis using immunohistochemistry, electrophysiology, and behavioral assays. They demonstrated that SWS1 protein is localized to cells beneath the chromatophore layer, in a position perfectly suited to monitor the light that has passed through (and been filtered by) the overlying pigment cells. When chromatophores expand or contract, they alter the spectrum of light reaching the SWS1-expressing cells, providing a real-time readout of the fish’s own color state.
This system — which the authors describe as “skin vision” or chromatophore-coupled photoreception — represents a fundamentally new mode of sensory feedback in vertebrate color change. It is conceptually analogous to the dermal photoreception long known from cephalopods, but with a different molecular architecture and a clear evolutionary independence. Crucially, the hogfish system links visual ecology directly to color pattern evolution: rapid color change requires not only chromatophore machinery but also a sensory feedback loop, and SWS1 in the skin appears to be that loop.
Several questions remain open and are excellent targets for the comparative work this clade enables:

Is dermal SWS1 expression unique to Lachnolaimus, or is it more widespread in hypsigenyines? Several Bodianus species also show rapid color change (e.g., during cleaning interactions or aggressive displays). Testing skin opsin expression across the clade would reveal whether this is a single derived feature or an ancestral hypsigenyine trait.
Does the presence of dermal photoreception correlate with the magnitude of color-pattern lability across species? Species with rapid color change (Lachnolaimus, some Bodianus) would be predicted to show higher dermal opsin expression than fixed-pattern species (e.g., Semicossyphus pulcher TP males).
How does dermal photoreception interact with depth? SWS1 is tuned to UV/violet wavelengths that attenuate rapidly with depth; deep-dwelling hypsigenyines might show shifts toward longer-wavelength dermal opsins (RH2, LWS).

These hypotheses are not currently testable with pavo and a phylogeny alone, but they provide rich background context for interpreting any color-evolution patterns you recover in your analysis.

title: Hypsigenyinae — Hogfishes, Tuskfishes, and Sheepheads
text:
Data Quality Warnings






Data quality: what to watch for



IP/TP dimorphism — moderate to strong, depending on species. Hypsigenyines are protogynous hermaphrodites, and most species show IP/TP color differences. The dimorphism is typically less extreme than in Scarinae or Cirrhilabrini but is real and can bias analyses:

Semicossyphus pulcher: TP males (black/red/black) and IP females (uniform pink) are essentially different “color phenotypes.” Use TP males consistently.
Bodianus species: TP males tend to be more intensely colored. The difference is subtle in some species but pronounced in others. Be consistent within your dataset.
Choerodon: Variable dimorphism. Use TP males where identifiable.

Rule of thumb: Use TP male images when available. If you cannot determine sex from the image, use the most intensely colored adult available for each species.
Juvenile cleaning livery. Juvenile Bodianus with cleaning livery look dramatically different from adults — typically a dark dorsum / pale ventrum bisected by a lateral stripe. This bicolor pattern is a cleaning advertisement (Harborne & Tholan, 2016), not the species’ “real” color pattern for comparative purposes. Exclude cleaning-livery juveniles from your pavo analysis. They will cluster together in color space regardless of species identity, biasing your results toward false convergence.
How to recognize juvenile cleaners:

Small body size (typically < 5 cm).
Bold bicolor pattern: dark (black, brown, or deep blue) upper body and white or yellow lower body, often with a prominent horizontal stripe.
May be photographed near or on the body of a larger client fish.

Rapid color change in Lachnolaimus. Adult hogfish can change color within seconds. A single individual photographed in different contexts can appear pale white, mottled brown, or vivid red. Choose a representative “neutral” image (mid-tone, mottled) if multiple are available, and note in your methods that Lachnolaimus coloration is plastic.
Small sample size. With 38 species, your statistical power for PGLS and model-comparison analyses is limited. Consider:

Using simpler models (BM vs. OU rather than multi-regime OU).
Emphasizing effect sizes and confidence intervals rather than p-values alone.
Supplementing quantitative analysis with qualitative pattern descriptions and phylogenetic trait mapping.

Taxonomic instability in Bodianus. Bodianus is paraphyletic with respect to Semicossyphus and Clepticus (Santini et al., 2016). If you use a tree that pre-dates the Santini et al. (2016) analysis, branch lengths and topology may be inaccurate. Confirm your tree source.

title: Hypsigenyinae — Hogfishes, Tuskfishes, and Sheepheads
text:
Promising Questions for This Clade

Depth and Color — Hypsigenyinae has the broadest depth range of any student clade, spanning from the intertidal to beyond 200 m. This is arguably the single best group for testing the depth–color hypothesis (Stieb et al., 2023). Do deep-dwelling species show reduced red/orange chroma and increased blue-shifted reflectance?
Discrete Trait Mapping — Map the presence/absence of juvenile cleaning livery onto the phylogeny. How many times has juvenile cleaning behavior (and its associated coloration) evolved in Bodianus? Is the cleaning livery pattern phylogenetically conserved or labile? Compare to the cleaner-mimic literature on Aspidontus and Plagiotremus (Estienne et al., 2024).
Body Size and Color Complexity — With body sizes ranging from small cleaner Bodianus (~10 cm) to the massive California sheephead (~90 cm), test whether larger species display different color metrics. Semicossyphus pulcher offers a built-in ontogenetic test: juveniles, females, and TP males span the full size range of the species and show dramatic color differences.
Cross-Family Comparison — Compare hypsigenyine color diversity to other labrid clades (Scarinae, Cirrhilabrini, Halichoerinae) to test whether the crusher feeding guild constrains color evolution relative to planktivores or herbivores. The clade also includes one planktivore (Clepticus) that you can compare to its durophagous relatives as an internal contrast (Floeter et al., 2018).

title: Project Recipe Book — From Data to Discovery
text: You have pavo metrics and a phylogeny. This cookbook helps you turn those into a testable research question, the R code to test it, and the interpretation framework to explain what you found.

title: Project Recipe Book — From Data to Discovery
text:
Prerequisites






What you need before you start



Before diving into any recipe, make sure you have all of the following:

FishView bundle — your clade’s directory with *-mini-tree.tre, picked_species.txt, and (optionally) species_traits.csv
pavo metrics CSV — the output from your Demo 7 / Demo 8 pavo analysis, with one row per species and columns including species, m, A, Jc, Jt, m_dS, m_dL
R packages installed: pavo, ape, phytools, caper, nlme, rfishbase, ggplot2

Install all packages at once:
install.packages(c("pavo", "ape", "phytools", "caper", "nlme", "rfishbase", "ggplot2"))

title: Project Recipe Book — From Data to Discovery
text:
Setup: Preparing Your Data






Do this BEFORE running any recipe



Your FishView bundle’s tree may have tip labels with specimen codes (e.g., Chaetodon_auriga2, Chaetodon_kleinii_PW4831). All recipes expect clean Genus_species format. The best way to normalize is to use the course crosswalk — a curated table that maps every tree tip to its canonical species name. The crosswalk handles edge cases (subgenus reassignments, spelling fixes, CF-prefix tips) that a regex heuristic gets wrong on ~3% of tips.
Run this once to normalize your tree and save it:
library(ape)

# 1. Load your tree (auto-detect Newick vs NEXUS)
tree_file <- list.files("path/to/your/bundle",
                        pattern = "-mini-tree\\.tre$", full.names = TRUE)[1]
tree <- tryCatch(read.nexus(tree_file),
                 error = function(e) read.tree(tree_file))
if (inherits(tree, "multiPhylo")) tree <- tree[[1]]

# 2. Load the course crosswalk (tip_label -> canonical Genus_species)
crosswalk_url <- "https://michaelalfaro.github.io/eeb187-demos/recipes/data/crosswalk.csv"
crosswalk <- tryCatch(
  read.csv(crosswalk_url, stringsAsFactors = FALSE),
  error = function(e) {
    message("Could not fetch crosswalk from URL: ", e$message)
    message("Falling back to a regex heuristic. Some tips may be mangled.")
    NULL
  }
)

# 3. Normalize tip labels — crosswalk-first, regex fallback
to_binomial_heuristic <- function(tips) {
  vapply(tips, function(t) {
    parts <- strsplit(t, "_", fixed = TRUE)[[1]]
    if (length(parts) < 2) return(parts[1])
    genus   <- parts[1]
    species <- sub("^([a-z]+).*", "\\1", parts[2])
    paste(genus, species, sep = "_")
  }, character(1), USE.NAMES = FALSE)
}

if (!is.null(crosswalk)) {
  lookup <- setNames(crosswalk$tree_species, crosswalk$tip_label)
  resolved <- lookup[tree$tip.label]
  n_missing <- sum(is.na(resolved))
  if (n_missing > 0) {
    message(n_missing, " tips not found in crosswalk — applying heuristic for those.")
    fallback <- to_binomial_heuristic(tree$tip.label[is.na(resolved)])
    resolved[is.na(resolved)] <- fallback
  }
  tree$tip.label <- unname(resolved)
} else {
  tree$tip.label <- to_binomial_heuristic(tree$tip.label)
}

# 4. Drop duplicates (keeps first occurrence) — after normalization,
# two specimen-coded tips may collapse to the same species name
dups <- duplicated(tree$tip.label)
if (any(dups)) {
  cat("Dropping", sum(dups), "duplicate tips\n")
  tree <- drop.tip(tree, tree$tip.label[dups])
}

cat("Tree ready:", length(tree$tip.label), "species\n")






Why bother with the crosswalk?



On the full 517-tip dataset, the regex heuristic alone silently mangles 16 tips (3.1%) — including Paracentropyge_multifasciata → Centropyge_multifasciata, Halichoeres_papillionaceous → papilionaceus, Anampses_temmincki → temminckii, and CF-prefix tips like Sparisoma_cf_atomarium. Pomacanthidae is hit worst (7/56 tips = 12.5%). The crosswalk fixes all of these.


Your pavo metrics CSV should have a species column using the same Genus_species format. If you ran Demo 8, your output already has this. Make sure the species names in your CSV exactly match the normalized tree tip labels.
Quick check:
traits <- read.csv("path/to/your/pavo_metrics.csv")
overlap <- intersect(tree$tip.label, traits$species)
cat(length(overlap), "of", nrow(traits), "species matched to tree\n")

Every group must complete these two recipes

title: Recipe 26: Rate-Trait Correlation
text: Do faster-diversifying lineages in my family have different color patterns?

title: Recipe 26: Rate-Trait Correlation
text: Do faster-diversifying lineages in my family have different color patterns?

title: Recipe 26: Rate-Trait Correlation
text:
This Is an Instance Of…






Rate-phenotype correlation



This analysis tests whether species that belong to fast-diversifying lineages differ systematically in their color patterns from species in slow-diversifying lineages. It bridges two domains of macroevolutionary analysis: diversification rate estimation (how fast lineages generate new species) and phenotypic evolution (how color patterns vary across the tree). A significant relationship would suggest that color and speciation are linked — either because color divergence promotes reproductive isolation and thus speciation, or because the same ecological factors that drive speciation also reshape color patterns.

title: Recipe 26: Rate-Trait Correlation
section: Why This Matters for Your Clade
text:
Why This Matters for Your Clade
The central question of your project is how color pattern diversity arose. If faster-diversifying lineages have systematically more complex (or simpler, or different) color patterns, that tells you something fundamental about the relationship between color and speciation in your family. It moves your poster beyond describing color variation to explaining it in the context of species diversification.






Clade-specific tips




Pomacanthidae (angelfishes): The species-rich Centropyge may show different color metrics than less diverse genera. If fast-diversifying Centropyge have lower transition density (simpler patterns), this suggests diversification favors streamlined phenotypes.
Cirrhilabrini (fairy wrasses): If the species-rich Cirrhilabrus have higher color complexity AND higher diversification rates, this is consistent with sexual selection driving both color elaboration and speciation.
Balistoidea (triggerfishes + filefishes): Monacanthidae have more species than Balistidae. Does this higher diversity correlate with different color patterns? The rate-trait correlation will tell you.
Scarinae (parrotfishes): If terminal-phase color complexity correlates with diversification rate, color display may play a role in reproductive isolation.

title: Recipe 26: Rate-Trait Correlation
text:
The Method
This recipe combines ClaDS1 tip-specific speciation rates (from Recipe 21) with pavo color metrics in a phylogenetic generalized least squares (PGLS) regression. PGLS accounts for the non-independence of species due to shared ancestry — essential because both speciation rates and color traits are phylogenetically structured.
The analysis proceeds in three steps. First, extract tip-specific speciation rates from your ClaDS1 results (you must have run Recipe 21 first). Second, merge these rates with your pavo color metrics. Third, use safe_pgls() from helpers.R to test whether log-transformed speciation rate predicts each color variable. We log-transform rates because speciation rates are typically right-skewed, and the log transformation improves the linearity of the relationship.
A significant positive slope means faster-diversifying lineages have higher values of that color metric. A significant negative slope means faster-diversifying lineages have lower values. No significance means diversification rate and color evolve independently.

title: Recipe 26: Rate-Trait Correlation
text:
How to Interpret Results








Result
Interpretation
What to say on your poster




Positive slope, p < 0.05
Faster-diversifying lineages have MORE complex/conspicuous color
“Species in rapidly diversifying lineages show higher color complexity, suggesting color may drive or accompany speciation in this family.”


Negative slope, p < 0.05
Faster-diversifying lineages have SIMPLER/less conspicuous color
“Faster diversification is associated with simpler color patterns, suggesting that rapid speciation in this family does not require color elaboration.”


p > 0.05
No detectable relationship
“Diversification rate and color pattern evolve independently — the tempo of speciation does not predict color complexity.”


Significant for some variables but not others
Color dimensions differ in their link to diversification
“The link between diversification and color is trait-specific: [variable X] correlates with speciation rate while [variable Y] does not.”









Common pitfalls




Correlation does not equal causation. Even a significant result does not tell you the direction of causality. Does color drive speciation (e.g., through reproductive isolation)? Or does rapid speciation drive color divergence (e.g., through character displacement)? Or does a third factor (ecology, habitat) drive both? State the correlation and discuss possible causal mechanisms, but do not claim causation.
You must have run Recipe 21 (ClaDS1) first. This recipe depends on tip-specific speciation rates from ClaDS. If you have not run ClaDS, go do that first.
Tip rates from ClaDS have uncertainty. The MAP estimates used here are point estimates from a posterior distribution. Ideally, you would propagate uncertainty by repeating the analysis across posterior samples, but for a course project the MAP estimates are sufficient.
PGLS corrects for phylogenetic non-independence. Do not use ordinary least squares (OLS) for this analysis — species are not independent data points. The safe_pgls() function handles this automatically.
Log-transforming rates is important. Speciation rates are right-skewed (most species have low rates, a few have high rates). Using raw rates can produce misleading regressions driven by a few fast-diversifying outliers. Always use log(rate).

title: Recipe 26: Rate-Trait Correlation
text:
The Code

# ── Recipe 26: Rate-Trait Correlation ─────────────────────────────
# DEPENDS ON: Recipe 21 (ClaDS1) — you must have tip rates ready.

source("https://michaelalfaro.github.io/eeb187-demos/recipes/code/helpers.R")   # loads ape, phytools, ggplot2, theme_poster

# ── 1. Load your tree and pavo data ───────────────────────────────
bundle   <- load_bundle("path/to/your-family-mini-bundle")
pavo_csv <- read.csv("path/to/your-pavo-metrics.csv",
                      stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

matched <- match_tree_data(bundle$tree, pavo_csv, species_col = "species")
tree    <- matched$tree
traits  <- matched$data

# ── 2. Load ClaDS1 tip rates from Recipe 21 ──────────────────────
# Option A: Load from CSV saved in Recipe 21
tip_rate_df <- read.csv("results/clads1-tip-rates.csv",
                         stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# Option B: Re-extract from saved ClaDS result (if CSV not available)
# clads1_res   <- readRDS("results/clads1-result.rds")
# maps         <- getMAPS_ClaDS(clads1_res, burn = 1/2, thin = 1)
# branch_rates <- maps[-(1:4)]
# n_tips       <- length(tree$tip.label)
# tip_edges    <- which(tree$edge[, 2] <= n_tips)
# tip_rates    <- branch_rates[tip_edges]
# names(tip_rates) <- tree$tip.label[tree$edge[tip_edges, 2]]
# tip_rate_df  <- data.frame(species = names(tip_rates),
#                             rate = tip_rates,
#                             stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# ── 3. Merge tip rates with pavo metrics ─────────────────────────
rate_df <- data.frame(
  species = tip_rate_df$species,
  speciation_rate = tip_rate_df$rate,
  log_rate = log(tip_rate_df$rate),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

merged <- merge(traits, rate_df, by = "species")
cat("Merged data:", nrow(merged), "species with both rates and pavo\n")

# ── 4. Match to tree ─────────────────────────────────────────────
matched2 <- match_tree_data(tree, merged, species_col = "species")
tree2    <- matched2$tree
dat2     <- matched2$data

# ── 5. PGLS: does speciation rate predict color complexity? ──────
# Start with transition density (m)
cat("\n── PGLS: m ~ log(speciation rate) ──────────────────────────\n")
model_m <- safe_pgls(m ~ log_rate, df = dat2, tree = tree2)

# ── 6. Scatter plot for transition density (m) ───────────────────
ggplot(dat2, aes(x = log_rate, y = m)) +
  geom_point(size = 4, alpha = 0.7, color = "#264653") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "#e76f51", linewidth = 1.2,
              se = TRUE) +
  labs(title = "Do faster-diversifying lineages have more complex color?",
       x = "log(Speciation rate) from ClaDS1",
       y = "Transition density (m)") +
  theme_poster

ggsave("results/recipe26-rate-vs-m.pdf", width = 8, height = 6)
cat("Saved: results/recipe26-rate-vs-m.pdf\n")

# ── 7. Run for all 6 pavo variables ──────────────────────────────
pavo_vars <- c("m", "A", "Jc", "Jt", "m_dS", "m_dL")

rate_trait_summary <- data.frame(
  Variable   = character(0),
  Slope      = numeric(0),
  SE         = numeric(0),
  t_value    = numeric(0),
  p_value    = numeric(0),
  Direction  = character(0),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

for (v in pavo_vars) {
  # Build formula dynamically
  frm <- as.formula(paste(v, "~ log_rate"))

  pgls_fit <- tryCatch(
    safe_pgls(frm, df = dat2, tree = tree2),
    error = function(e) {
      message(v, ": PGLS failed — ", e$message)
      NULL
    }
  )

  if (!is.null(pgls_fit)) {
    coefs <- summary(pgls_fit)$tTable
    sl    <- coefs["log_rate", "Value"]
    se    <- coefs["log_rate", "Std.Error"]
    tv    <- coefs["log_rate", "t-value"]
    pv    <- coefs["log_rate", "p-value"]

    direction <- "No relationship"
    if (pv < 0.05 && sl > 0) direction <- "Positive"
    if (pv < 0.05 && sl < 0) direction <- "Negative"

    rate_trait_summary <- rbind(rate_trait_summary, data.frame(
      Variable  = v,
      Slope     = round(sl, 4),
      SE        = round(se, 4),
      t_value   = round(tv, 3),
      p_value   = round(pv, 4),
      Direction = direction,
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    ))
  }
}

cat("\n── Rate-Trait Correlation Summary ──────────────────────────\n")
print(rate_trait_summary, row.names = FALSE)

# ── 8. Six-panel scatter plot ─────────────────────────────────────
library(gridExtra)

plot_list <- list()
for (v in pavo_vars) {
  p <- ggplot(dat2, aes(x = log_rate, y = .data[[v]])) +
    geom_point(size = 3, alpha = 0.6, color = "#264653") +
    geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "#e76f51",
                linewidth = 1, se = TRUE) +
    labs(title = v,
         x = "log(Speciation rate)",
         y = v) +
    theme_poster +
    theme(plot.title = element_text(size = 14))
  plot_list[[v]] <- p
}

pdf("results/recipe26-rate-trait-all.pdf", width = 14, height = 10)
grid.arrange(grobs = plot_list, ncol = 3)
dev.off()
cat("Saved: results/recipe26-rate-trait-all.pdf\n")

# ── 9. Highlight significant results ─────────────────────────────
sig_vars <- rate_trait_summary$Variable[rate_trait_summary$p_value < 0.05]
if (length(sig_vars) > 0) {
  cat("\nSignificant rate-trait correlations found for:",
      paste(sig_vars, collapse = ", "), "\n")
  cat("These color variables are associated with diversification rate.\n")
} else {
  cat("\nNo significant rate-trait correlations detected.\n")
  cat("Diversification rate and color appear to evolve independently.\n")
}

From the Literature

Rabosky, D. L., & Huang, H. (2016) — Developed a semiparametric test (STRAPP) for detecting associations between speciation rates and continuous traits on phylogenies. The method permutes trait values across rate regimes to build a null distribution, providing a robust test for rate-phenotype correlations. Systematic Biology, 65(2), 181–193. DOI


Maliet, O., Hartig, F., & Morlon, H. (2019) — Introduced the ClaDS models for estimating branch-specific diversification rates, which provide the tip rates used as the predictor variable in this recipe. Nature Ecology & Evolution, 3(7), 1086–1092. DOI

title: Recipe 20: Evolutionary Model Comparison
text: Is the macroevolutionary trajectory of color pattern in my family best described by neutral random drift along the tree (Brownian motion), by stabilizing selection pulling colors toward an optimum (Ornstein-Uhlenbeck), or by rapid early diversification that has since slowed down (Early Burst)?

title: Recipe 20: Evolutionary Model Comparison
text: Is the macroevolutionary trajectory of color pattern in my family best described by neutral random drift along the tree (Brownian motion), by stabilizing selection pulling colors toward an optimum (Ornstein-Uhlenbeck), or by rapid early diversification that has since slowed down (Early Burst)?

title: Recipe 20: Evolutionary Model Comparison
text:
This Is an Instance Of…






Evolutionary model fitting / model selection



This analysis fits competing mathematical models of trait evolution to your tree and data, then uses information-theoretic model selection (AIC) to determine which model the data support most strongly. The three models represent three fundamental macroevolutionary regimes. Brownian motion (BM) assumes color evolves as a random walk — each branch accumulates change at a constant rate with no directional pressure. Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) adds a “rubber band” that pulls trait values toward an adaptive optimum, mimicking stabilizing selection. Early Burst (EB) allows the rate of evolution to slow exponentially from root to tips, capturing the signature of an adaptive radiation that “used up” available niche space early. By comparing these three models with AIC, you are asking which evolutionary process best explains the pattern of color diversity you observe today.

title: Recipe 20: Evolutionary Model Comparison
section: Why This Matters for Your Clade
text:
Why This Matters for Your Clade
Model comparison translates qualitative statements about color evolution into testable hypotheses. If OU wins, you can claim there is a macroevolutionary constraint on color — something limits how far from a central color pattern species can stray. If EB wins, the story is one of explosive early diversification followed by stasis. If BM wins, neither constraint nor early-burst is detectable — color evolution looks like neutral drift along the tree. These results connect directly to the lecture on macroevolutionary drivers of color (Lec 18) and provide the most mechanistically explicit claim you can put on your poster.






Clade-specific tips




Pomacanthidae (angelfishes): OU is biologically plausible if angelfishes share a common “angelfish gestalt” — banded juveniles and bright-rimmed adults — that constrains color variation around a family-level optimum. Watch for whether the OU alpha parameter is large (strong pull) or small (weak pull near BM).
Cirrhilabrini (fairy wrasses): The extreme color diversification in Cirrhilabrus might favor EB if the tribe’s color burst happened early in its history. But if ongoing sexual selection is continually generating new male color morphs, BM or OU might fit better.
Hypsigenyinae (hogfishes and allies): With ~38 species you are right at the boundary where OU and EB become difficult to distinguish from BM. Treat your results as suggestive and emphasize the direction of effects rather than statistical significance alone.
Scarinae (parrotfishes): Complex phase-based color changes (initial phase, terminal phase) mean your pavo metrics describe whichever phase was photographed. If your images mix phases, OU might appear to win simply because within-phase variation is constrained — check your image metadata.

title: Recipe 20: Evolutionary Model Comparison
text:
The Method
You use fitContinuous() from the geiger package to fit all three models to the same trait data. Rather than running the analysis on six pavo variables separately (which multiplies the number of comparisons and makes interpretation difficult), the recipe uses PC1 of the six pavo variables as the focal trait. PC1 captures the main axis of color pattern variation across your species and gives you a single, biologically meaningful number per species that summarizes their overall color pattern position.
The AIC (Akaike Information Criterion) from each model is then compared. A model with lower AIC is preferred. The delta-AIC (difference from the best model) quantifies how much worse each alternative is: delta-AIC < 2 means the models are essentially indistinguishable; delta-AIC 2–7 means moderate support for the better model; delta-AIC > 10 means strong support.
This analysis requires the geiger package. If it is not installed, run install.packages("geiger") once before sourcing helpers.

title: Recipe 20: Evolutionary Model Comparison
text:
How to Interpret Results








Best model
Interpretation
What to say on your poster




BM
Color evolves neutrally — no directional or stabilizing selection detected
“Color pattern evolution is consistent with neutral Brownian motion drift; we find no evidence for stabilizing selection or early-burst dynamics.”


OU
Stabilizing selection constrains color toward an optimum — limited color space explored
“The Ornstein-Uhlenbeck model best fits color evolution, suggesting a macroevolutionary constraint that pulls color patterns toward a family-level optimum.”


EB
Rapid early diversification, slowing recently — main color axes established early
“Color pattern diversity shows an early-burst signature: rapid early diversification has slowed toward the present, consistent with early niche filling.”


deltaAIC < 2 between top models
Models are statistically indistinguishable
“AIC values differ by less than 2 units between models, indicating we cannot distinguish among evolutionary regimes with our current sample.”









Power warning: small sample sizes make model comparison unreliable



With fewer than 40 species, OU and EB are often statistically indistinguishable from BM. The OU alpha and EB rate-decay parameters are difficult to estimate precisely with small trees, and AIC comparisons may favor OU or EB simply due to chance variation in the data rather than genuine signal.
Hypsigenyinae (~38 spp) should interpret these results with particular caution. Even for larger clades (Balistoidea ~100 spp, Pomacanthidae ~90 spp), model comparison results should be viewed as suggestive rather than definitive without additional validation.
If OU wins, always report the alpha parameter: near-zero alpha is essentially BM and should be described as such. If EB wins, report the rate parameter (a): values near zero indicate the “early burst” is barely distinguishable from BM.








Common pitfalls




OU can overfit small trees. The OU model has one more parameter than BM, so it will almost always fit slightly better. AIC corrects for this, but with small n the correction may be insufficient. BM should be your prior expectation unless delta-AIC strongly favors OU.
Do not run model comparison on each pavo variable separately and then count “wins.” This inflates Type I error and is hard to interpret. Stick to PC1 as your focal variable.
Check that your tree is ultrametric before running fitContinuous(). Use ape::is.ultrametric(tree) and correct if needed.
PC1 direction is arbitrary. PCA can flip the sign of PC1 depending on your data. This does not affect the model comparison results (all three models are symmetric), but be careful when interpreting the OU optimum parameter (theta) — its sign means nothing on its own.

title: Recipe 20: Evolutionary Model Comparison
text:
The Code

# ── Recipe 20: Evolutionary Model Comparison ────────────────────
# Requires the geiger package.
# If not installed: install.packages("geiger")

source("https://michaelalfaro.github.io/eeb187-demos/recipes/code/helpers.R")   # loads ape, phytools, ggplot2, theme_poster
library(geiger)

# ── 1. Load your tree and pavo data ─────────────────────────────
bundle   <- load_bundle("path/to/your-family-mini-bundle")
pavo_csv <- read.csv("path/to/your-pavo-metrics.csv",
                      stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# ── 2. Match tree to data ───────────────────────────────────────
matched <- match_tree_data(bundle$tree, pavo_csv, species_col = "species")
tree    <- matched$tree
dat     <- matched$data

cat("Working with", length(tree$tip.label), "species\n")

# ── 3. Check ultrametric ─────────────────────────────────────────
if (!ape::is.ultrametric(tree)) {
  cat("Forcing ultrametric tree (small numerical correction)\n")
  tree <- phytools::force.ultrametric(tree, method = "extend")
}

# ── 4. Build PC1 as focal trait ──────────────────────────────────
pavo_vars <- c("m", "A", "Jc", "Jt", "m_dS", "m_dL")

# Remove species with any missing pavo values
complete  <- complete.cases(dat[, pavo_vars])
if (any(!complete)) {
  cat("Dropping", sum(!complete), "species with missing values\n")
}
dat_complete <- dat[complete, ]
tree         <- ape::drop.tip(tree,
                              setdiff(tree$tip.label, dat_complete$species))

trait_mat            <- dat_complete[, pavo_vars]
rownames(trait_mat)  <- dat_complete$species
trait_mat            <- trait_mat[tree$tip.label, ]   # align row order

# PCA on the 6 pavo variables (scaled)
pca   <- prcomp(trait_mat, scale. = TRUE)
pc1   <- setNames(pca$x[, 1], rownames(pca$x))

# Report variance explained by PC1
var_explained <- round(summary(pca)$importance[2, 1] * 100, 1)
cat("PC1 explains", var_explained, "% of color pattern variance\n")
cat("Loadings:\n")
print(round(pca$rotation[, 1], 3))

# ── 5. Fit three evolutionary models ────────────────────────────
cat("\nFitting models (this may take a moment) ...\n")

fit_bm <- fitContinuous(tree, pc1, model = "BM")
fit_ou <- fitContinuous(tree, pc1, model = "OU")
fit_eb <- fitContinuous(tree, pc1, model = "EB")

# ── 6. Build and print AIC comparison table ──────────────────────
aic_table <- data.frame(
  Model = c("Brownian Motion", "Ornstein-Uhlenbeck", "Early Burst"),
  AIC   = c(fit_bm$opt$aic, fit_ou$opt$aic, fit_eb$opt$aic),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
aic_table$deltaAIC <- round(aic_table$AIC - min(aic_table$AIC), 2)
aic_table$AIC      <- round(aic_table$AIC, 2)
aic_table          <- aic_table[order(aic_table$deltaAIC), ]

cat("\n── Model Comparison ──────────────────────────────────────────\n")
print(aic_table, row.names = FALSE)

best <- aic_table$Model[1]
cat("\nBest model:", best, "\n")
cat("  BM = neutral drift along the tree\n")
cat("  OU = stabilizing selection toward an optimum\n")
cat("  EB = rapid early diversification, slowing toward present\n")

# ── 7. Report key parameters for the best model ─────────────────
cat("\n── Best model parameters ──────────────────────────────────────\n")
if (best == "Brownian Motion") {
  cat("  sigsq (rate):", round(fit_bm$opt$sigsq, 4), "\n")
} else if (best == "Ornstein-Uhlenbeck") {
  cat("  sigsq (rate):", round(fit_ou$opt$sigsq, 4), "\n")
  cat("  alpha (pull strength):", round(fit_ou$opt$alpha, 4), "\n")
  cat("  theta (optimum):", round(fit_ou$opt$z0, 4), "\n")
  if (fit_ou$opt$alpha < 0.01) {
    cat("  NOTE: alpha is near zero --- OU is essentially equivalent to BM.\n")
  }
} else if (best == "Early Burst") {
  cat("  sigsq (initial rate):", round(fit_eb$opt$sigsq, 4), "\n")
  cat("  a (rate decay):", round(fit_eb$opt$a, 4), "\n")
  if (abs(fit_eb$opt$a) < 0.001) {
    cat("  NOTE: a is near zero --- EB is essentially equivalent to BM.\n")
  }
}

# ── 8. Warning for small sample sizes ───────────────────────────
n_spp <- length(tree$tip.label)
if (n_spp < 40) {
  cat("\n[WARNING] Only", n_spp, "species in analysis.\n")
  cat("  With < 40 species, OU and EB are often indistinguishable from BM.\n")
  cat("  Treat these results as suggestive, not definitive.\n")
}

# ── 9. Bar chart of deltaAIC ─────────────────────────────────────
aic_table$Model <- factor(aic_table$Model,
                          levels = c("Brownian Motion",
                                     "Ornstein-Uhlenbeck",
                                     "Early Burst"))

ggplot(aic_table, aes(x = Model, y = deltaAIC, fill = Model)) +
  geom_col(alpha = 0.85, width = 0.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 2, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "gray40", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.6, y = 2.3, label = "deltaAIC = 2 threshold",
           hjust = 0, size = 4, color = "gray40") +
  labs(
    title = "Evolutionary model comparison (color PC1)",
    x     = "",
    y     = expression(Delta * "AIC")
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(
    "Brownian Motion"    = "#4e9af1",
    "Ornstein-Uhlenbeck" = "#e76f51",
    "Early Burst"        = "#2a9d8f"
  )) +
  theme_poster +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

ggsave("results/recipe20-model-comparison.pdf", width = 7, height = 6)
cat("Saved: results/recipe20-model-comparison.pdf\n")

title: Recipe 20: Evolutionary Model Comparison
text:
From the Literature

Harmon, L. J., Losos, J. B., Davies, T. J., Gillespie, R. G., Gittleman, J. L., Jennings, W. B., … & Mooers, A. O. (2010) — Systematically evaluated whether early-burst body size and shape evolution is common in comparative datasets, fitting BM, OU, and EB models to hundreds of clades. Found that early burst is surprisingly rare and that OU is more commonly supported than expected under neutrality. The primary reference for the fitContinuous() model comparison framework. Evolution, 64(8), 2385–2396. DOI


Butler, M. A., & King, A. A. (2004) — Developed and formalized the OU model for comparative biology (the “Hansen model”), showing how multiple OU optima on a phylogeny can represent distinct selective regimes. Essential background for interpreting the OU result from fitContinuous(). American Naturalist, 164(6), 683–695. DOI


Cooper, N., Thomas, G. H., Venditti, C., Meade, A., & Freckleton, R. P. (2016) — Showed that standard single-optimum OU model tests are frequently overconfident in small comparative datasets, echoing the power warning in this recipe. Provides practical recommendations for interpreting model comparison results when sample sizes are modest. Methods in Ecology and Evolution, 7(6), 656–665. DOI

title: Recipe 21: ClaDS1 — Lineage-Specific Diversification Rates
text: Do diversification rates vary across lineages in my family, and which lineages are diversifying fastest?

title: Recipe 21: ClaDS1 — Lineage-Specific Diversification Rates
text: Do diversification rates vary across lineages in my family, and which lineages are diversifying fastest?

title: Recipe 21: ClaDS1 — Lineage-Specific Diversification Rates
text:
This Is an Instance Of…






Diversification rate heterogeneity



Most models of species diversification assume a single rate for the entire tree, but real clades rarely diversify at a constant pace. Some lineages explode with new species while others stagnate. ClaDS (Cladogenetic Diversification rate Shift) models allow the speciation rate to change at every single node in the tree, producing a branch-by-branch portrait of where diversification has been fast and where it has been slow. This is one of the most detailed views of diversification rate variation available in comparative biology.

title: Recipe 21: ClaDS1 — Lineage-Specific Diversification Rates
section: Why This Matters for Your Clade
text:
Why This Matters for Your Clade
Every reef fish family has lineages that seem to have generated species rapidly (think of the species-rich Cirrhilabrus within wrasses, or the Centropyge dwarfs within angelfishes) and lineages that have barely diversified at all. ClaDS1 lets you quantify this variation rather than relying on intuition from looking at tree shape. The branch-specific rates it produces can also feed into downstream analyses — for example, testing whether faster-diversifying lineages have different color patterns (see Recipe 26).






Clade-specific tips




Pomacanthidae (angelfishes): Expect the Centropyge radiation to show elevated tip rates relative to the larger-bodied genera. If alpha < 1, the whole family may show decelerating diversification consistent with early ecological opportunity.
Cirrhilabrini (fairy wrasses): The tribe’s species-rich genera (Cirrhilabrus, Paracheilinus) should stand out with high tip rates. Compare these to the rest of the Labridae if your tree includes outgroup context.
Balistoidea (triggerfishes + filefishes): The Monacanthidae (filefishes) have far more species than Balistidae. ClaDS will quantify whether this reflects genuinely higher speciation rates or just a longer time for accumulation.
Acanthuridae (surgeonfishes): A relatively species-poor family — ClaDS may reveal uniformly low rates, or a single burst in one subclade (e.g., Acanthurus).
Hypsigenyinae (hogfishes and allies): With ~38 species, your tree is small for ClaDS. Results will have wider uncertainty — report them honestly and note the sample size limitation.

title: Recipe 21: ClaDS1 — Lineage-Specific Diversification Rates
text:
The Method
ClaDS1 is a Bayesian model implemented in the RPANDA package. Unlike models that assume a few large rate shifts (like BAMM), ClaDS allows the speciation rate to change at every speciation event. Each daughter lineage inherits a modified rate from its parent, and the model estimates how rates shift across the entire tree.
ClaDS1 estimates four key quantities. The trend parameter (alpha) tells you whether rates systematically increase or decrease through time: alpha < 1 means rates decelerate (early burst of diversification), alpha = 1 means no trend, and alpha > 1 means acceleration. The stochasticity parameter (sigma) describes how much rates jump at each node. A global extinction rate (mu) applies across the whole tree (ClaDS1 assumes constant extinction, unlike ClaDS2 which allows variable extinction). Finally, branch-specific speciation rates (lambda_i) give you a rate for every single branch in the phylogeny.
The model is fit using MCMC sampling, which means it takes significant computation time (20–60 minutes for a typical reef fish family tree of 60–100 tips). You must check that the MCMC chains have converged before interpreting results.






Runtime warning



ClaDS1 takes 20–60 minutes for a tree with 60–100 tips. Start this analysis early in your workflow and work on other recipes while it runs. Save the results object so you do not need to re-run it.

title: Recipe 21: ClaDS1 — Lineage-Specific Diversification Rates
text:
How to Interpret Results








Parameter
Value
Meaning




alpha < 1
Rates decelerate
Early burst of diversification — speciation was faster in the past


alpha ~ 1
No trend
Speciation rates have been roughly constant through time


alpha > 1
Rates accelerate
Late burst — speciation is speeding up toward the present


sigma near 0
Low stochasticity
Rates change little between parent and daughter — relatively homogeneous


sigma large
High stochasticity
Rates jump substantially at each node — heterogeneous diversification


mu near 0
Low extinction
Few lineages have gone extinct relative to the number that originated









Common pitfalls




MCMC convergence: Always check the trace plots with plot_ClaDS_chains(). If the chains have not converged (traces still trending, not mixing around a stable value), increase the number of iterations. Do not interpret results from unconverged chains.
Small trees (<30 tips): ClaDS may lack statistical power to reliably estimate branch-specific rates. Report your results cautiously and note the sample size limitation.
RPANDA installation: If RPANDA fails to install, try: install.packages('RPANDA', repos = 'https://cran.r-project.org'). On some systems you may also need to install system dependencies for C++ compilation.
Runtime: ClaDS1 takes 20–60 minutes for ~60–100 tips. Start it running and work on other recipes while you wait. Save the output with saveRDS() so you never have to re-run it.

title: Recipe 21: ClaDS1 — Lineage-Specific Diversification Rates
text:
The Code

# ── Recipe 21: ClaDS1 — Lineage-Specific Diversification Rates ──
# Requires the RPANDA package.
# If not installed: install.packages("RPANDA")

source("https://michaelalfaro.github.io/eeb187-demos/recipes/code/helpers.R")   # loads ape, phytools, ggplot2, theme_poster
library(RPANDA)

# ── 1. Load your tree and data ────────────────────────────────────
bundle   <- load_bundle("path/to/your-family-mini-bundle")
pavo_csv <- read.csv("path/to/your-pavo-metrics.csv",
                      stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# ── 2. Match tree to data ─────────────────────────────────────────
matched <- match_tree_data(bundle$tree, pavo_csv, species_col = "species")
tree    <- matched$tree
dat     <- matched$data

cat("Working with", length(tree$tip.label), "species\n")

# ── 3. Check that tree is ultrametric ─────────────────────────────
if (!ape::is.ultrametric(tree)) {
  cat("Forcing ultrametric tree (small numerical correction)\n")
  tree <- phytools::force.ultrametric(tree, method = "extend")
}

# ── 4. Run ClaDS1 ────────────────────────────────────────────────
# ClaDS1: variable speciation, constant extinction
# This takes 20-60 minutes depending on tree size — be patient!
cat("Starting ClaDS1 MCMC — this will take 20-60 minutes...\n")
cat("Start time:", format(Sys.time()), "\n")

set.seed(42)   # for reproducibility (fit_ClaDS has no seed argument)

clads1_res <- fit_ClaDS(tree,
                         sample_fraction = 1,     # 1.0 = complete sampling
                         iterations = 5e6,        # 5 million MCMC steps
                         thin = 10000,
                         file_name = "my_clads1", # backup file (NULL to disable)
                         model_id = "ClaDS1",
                         nCPU = 1)

cat("Finished at:", format(Sys.time()), "\n")

# ── 5. Save the result so you never have to re-run ───────────────
saveRDS(clads1_res, "results/clads1-result.rds")
cat("Saved: results/clads1-result.rds\n")

# ── 6. Check MCMC convergence ─────────────────────────────────────
# ALWAYS inspect trace plots before interpreting results
pdf("results/recipe21-mcmc-traces.pdf", width = 10, height = 8)
plot_ClaDS_chains(clads1_res)
dev.off()
cat("Saved: results/recipe21-mcmc-traces.pdf\n")
cat("CHECK: Do the traces look stationary (flat, mixing well)?\n")
cat("If they are still trending, increase iterations and re-run.\n")

# ── 7. Extract MAP (maximum a posteriori) estimates ───────────────
# burn = 1/2 discards first half of MCMC as burn-in
maps <- getMAPS_ClaDS(clads1_res, burn = 1/2, thin = 1)

# maps contains: [1] sigma, [2] alpha, [3] epsilon, [4] lambda_0,
# then branch-specific rates in edge-matrix order
sigma_map    <- maps[1]   # rate stochasticity
alpha_map    <- maps[2]   # rate trend (alpha < 1 = deceleration)
mu_map       <- maps[3]   # turnover rate (epsilon)
lambda0_map  <- maps[4]   # initial speciation rate
branch_rates <- maps[-(1:4)]   # per-branch speciation rates

cat("\n── ClaDS1 Results ──────────────────────────────────────────\n")
cat("Trend (alpha):", round(alpha_map, 3),
    ifelse(alpha_map < 1, "(rates decelerating)",
    ifelse(alpha_map > 1, "(rates accelerating)", "(no trend)")), "\n")
cat("Stochasticity (sigma):", round(sigma_map, 4), "\n")
cat("Extinction (mu):", round(mu_map, 4), "\n")
cat("Rate range:", round(range(branch_rates), 4), "\n")

# ── 8. Plot rate tree — branches colored by speciation rate ───────
pdf("results/recipe21-rate-tree.pdf", width = 10, height = 10)
plot_ClaDS_phylo(tree, branch_rates, lwd = 2.5, log = TRUE)
title("ClaDS1: branch-specific speciation rates")
dev.off()
cat("Saved: results/recipe21-rate-tree.pdf\n")

# ── 9. Extract tip-specific rates ────────────────────────────────
# Branch rates are in tree$edge order. Tip branches are those where
# the child node (edge[,2]) is a tip (numbered 1..N).
n_tips     <- length(tree$tip.label)
tip_edges  <- which(tree$edge[, 2] <= n_tips)
tip_rates  <- branch_rates[tip_edges]
names(tip_rates) <- tree$tip.label[tree$edge[tip_edges, 2]]

# Sort by rate for inspection
tip_rate_df <- data.frame(
  species = names(tip_rates),
  rate    = tip_rates,
  genus   = sub("_.*", "", names(tip_rates)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
tip_rate_df <- tip_rate_df[order(tip_rate_df$rate, decreasing = TRUE), ]
tip_rate_df$species <- factor(tip_rate_df$species,
                               levels = tip_rate_df$species)

cat("\n── Top 10 fastest-diversifying tips ────────────────────────\n")
print(head(tip_rate_df, 10), row.names = FALSE)

cat("\n── Bottom 5 slowest-diversifying tips ──────────────────────\n")
print(tail(tip_rate_df, 5), row.names = FALSE)

# ── 10. Bar chart of tip rates colored by genus ──────────────────
ggplot(tip_rate_df, aes(x = species, y = rate, fill = genus)) +
  geom_col(alpha = 0.85) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(title = "ClaDS1 tip-specific speciation rates",
       x = "", y = "Speciation rate (events / Myr)") +
  theme_poster +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 7, face = "italic"),
        legend.position = "right")

ggsave("results/recipe21-tip-rates-barplot.pdf", width = 10, height = 12)
cat("Saved: results/recipe21-tip-rates-barplot.pdf\n")

# ── 11. Save tip rates for use in Recipe 26 ──────────────────────
write.csv(tip_rate_df, "results/clads1-tip-rates.csv", row.names = FALSE)
cat("Saved: results/clads1-tip-rates.csv\n")
cat("You can use these tip rates in Recipe 26 (Rate-Trait Correlation).\n")

From the Literature

Maliet, O., Hartig, F., & Morlon, H. (2019) — Introduced the ClaDS family of models, which allow speciation rates to shift at every cladogenesis event rather than at a few discrete breakpoints. Applied to birds, they showed that diversification rates are remarkably heterogeneous even within small clades, and that the “many small shifts” model outperforms “few large shifts” approaches. Nature Ecology & Evolution, 3(7), 1086–1092. DOI

The package provides the R implementation of ClaDS used in this recipe. Methods in Ecology and Evolution, 7(5), 589–597. DOI

title: Recipe 4: Cross-Family Comparison
text: Is the tempo of color pattern evolution in my family similar to what has been documented in butterflyfishes and surgeonfishes, or does my family follow a different evolutionary script?

title: Recipe 4: Cross-Family Comparison
text: Is the tempo of color pattern evolution in my family similar to what has been documented in butterflyfishes and surgeonfishes, or does my family follow a different evolutionary script?

title: Recipe 4: Cross-Family Comparison
text:
This Is an Instance Of…






Cross-system comparative inference



Science advances by replication. When a pattern is documented in one system (e.g., “butterflyfish color evolves fast, with K well below 1”), the natural next question is whether the same pattern holds in other lineages. Cross-family comparison tests the generality of an evolutionary finding. If the same low K values appear in triggerfishes, angelfishes, and wrasses, the pattern may reflect something fundamental about reef fish color evolution. If some families show high K while others show low K, the contrast tells you that lineage-specific biology — not a universal rule — is driving color evolution.

title: Recipe 4: Cross-Family Comparison
section: Why This Matters for Your Clade
text:
Why This Matters for Your Clade
Your family is one of seven groups contributing to the EEB 187 class dataset. By comparing your K values to published benchmarks and to the other groups’ results, you are participating in a genuine comparative analysis of reef fish color evolution across multiple families. This comparison is what makes the class project more than a single-family case study — it is a test of whether the “color evolves fast on reefs” narrative is universal or clade-specific.






A note for labrid subgroups (Scarinae, Cirrhilabrini, Hypsigenyinae, Halichoerine)



Michael will pool the pavo data from all four labrid subgroups into a single mega-analysis on the full labrid phylogeny. Your group’s within-clade K values are the building blocks for that combined analysis. You will see your data in two contexts: (1) your own mini-tree analysis from Recipe 1, and (2) the combined labrid dataset that spans all four subgroups. If K differs between your subgroup and the full labrid analysis, that tells you something about how clade boundaries affect signal estimates.

title: Recipe 4: Cross-Family Comparison
text:
The Method
This recipe is conceptually simple: compute your family’s K values (from Recipe 1), place them next to published benchmark values, and ask whether the numbers are in the same regime. There is no formal statistical test for “are two K values from different families significantly different” — the comparison is qualitative, based on whether your family’s values fall in the same order-of-magnitude zone as the benchmarks.
The benchmark table below compiles published K values from two reef fish families that have been analyzed with the same pavo adjacency statistics or closely related methods. Chaetodontidae (butterflyfishes) is the primary benchmark because Alfaro et al. (2019) used the same six pavo variables and the same phyloPCA framework. Acanthuridae (surgeonfishes) provides a second benchmark from Frederich et al., though their analysis used binary motif presence/absence rather than continuous adjacency statistics, so the comparison is at the level of “order of magnitude of signal strength” rather than direct numerical equivalence.
The visual output is a grouped bar plot: your family’s K values side-by-side with the benchmarks, one cluster per pavo variable (or PC axis). The Brownian motion expectation (K = 1) is marked as a reference line. The viewer can immediately see whether all families cluster below 1 (fast evolution across the board), whether your family diverges, or whether the pattern is variable-specific.

title: Recipe 4: Cross-Family Comparison
text:
How to Interpret Results








Comparison
Interpretation
What to say on your poster




Your K values cluster with Chaetodontidae (~0.1–0.2)
Color evolves fast across reef fish families
“The low phylogenetic signal found in butterflyfishes generalizes to [family], suggesting a shared pattern of rapid color evolution on coral reefs.”


Your K values are much higher (> 0.5)
Your family conserves color more than butterflyfishes
“[Family] retains ancestral color patterns more strongly than butterflyfishes, possibly due to [stabilizing selection / developmental constraint / smaller effective population sizes].”


Mixed pattern: some variables match, others diverge
Mosaic evolution
“Color evolution in [family] is mosaic: [variable] evolves as fast as in butterflyfishes, but [other variable] is more conserved, suggesting different evolutionary pressures act on different aspects of pattern.”


All seven EEB 187 families show K < 0.3
General pattern across reef fish
“Across all seven families surveyed, color patterns show weak phylogenetic signal, consistent with a general pattern of rapid color evolution in reef fishes.”









Common pitfalls




Apples and oranges. The Alfaro et al. (2019) benchmarks used the same pavo adjacency framework as your analysis. The Frederich et al. benchmarks used binary motif coding. Always state the method alongside the number when making comparisons.
Tree size matters. K estimates from a 15-species tree are much noisier than from a 60-species tree. If your family has far fewer tips than the benchmark study, a K difference might reflect sample size rather than biology.
Do not claim statistical significance for qualitative comparisons. You are not running a formal test of “K_family1 vs. K_family2.” You are making a visual, order-of-magnitude comparison. Use language like “similar to,” “in the same regime as,” or “notably higher than” — not “significantly different from.”

title: Recipe 4: Cross-Family Comparison
text:
The Code

# ── Recipe 4: Cross-Family Comparison ──────────────────────────
source("https://michaelalfaro.github.io/eeb187-demos/recipes/code/helpers.R")   # loads ape, phytools, ggplot2, theme_poster

# ── 1. Load your bundle and pavo data ──────────────────────────
bundle   <- load_bundle("path/to/your-family-mini-bundle")
pavo_csv <- read.csv("path/to/your-pavo-metrics.csv",
                      stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# ── 2. Match tree to data ──────────────────────────────────────
matched <- match_tree_data(bundle$tree, pavo_csv, species_col = "species")
tree    <- matched$tree
dat     <- matched$data

# ── 3. Compute your K values ──────────────────────────────────
K_table <- format_K_table(dat, tree,
                          vars = c("m", "A", "Jc", "Jt", "m_dS", "m_dL"))

# ── 4. Full benchmark table ───────────────────────────────────
# All published K values from reef fish color pattern studies
# using pavo or comparable methods.
benchmarks <- data.frame(
  family   = c(rep("Chaetodontidae", 6), "Acanthuridae"),
  variable = c("PC1", "PC2", "PC3", "m (complexity)", "A (aspect ratio)",
               "m_dS (chrom. boundary)", "multivariate (binary motifs)"),
  K        = c(0.122, 0.192, 0.136, 0.15, 1.30, 0.20, 0.10),
  method   = c(rep("pavo + phyloPCA", 3), rep("pavo per-variable", 3),
               "binary motif coding"),
  source   = c(rep("Alfaro et al. 2019", 6), "Frederich et al."),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

cat("── Published benchmarks ──\n")
print(benchmarks)

# ── 5. Build comparison data frame ─────────────────────────────
your_family <- gsub("-mini-bundle", "",
                    basename(normalizePath("path/to/your-family-mini-bundle")))
my_K <- data.frame(
  family   = your_family,
  variable = K_table$Variable,
  K        = K_table$K,
  method   = "pavo per-variable",
  source   = "Your analysis",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

compare_df <- rbind(benchmarks, my_K)

# ── 6. Grouped comparison plot ─────────────────────────────────
# Subset to per-variable comparisons (matching measurement scales)
per_var <- compare_df[compare_df$method == "pavo per-variable", ]

p <- ggplot(per_var,
            aes(x = reorder(variable, K), y = K, fill = family)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.75), width = 0.65) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dotted", color = "grey40") +
  coord_flip(ylim = c(0, max(per_var$K, 1) * 1.15)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Chaetodontidae" = "#d4a853",
                                setNames("#0a66c2", your_family))) +
  labs(
    title    = paste("Cross-family comparison:", your_family,
                     "vs. Chaetodontidae"),
    subtitle = "Dotted line = K = 1 (Brownian motion expectation)",
    x = NULL, y = "Blomberg's K", fill = "Family"
  ) +
  theme_poster

print(p)

# ── 7. Save poster-quality PDF ─────────────────────────────────
ggsave("results/recipe4-cross-family.pdf", p, width = 12, height = 8)
cat("Saved: results/recipe4-cross-family.pdf\n")

# ── 8. Summary interpretation ─────────────────────────────────
cat("\n── Quick comparison ──\n")
cat("Chaetodontidae average K (per-variable):",
    round(mean(benchmarks$K[benchmarks$method == "pavo per-variable"]), 3), "\n")
cat("Your family average K:", round(mean(K_table$K), 3), "\n")

ratio <- mean(K_table$K) / mean(benchmarks$K[benchmarks$method == "pavo per-variable"])
if (ratio < 0.5) {
  cat("Your family's signal is much WEAKER than butterflyfishes.\n")
} else if (ratio < 1.5) {
  cat("Your family's signal is in the SAME REGIME as butterflyfishes.\n")
} else {
  cat("Your family's signal is STRONGER than butterflyfishes.\n")
}

title: Recipe 4: Cross-Family Comparison
text:
From the Literature

Alfaro, M. E., Karan, E. A., Schwartz, S. T., & Shultz, A. J. (2019) — The primary benchmark for this recipe: analyzed 95 butterflyfish species with the same pavo adjacency statistics, finding K ~ 0.12–0.19 across phyloPCA axes and documenting that most color diversity is not predicted by ecology. Integrative and Comparative Biology, 59(3), 604–615. DOI


Blomberg, S. P., Garland, T., Jr., & Ives, A. R. (2003) — Provided the K statistic and the conceptual framework for comparing phylogenetic signal across traits and across clades. Evolution, 57(4), 717–745. DOI


Revell, L. J. (2012) — The phytools package that implements phylosig() for computing K and lambda, enabling consistent methodology across the family comparisons in this recipe. Methods in Ecology and Evolution, 3(2), 217–223. DOI

title: Recipe 1: Phylogenetic Signal
text: Do closely related species in my family share similar color patterns, or has color evolved so fast that the phylogeny tells us nothing about who looks like whom?

title: Recipe 1: Phylogenetic Signal
text: Do closely related species in my family share similar color patterns, or has color evolved so fast that the phylogeny tells us nothing about who looks like whom?

title: Recipe 1: Phylogenetic Signal
text:
This Is an Instance Of…






Phylogenetic signal testing



This is the most fundamental question in phylogenetic comparative biology: does the evolutionary tree predict trait similarity? Phylogenetic signal quantifies whether close relatives resemble each other more than expected by chance. It is the starting point for nearly every comparative analysis because it determines how you should interpret all downstream results — if signal is strong, you must account for shared ancestry in every statistical test; if signal is weak, the trait is evolving fast enough that history alone does not constrain it.

title: Recipe 1: Phylogenetic Signal
section: Why This Matters for Your Clade
text:
Why This Matters for Your Clade
Color patterns serve many functions on a reef — camouflage, species recognition, mate attraction, warning signals. Whether these functions produce conserved or rapidly evolving patterns depends on the ecological and social pressures acting on each lineage. Testing for phylogenetic signal tells you whether your family’s color diversity is the product of deep evolutionary inertia or recent, lineage-specific innovation.






Clade-specific tips




Pomacanthidae (angelfishes): Dramatic ontogenetic color changes (juveniles look completely different from adults) might weaken signal if your images mix life stages. Make sure all exemplars are adults.
Cirrhilabrini (fairy wrasses): Strong sexual dichromatism means male display colors may have different signal than female cryptic colors. If your bundle has mostly males, your K values describe male display evolution.
Balistoidea (triggerfishes + filefishes): This group spans two families with very different body plans. Expect signal to differ depending on whether the triggerfishes or filefishes dominate your species sample.

title: Recipe 1: Phylogenetic Signal
text:
The Method
We use two complementary statistics. Blomberg’s K compares the observed variance of a trait on the tree to the variance expected if the trait evolved by Brownian motion (random drift along branches). K = 1 means the trait matches Brownian motion exactly. K > 1 means close relatives are more similar than drift predicts — the trait is conserved. K < 1 means close relatives are less similar than drift predicts — the trait is evolving faster than expected, perhaps driven by natural or sexual selection, or by convergent evolution across distantly related lineages. A permutation test (shuffling trait values across tips 1,000 times) produces a p-value testing whether K is significantly different from zero (no signal at all).
Pagel’s lambda asks the same question from a different angle. It transforms the tree’s internal branch lengths until the tree best fits the observed trait data. Lambda = 1 means the original tree is optimal — full phylogenetic signal. Lambda = 0 means a “star phylogeny” (all species equally unrelated) fits just as well — no signal. Values between 0 and 1 indicate partial signal. A likelihood-ratio test produces the p-value.
Using both metrics is standard practice because they are sensitive to different aspects of the data. K is more influenced by tip-level similarity (it detects whether sister species resemble each other), while lambda is more sensitive to deep phylogenetic structure (it detects whether major clades differ). If both are significant, you can confidently claim phylogenetic signal. If they disagree, that disagreement is itself informative about where on the tree the signal lives.

title: Recipe 1: Phylogenetic Signal
text:
How to Interpret Results








Result
Interpretation
What to say on your poster




K < 1, p < 0.05
Significant signal, but weaker than Brownian motion
“Color evolves faster than expected under drift — selection or convergence is reshaping patterns across the tree.”


K ~ 1, p < 0.05
Signal consistent with Brownian motion
“Color diversity is consistent with neutral evolutionary drift along the phylogeny.”


K > 1, p < 0.05
Signal stronger than Brownian motion
“Color is phylogenetically conserved — close relatives look strikingly similar, more so than drift alone would produce.”


p > 0.05
No significant signal detected
“We lack statistical evidence for phylogenetic signal, either because it is genuinely absent or because our sample is too small to detect it.”









Common pitfalls




“Non-significant does not mean no signal.” With fewer than ~20 species, K tests have low statistical power. A non-significant result might simply mean you cannot distinguish signal from noise with your sample size — not that signal is absent. Always report the K value alongside the p-value, and note your sample size.
“K < 1 does NOT mean color doesn’t matter.” K < 1 means color is less phylogenetically structured than Brownian motion predicts. That is often the most interesting result — it implies selection, adaptation, or convergence is actively driving color evolution beyond what shared ancestry would produce.
Do not compare raw K values across variables without context. K for transition density (m) and K for aspect ratio (A) are on different scales because the traits themselves have different distributions. Compare the pattern (significant vs. not) rather than the raw numbers.

title: Recipe 1: Phylogenetic Signal
text:
The Code

# ── Recipe 1: Phylogenetic Signal ───────────────────────────────
source("https://michaelalfaro.github.io/eeb187-demos/recipes/code/helpers.R")   # loads ape, phytools, ggplot2, theme_poster

# ── 1. Load your bundle and pavo data ───────────────────────────
bundle   <- load_bundle("path/to/your-family-mini-bundle")
pavo_csv <- read.csv("path/to/your-pavo-metrics.csv",
                      stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# ── 2. Match tree to data ───────────────────────────────────────
matched <- match_tree_data(bundle$tree, pavo_csv, species_col = "species")
tree    <- matched$tree
dat     <- matched$data

cat("Working with", length(tree$tip.label), "species\n")

# ── 3. Blomberg's K for all 6 pavo variables ───────────────────
K_table <- format_K_table(dat, tree,
                          vars = c("m", "A", "Jc", "Jt", "m_dS", "m_dL"))
print(K_table)

# ── 4. Pagel's lambda for comparison ───────────────────────────
lambda_results <- data.frame(
  Variable = character(0),
  lambda   = numeric(0),
  p_value  = numeric(0),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

for (v in c("m", "A", "Jc", "Jt", "m_dS", "m_dL")) {
  x <- setNames(dat[[v]], dat$species)
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]
  # Prune tree to species with data for this variable
  overlap  <- intersect(names(x), tree$tip.label)
  t_pruned <- ape::drop.tip(tree, setdiff(tree$tip.label, overlap))
  x <- x[t_pruned$tip.label]

  res <- phytools::phylosig(t_pruned, x, method = "lambda", test = TRUE)
  lambda_results <- rbind(lambda_results, data.frame(
    Variable = v,
    lambda   = round(res$lambda, 3),
    p_value  = round(res$P, 4),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  ))
}
print(lambda_results)

# ── 5. Run a quick PCA to get PC1 for the contMap ──────────────
pavo_vars <- c("m", "A", "Jc", "Jt", "m_dS", "m_dL")
trait_mat <- dat[, pavo_vars]
rownames(trait_mat) <- dat$species

# Remove any rows with NA before PCA
complete <- complete.cases(trait_mat)
trait_mat <- trait_mat[complete, ]
tree_pca  <- ape::drop.tip(tree, setdiff(tree$tip.label,
                                          rownames(trait_mat)))
trait_mat <- trait_mat[tree_pca$tip.label, ]

pc <- prcomp(trait_mat, scale. = TRUE)
pc1 <- setNames(pc$x[, "PC1"], rownames(pc$x))

# ── 6. contMap: paint PC1 onto the tree (fan layout) ───────────
cm <- phytools::contMap(tree_pca, pc1, plot = FALSE)

# On-screen plot
plot(cm, type = "fan", fsize = 0.5, lwd = 3,
     legend = 0.7 * max(nodeHeights(tree_pca)))
title("PC1 of color pattern mapped on phylogeny")

# ── 7. Save a poster-quality PDF ───────────────────────────────
pdf("results/recipe1-contmap-pc1.pdf", width = 10, height = 10)
plot(cm, type = "fan", fsize = 0.5, lwd = 3,
     legend = 0.7 * max(nodeHeights(tree_pca)))
title("PC1 of color pattern mapped on phylogeny")
dev.off()
cat("Saved: results/recipe1-contmap-pc1.pdf\n")

# ── 8. Print a combined summary table ──────────────────────────
summary_table <- merge(K_table, lambda_results, by = "Variable",
                       suffixes = c("_K", "_lambda"))
print(summary_table)
