text:
From the Literature

Blomberg, S. P., Garland, T., Jr., & Ives, A. R. (2003) — Introduced the K statistic and permutation test for phylogenetic signal, showing that behavioral traits tend to be more evolutionarily labile than morphological ones. Evolution, 57(4), 717–745. DOI


Pagel, M. (1999) — Developed the lambda transformation for estimating the degree to which shared evolutionary history explains trait similarity among species. Nature, 401(6756), 877–884. DOI


Munkemuller, T., Lavergne, S., Bzeznik, B., Dray, S., Jombart, T., Schiffers, K., & Thuiller, W. (2012) — Compared the performance of K, lambda, and other phylogenetic signal indices across simulated trees, providing practical guidance on when each metric is most reliable. Methods in Ecology and Evolution, 3(4), 743–756. DOI

title: Recipe 2: Rates of Evolution
text: How fast is color pattern evolving in my family compared to other reef fish families — and what does that speed tell us about the forces shaping color diversity?

title: Recipe 2: Rates of Evolution
text: How fast is color pattern evolving in my family compared to other reef fish families — and what does that speed tell us about the forces shaping color diversity?

title: Recipe 2: Rates of Evolution
text:
This Is an Instance Of…






Evolutionary rate inference



Comparing observed rates of trait evolution to theoretical expectations and to published benchmarks is a core task in macroevolution. Brownian motion provides the null model: traits drifting at a constant rate along the tree. When K is much less than 1, the trait is evolving faster than drift alone would produce, pointing to directional selection, adaptive radiation, or convergent evolution. By placing your family’s K values next to published values from other reef fish families, you can ask whether your clade’s color evolution is typical or exceptional.

title: Recipe 2: Rates of Evolution
section: Why This Matters for Your Clade
text:
Why This Matters for Your Clade
Reef fish families differ enormously in how quickly their color patterns evolve. Butterflyfishes (Chaetodontidae) show very weak phylogenetic signal — color changes rapidly, with distantly related species converging on similar patterns. If your family shows similarly low K values, the same ecological forces (mimicry, habitat matching, rapid speciation) may be at work. If your family shows much higher K, something is constraining color evolution — perhaps strong stabilizing selection or developmental limits on pattern variation.






Clade-specific tips




Acanthuridae (surgeonfishes): Your family was analyzed by Frederich et al. using binary pattern traits. Compare your pavo-based K values to their results for a methods comparison (binary motif coding vs. continuous adjacency statistics).
Scarinae (parrotfishes): Parrotfish undergo dramatic color changes between initial and terminal phase. If your bundle uses terminal-phase males, your K values describe the rate of evolution of the most sexually selected color state.
Halichoerine (Coris-allies): With ~140 tips, this is the largest group. Larger trees generally give tighter K estimates, so your comparisons to published benchmarks are on firmer statistical ground.

title: Recipe 2: Rates of Evolution
text:
The Method
This recipe builds directly on Recipe 1. You already have K values for each pavo variable. The new step is to place those values in context by comparing them to published benchmarks — K values from the same pavo variables measured on other reef fish families.
The key benchmark comes from Alfaro et al. (2019), who measured the same six pavo adjacency statistics on Chaetodontidae (butterflyfishes) and reported per-variable K values from a phyloPCA. Their PC1 K was 0.122, PC2 K was 0.192, and PC3 K was 0.136 — all far below 1, indicating that butterflyfish color patterns evolve much faster than Brownian motion predicts. For Acanthuridae, Frederich et al. reported a multivariate K of approximately 0.10 using binary pattern coding, which is consistent with the butterflyfish story of fast color evolution.
The comparison is qualitative, not a formal statistical test. You are asking: does my family’s K sit in the same low-signal zone as butterflyfishes, or does it diverge? A bar plot with your K values next to the published benchmarks makes this comparison visual and immediate. If your K values cluster near the benchmarks, your family follows the same “fast color evolution” narrative. If they are notably higher, your family may be under different evolutionary pressures that conserve color patterns.

title: Recipe 2: Rates of Evolution
text:
How to Interpret Results








Your K vs. benchmarks
Interpretation
What to say on your poster




Your K similar to Chaetodontidae (~0.1–0.2)
Your family’s color evolves at a similar fast rate
“Color pattern evolution in [family] follows the fast-evolution pattern seen in butterflyfishes, consistent with rapid adaptation or convergence.”


Your K much lower than benchmarks (< 0.1)
Even faster evolution than butterflyfishes
“Color in [family] evolves exceptionally fast — even less phylogenetically structured than the already-labile butterflyfish patterns.”


Your K much higher than benchmarks (> 0.5)
Slower evolution, more phylogenetically conserved
“Unlike butterflyfishes, [family] retains ancestral color patterns — close relatives look similar, suggesting stabilizing selection or developmental constraints.”


K varies widely across pavo variables
Different aspects of color evolve at different rates
“Color evolution in [family] is mosaic: some pattern features (e.g., aspect ratio) are conserved while others (e.g., complexity) evolve rapidly.”









Common pitfalls




Your K and the published K are not on identical scales unless measured the same way. Alfaro et al. (2019) used the same pavo adjacency statistics and phyloPCA, so the comparison is appropriate for PC-level K. Frederich et al. used binary motif presence/absence and a multivariate K, which is a different estimand. Note this distinction on your poster.
Sample size affects K. A family with 15 species will produce noisier K estimates than one with 60 species. The comparison is most informative if your species count is in the same ballpark as the benchmark studies.
Do not over-interpret small differences. K = 0.15 vs. K = 0.12 is not a meaningful difference. Focus on order-of-magnitude contrasts (K ~ 0.1 vs. K ~ 0.8).

title: Recipe 2: Rates of Evolution
text:
The Code

# ── Recipe 2: Rates of Evolution ────────────────────────────────
source("https://michaelalfaro.github.io/eeb187-demos/recipes/code/helpers.R")   # loads ape, phytools, ggplot2, theme_poster

# ── 1. Load your bundle and pavo data ───────────────────────────
bundle   <- load_bundle("path/to/your-family-mini-bundle")
pavo_csv <- read.csv("path/to/your-pavo-metrics.csv",
                      stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# ── 2. Match tree to data ───────────────────────────────────────
matched <- match_tree_data(bundle$tree, pavo_csv, species_col = "species")
tree    <- matched$tree
dat     <- matched$data

# ── 3. Compute K for all 6 pavo variables ──────────────────────
K_table <- format_K_table(dat, tree,
                          vars = c("m", "A", "Jc", "Jt", "m_dS", "m_dL"))

# ── 4. Build the benchmark data frame ──────────────────────────
# Published K values from Alfaro et al. 2019 (Chaetodontidae, pavo)
# and Frederich et al. (Acanthuridae, binary motifs — multivariate K)
benchmarks <- data.frame(
  family   = c("Chaetodontidae", "Chaetodontidae", "Chaetodontidae",
               "Acanthuridae"),
  variable = c("PC1", "PC2", "PC3", "multivariate"),
  K        = c(0.122, 0.192, 0.136, 0.10),
  source   = c(rep("Alfaro et al. 2019", 3), "Frederich et al."),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

# ── 5. Combine your results with benchmarks ─────────────────────
your_family <- gsub("-mini-bundle", "",
                    basename(normalizePath("path/to/your-family-mini-bundle")))
my_K <- data.frame(
  family   = your_family,
  variable = K_table$Variable,
  K        = K_table$K,
  source   = "Your analysis",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

compare_df <- rbind(benchmarks, my_K)
compare_df$label <- paste(compare_df$family, compare_df$variable, sep = " — ")

# ── 6. Bar plot: your K vs. published benchmarks ───────────────
p <- ggplot(compare_df,
            aes(x = reorder(label, K), y = K, fill = source)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.7) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dotted", color = "grey40") +
  coord_flip(ylim = c(0, max(compare_df$K, 1) * 1.15)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Alfaro et al. 2019" = "#d4a853",
                                "Frederich et al."   = "#a0c4e8",
                                "Your analysis"      = "#0a66c2")) +
  labs(
    title    = paste("Blomberg's K:", your_family, "vs. published benchmarks"),
    subtitle = "Dotted line = K = 1 (Brownian motion expectation)",
    x = NULL, y = "Blomberg's K", fill = "Source"
  ) +
  theme_poster

print(p)

# ── 7. Save poster-quality PDF ──────────────────────────────────
ggsave("results/recipe2-K-comparison.pdf", p, width = 12, height = 8)
cat("Saved: results/recipe2-K-comparison.pdf\n")

# ── 8. Print interpretation text ────────────────────────────────
cat("\n── Interpretation ──\n")
avg_K <- mean(K_table$K, na.rm = TRUE)
if (avg_K < 0.2) {
  cat("Your family's average K (", round(avg_K, 3), ") is in the same\n",
      "low-signal zone as Chaetodontidae. Color evolves fast.\n")
} else if (avg_K < 0.5) {
  cat("Your family's average K (", round(avg_K, 3), ") shows moderate\n",
      "signal — more conserved than butterflyfishes but still below BM.\n")
} else {
  cat("Your family's average K (", round(avg_K, 3), ") is notably higher\n",
      "than Chaetodontidae. Color patterns are phylogenetically conserved.\n")
}

title: Recipe 2: Rates of Evolution
text:
From the Literature

Alfaro, M. E., Karan, E. A., Schwartz, S. T., & Shultz, A. J. (2019) — Quantified color pattern geometry in butterflyfishes using pavo adjacency statistics and found weak phylogenetic signal (K ~ 0.12–0.19), indicating rapid, convergent color evolution. Integrative and Comparative Biology, 59(3), 604–615. DOI


Blomberg, S. P., Garland, T., Jr., & Ives, A. R. (2003) — Established the K statistic framework and showed that morphological traits typically have higher K than behavioral traits across vertebrates, providing the theoretical baseline for rate comparisons. Evolution, 57(4), 717–745. DOI


Harmon, L. J., Losos, J. B., Davies, T. J., Gillespie, R. G., Gittleman, J. L., Jennings, W. B., … & Mooers, A. O. (2010) — Found that early bursts of morphological evolution are rare across animal clades, suggesting that most trait diversification accumulates gradually rather than in ancient adaptive radiations. Evolution, 64(8), 2385–2396. DOI

title: Recipe 23: Continuous Ancestral State Reconstruction
text: What color pattern did the ancestor of my family likely have, and how have traits changed along the phylogeny?

title: Recipe 23: Continuous Ancestral State Reconstruction
text: What color pattern did the ancestor of my family likely have, and how have traits changed along the phylogeny?

title: Recipe 23: Continuous Ancestral State Reconstruction
text:
This Is an Instance Of…






Ancestral state estimation for continuous traits



Ancestral state reconstruction (ASR) uses the observed trait values at the tips of a phylogeny and a model of evolution (here, Brownian motion) to estimate the most likely trait values at internal nodes — including the root. This tells you what the ancestor probably looked like and identifies where on the tree the largest changes occurred. For continuous traits like pavo color metrics, maximum likelihood ASR produces point estimates with 95% confidence intervals at every internal node, letting you quantify uncertainty about ancestral phenotypes.

title: Recipe 23: Continuous Ancestral State Reconstruction
section: Why This Matters for Your Clade
text:
Why This Matters for Your Clade
Every poster tells a story about how color diversity arose. Ancestral state reconstruction lets you anchor that story at the root: “The ancestor of my family likely had [low/moderate/high] color complexity, and derived lineages evolved [toward/away from] that ancestral condition.” It also identifies which branches on the tree experienced the largest evolutionary changes, pointing you toward the lineages where color evolution was most dramatic.






Clade-specific tips




Pomacanthidae (angelfishes): Was the ancestor drab or colorful? If the root reconstruction is moderate and derived genera diverge in both directions, you have evidence for bidirectional evolution from a generalized ancestral pattern.
Cirrhilabrini (fairy wrasses): If the root value for color metrics like Jc (color adjacency) is low but tip values span a wide range, the ancestor was likely relatively plain and the spectacular male display colors are derived.
Balistoidea (triggerfishes + filefishes): Reconstruct the MRCA of each family separately — did triggerfishes and filefishes diverge from a similar ancestral color pattern, or were they already different at the split?
Scarinae (parrotfishes): The root value may reflect a more cryptic initial-phase-like pattern if early diverging species are less colorful, with terminal-phase brilliance evolving later.

title: Recipe 23: Continuous Ancestral State Reconstruction
text:
The Method
We use phytools::fastAnc() to perform maximum likelihood ancestral state reconstruction under Brownian motion. This function estimates the trait value at every internal node that maximizes the likelihood of observing the tip data, given the tree topology and branch lengths. When called with CI = TRUE, it also returns 95% confidence intervals for each node estimate.
The root node estimate is the single most informative result — it tells you what the common ancestor of your entire family probably looked like for each color variable. But the internal node estimates are also valuable: by comparing a node’s value to its descendants’ values, you can identify where on the tree the biggest evolutionary shifts happened.
We complement the numerical estimates with contMap() visualizations, which paint the tree with a continuous color gradient showing how each trait changes from root to tips. The combination of numerical estimates (with CIs) and visual maps gives you both the precision to make quantitative claims and the visual impact needed for a poster.

title: Recipe 23: Continuous Ancestral State Reconstruction
text:
How to Interpret Results








Pattern
Interpretation
What to say on your poster




Root value near center of tip range
Ancestor was intermediate; derived lineages diverged in both directions
“The ancestral color pattern was moderate, and descendent lineages evolved both increased and decreased complexity.”


Root value at one extreme
Ancestor was at one end of the spectrum; evolution has been predominantly directional
“The ancestor had [low/high] color complexity, and evolution has been predominantly toward [higher/lower] values.”


Narrow CI at root
Confident reconstruction
“We can reconstruct the ancestral condition with high confidence.”


Wide CI at root
Uncertain reconstruction
“The ancestral state is uncertain, reflecting the lability of color evolution in this family.”


Large jumps at specific nodes
Major evolutionary shifts at particular branches
“The largest color shifts occurred at the base of [clade X], suggesting a key transition in color strategy.”









Common pitfalls




ASR assumes Brownian motion by default. If your Recipe 20/22 results show that OU or another model fits better, the BM-based reconstruction may be biased. For OU-favored traits, consider that reconstructions near the root are pulled toward the OU optimum and may be overconfident.
Wide confidence intervals are the norm, not the exception. Deep nodes (near the root) accumulate uncertainty from both sides of the tree. A wide CI does not mean the analysis failed — it means the trait is genuinely uncertain at that point, which is itself informative.
Do not over-interpret small differences between nodes. If two internal nodes differ by 0.05 in transition density (m) but both have CIs spanning 0.3 units, that difference is not meaningful. Focus on large, CI-non-overlapping shifts.
Tip values drive everything. If your pavo data has errors at the tips, those errors propagate into the ancestral estimates. Double-check any species whose reconstructed value seems anomalous.

title: Recipe 23: Continuous Ancestral State Reconstruction
text:
The Code

# ── Recipe 23: Continuous Ancestral State Reconstruction ──────────
source("https://michaelalfaro.github.io/eeb187-demos/recipes/code/helpers.R")   # loads ape, phytools, ggplot2, theme_poster

# ── 1. Load your tree and pavo data ───────────────────────────────
bundle   <- load_bundle("path/to/your-family-mini-bundle")
pavo_csv <- read.csv("path/to/your-pavo-metrics.csv",
                      stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# ── 2. Match tree to data ─────────────────────────────────────────
matched <- match_tree_data(bundle$tree, pavo_csv, species_col = "species")
tree    <- matched$tree
dat     <- matched$data

cat("Working with", length(tree$tip.label), "species\n")

# ── 3. Check ultrametric ──────────────────────────────────────────
if (!ape::is.ultrametric(tree)) {
  cat("Forcing ultrametric tree (small numerical correction)\n")
  tree <- phytools::force.ultrametric(tree, method = "extend")
}

# ── 4. Ancestral state reconstruction for transition density (m) ──
trait_vec <- setNames(dat$m, dat$species)
trait_vec <- trait_vec[tree$tip.label]   # align to tree order

asr <- fastAnc(tree, trait_vec, CI = TRUE)

# Root estimate
cat("\n── Root Ancestral State ────────────────────────────────────\n")
cat("Estimated root value (m):", round(asr$ace[1], 3), "\n")
cat("95% CI:", round(asr$CI95[1, ], 3), "\n")
cat("Observed tip range:", round(range(trait_vec), 3), "\n")

# ── 5. Ancestral values at genus-level MRCAs ─────────────────────
# Get all genera in the tree
genera <- unique(sub("_.*", "", tree$tip.label))
n_tips <- length(tree$tip.label)

mrca_table <- data.frame(
  Genus        = character(0),
  N_species    = integer(0),
  MRCA_node    = integer(0),
  Ancestral_m  = numeric(0),
  CI_lower     = numeric(0),
  CI_upper     = numeric(0),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

for (g in genera) {
  genus_tips <- tree$tip.label[grepl(paste0("^", g, "_"), tree$tip.label)]
  if (length(genus_tips) < 2) next   # need at least 2 tips for an MRCA

  mrca_node <- getMRCA(tree, genus_tips)
  node_idx  <- mrca_node - n_tips   # internal node index for asr$ace

  mrca_table <- rbind(mrca_table, data.frame(
    Genus       = g,
    N_species   = length(genus_tips),
    MRCA_node   = mrca_node,
    Ancestral_m = round(asr$ace[node_idx], 3),
    CI_lower    = round(asr$CI95[node_idx, 1], 3),
    CI_upper    = round(asr$CI95[node_idx, 2], 3),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  ))
}

cat("\n── Genus-Level Ancestral Estimates ─────────────────────────\n")
print(mrca_table, row.names = FALSE)

# ── 6. contMap visualization with labeled key nodes ───────────────
cm <- contMap(tree, trait_vec, plot = FALSE)

pdf("results/recipe23-contmap-m.pdf", width = 10, height = 10)
plot(cm, type = "fan", fsize = 0.5, lwd = 3,
     legend = 0.7 * max(nodeHeights(tree)))
title("Ancestral reconstruction: transition density (m)")

# Label key nodes with their estimated values
for (i in seq_len(nrow(mrca_table))) {
  nodelabels(text = round(mrca_table$Ancestral_m[i], 2),
             node = mrca_table$MRCA_node[i],
             bg = "white", cex = 0.6, frame = "rect")
}
dev.off()
cat("Saved: results/recipe23-contmap-m.pdf\n")

# ── 7. Six-panel figure: one contMap per pavo variable ────────────
pavo_vars <- c("m", "A", "Jc", "Jt", "m_dS", "m_dL")

# Remove species with missing data in any variable
complete <- complete.cases(dat[, pavo_vars])
dat_sub  <- dat[complete, ]
tree_sub <- ape::drop.tip(tree, setdiff(tree$tip.label, dat_sub$species))

pdf("results/recipe23-contmaps-all-variables.pdf", width = 14, height = 10)
par(mfrow = c(2, 3))
for (v in pavo_vars) {
  x <- setNames(dat_sub[[v]], dat_sub$species)
  x <- x[tree_sub$tip.label]

  cm_v <- contMap(tree_sub, x, plot = FALSE)
  plot(cm_v, type = "fan", fsize = 0.35, lwd = 2,
       legend = 0.6 * max(nodeHeights(tree_sub)))
  title(v, cex.main = 1.2)
}
dev.off()
cat("Saved: results/recipe23-contmaps-all-variables.pdf\n")

# ── 8. Summary table: root values for all 6 variables ────────────
root_summary <- data.frame(
  Variable  = character(0),
  Root_est  = numeric(0),
  CI_lower  = numeric(0),
  CI_upper  = numeric(0),
  Tip_min   = numeric(0),
  Tip_max   = numeric(0),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

for (v in pavo_vars) {
  x <- setNames(dat_sub[[v]], dat_sub$species)
  x <- x[tree_sub$tip.label]
  asr_v <- fastAnc(tree_sub, x, CI = TRUE)

  root_summary <- rbind(root_summary, data.frame(
    Variable = v,
    Root_est = round(asr_v$ace[1], 3),
    CI_lower = round(asr_v$CI95[1, 1], 3),
    CI_upper = round(asr_v$CI95[1, 2], 3),
    Tip_min  = round(min(x), 3),
    Tip_max  = round(max(x), 3),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  ))
}

cat("\n── Root Ancestral Values for All 6 Color Variables ────────\n")
print(root_summary, row.names = FALSE)

title: Recipe 23: Continuous Ancestral State Reconstruction
text:
From the Literature

Revell, L. J. (2012) — Presented the phytools R package, which provides fastAnc() for fast maximum likelihood ancestral state estimation and contMap() for continuous trait mapping on phylogenies. Methods in Ecology and Evolution, 3(2), 217–223. DOI


Schluter, D., Price, T., Mooers, A. O., & Ludwig, D. (1997) — Developed the likelihood framework for reconstructing ancestral states of continuous characters, showing how ML estimates and confidence intervals can be derived from phylogenetic data. This paper provides the statistical foundation underlying fastAnc(). Evolution, 51(5), 1699–1711. DOI


Paradis, E., & Schliep, K. (2019) — ape 5.0: an environment for modern phylogenetics and evolutionary analyses in R. Provides the core tree manipulation and plotting functions used throughout this recipe. Bioinformatics, 35(3), 526–528. DOI

title: Recipe 13: Sexual System and Color Complexity
text: Do protogynous (female-to-male sex-changing) species have more complex color patterns than gonochoristic (fixed-sex) species, consistent with stronger sexual selection on terminal-phase males?

title: Recipe 13: Sexual System and Color Complexity
text: Do protogynous (female-to-male sex-changing) species have more complex color patterns than gonochoristic (fixed-sex) species, consistent with stronger sexual selection on terminal-phase males?
crumbs: Recipe 13: Sexual System and Color Complexity

title: Recipe 13: Sexual System and Color Complexity
text:
This Is an Instance Of…






Categorical PGLS — testing whether a discrete life history state predicts a continuous color metric



You are asking whether membership in a sexual-system category predicts color pattern complexity after accounting for phylogeny. This is a phylogenetic ANOVA (implemented as PGLS with a categorical predictor). The logic is: if sexual selection drives color complexity, then species in which males compete intensely for females — especially protogynous species where terminal-phase males achieve dominance after a life spent as female — should show higher pattern complexity than species where sex is fixed from birth and male-male competition is less extreme.
crumbs: Recipe 13: Sexual System and Color Complexity

title: Recipe 13: Sexual System and Color Complexity
section: Why This Matters for Your Clade
text:
Why This Matters for Your Clade
Protogyny is not randomly distributed across reef fishes. It is concentrated in groups where male body size or territory quality strongly determines reproductive success, exactly the conditions predicted by the size-advantage model of sex change. These are also groups with striking sexual dichromatism — initial-phase versus terminal-phase color differences that can be among the most dramatic on the reef.
Measuring pattern complexity (m, transition density) rather than just hue or brightness lets you ask a more nuanced question: is it just that terminal-phase males are brighter, or are they also more intricately patterned? Theory predicts both — sexual selection should favor conspicuous, complex signals that are hard for females to miss and hard for rival males to fake.






Clade-specific tips




Scarinae (parrotfishes): The IP/TP distinction is extreme — initial-phase fish can be female, primary male, or juveniles all sharing the same drab pattern; terminal-phase males are often brilliant blue-green or red. If your images are IP only or TP only, note this clearly and explain what your PGLS result actually tests.
Cirrhilabrini (fairy wrasses): Cirrhilabrus males in nuptial display coloration are among the most extravagantly patterned fish on the reef. The genus is largely protogynous. Expect this recipe to be highly relevant to your clade story.
Halichoerinae (hogfishes and kin): Some species have dramatic TP males (Lachnolaimus, Bodianus) while others are less dimorphic. Variation within this subfamily makes the between-species contrast especially interesting.
Hypsigenyinae (hogfishes, dragon wrasses): Includes species with extreme ontogenetic change (Novaculichthys) and others that are more subtly dichromatic. Mixed sexual systems within the subfamily make this a natural test case.
Pomacanthidae (angelfishes): Most angelfishes are gonochoristic, but a few genera (Centropyge, Genicanthus) include protogynous species. If your sample spans both, you can run this recipe directly.
Balistoidea (triggerfishes + filefishes): Most are gonochoristic. Expect the “protogynous” category to be very small or absent. If you have fewer than 5 species in one category, report the sample size prominently and interpret with caution.
crumbs: Recipe 13: Sexual System and Color Complexity

title: Recipe 13: Sexual System and Color Complexity
text:
The Method
You will pull the reproduction table from FishBase for your species, extract the ReproMode column describing the sexual system, and collapse it into a binary predictor: protogynous versus gonochoristic. Species coded as protandrous, simultaneous hermaphrodites, or with missing data are dropped for this analysis (you can note how many were excluded and why).






ReproMode, not Mode



In rfishbase ≤ 3.x the column was called Mode. From rfishbase 5.x onward it was renamed ReproMode. The recipe below uses the 5.x name.


You then run a PGLS with m (transition density, your measure of pattern complexity) as the response and sexual_system as the categorical predictor. PGLS accounts for the fact that related species are not statistically independent — without this correction, a single protogynous clade with high-m species could appear to “explain” variance that is really just phylogenetic clustering.
The boxplot visualizes the distribution of m values in each sexual-system category with individual points overlaid so reviewers can see your raw sample sizes directly.
crumbs: Recipe 13: Sexual System and Color Complexity

title: Recipe 13: Sexual System and Color Complexity
text:
How to Interpret Results








Result
Interpretation
What to say on your poster




Protogynous m > gonochoristic m, p < 0.05
Sex-changing species have significantly more complex patterns
“Pattern complexity is significantly higher in protogynous species, consistent with stronger sexual selection on terminal-phase males.”


No significant difference, p > 0.05
Sexual system does not predict pattern complexity in this clade
“We find no significant relationship between sexual system and pattern complexity, suggesting other factors (habitat, diet, crypsis) may dominate color evolution in our clade.”


Protogynous m < gonochoristic m
Unexpected — gonochoristic species are more complex
“Gonochoristic species show higher pattern complexity; this could reflect intense male-male competition in species with fixed sex, or it may reflect sampling bias if our protogynous sample is dominated by initial-phase images.”


Very small sample in one category (< 5)
Underpowered — result is suggestive only
“With only N = [X] protogynous species, statistical power is limited. Results are preliminary and should be interpreted cautiously.”









Common pitfalls




Image phase matters enormously. If your pavo metrics were computed from initial-phase images (drab, female-like coloration), you are measuring female pattern complexity, not the male display that sexual selection acts on. Check your image sources and describe clearly which phase your metrics represent.
FishBase ReproMode codes are not always clean. The column uses varied free-text entries. The cleaning regex in the code below catches the most common variants, but print table(merged$ReproMode) before cleaning and check for unusual entries (e.g., “hermaphrodite” without direction, “bidirectional sex change”).
Dropping species changes your phylogenetic context. When you filter to only protogynous + gonochoristic species, match_tree_data() will prune the tree accordingly. The pruned tree is what PGLS uses — this is correct, but note that your reported N after filtering may be substantially smaller than your total pavo dataset.
PGLS with small N is sensitive to outliers. Plot the residuals. If one or two species are driving the result, your interpretation should flag this.
crumbs: Recipe 13: Sexual System and Color Complexity

title: Recipe 13: Sexual System and Color Complexity
text:
The Code

# ── Recipe 13: Sexual System and Color Complexity ────────────────
source("https://michaelalfaro.github.io/eeb187-demos/recipes/code/helpers.R")   # loads ape, phytools, nlme, ggplot2, theme_poster

# ── 1. Load your pavo metrics and tree ──────────────────────────
traits <- read.csv("path/to/your-pavo-metrics.csv",
                   stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
tree   <- ape::read.tree("path/to/your-family-mini-tree.tre")

# ── 2. Pull sexual system data from FishBase ─────────────────────
# rfishbase 5.x uses `ReproMode` (older versions used `Mode`).
fb <- pull_fishbase(traits$species,
                    fields = list(reproduction = c("ReproMode")))

cat("Raw ReproMode values from FishBase:\n")
print(table(fb$ReproMode, useNA = "always"))

# ── 3. Merge and clean to binary predictor ──────────────────────
merged <- merge(traits, fb, by = "species")

merged$sexual_system <- ifelse(
  grepl("protogyn", merged$ReproMode, ignore.case = TRUE), "protogynous",
  ifelse(grepl("dioec|gonochor", merged$ReproMode, ignore.case = TRUE),
         "gonochoristic", NA))

cat("\nSpecies retained by sexual system:\n")
print(table(merged$sexual_system, useNA = "always"))

# Drop species with NA sexual system (protandrous, simultaneous, missing)
n_before <- nrow(merged)
merged   <- merged[!is.na(merged$sexual_system), ]
cat("\nDropped", n_before - nrow(merged), "species with NA or other sexual system\n")
cat("Final N:", nrow(merged), "\n")

# ── 4. Match tree to filtered data ──────────────────────────────
matched <- match_tree_data(tree, merged, species_col = "species")
cat("Species in PGLS:", nrow(matched$data), "\n")
cat("  Protogynous:", sum(matched$data$sexual_system == "protogynous"), "\n")
cat("  Gonochoristic:", sum(matched$data$sexual_system == "gonochoristic"), "\n")

# ── 5. PGLS: pattern complexity ~ sexual system ──────────────────
model <- safe_pgls(m ~ sexual_system, df = matched$data, tree = matched$tree)
print(summary(model))

# ── 6. Boxplot ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
ggplot(matched$data,
       aes(x = sexual_system, y = m, fill = sexual_system)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, outlier.shape = NA) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, size = 3, alpha = 0.6, color = "grey30") +
  labs(
    title = "Pattern complexity by sexual system",
    x     = "",
    y     = "Transition density (m)"
  ) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("gonochoristic" = "#264653",
                                "protogynous"   = "#e9c46a")) +
  theme_poster +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

ggsave("results/recipe13-sexual-system-boxplot.pdf",
       width = 6, height = 5)
cat("Saved: results/recipe13-sexual-system-boxplot.pdf\n")

# ── 7. Optional: repeat for other pavo variables ─────────────────
# You can swap m for A, Jc, Jt, m_dS, or m_dL depending on
# whether you have a specific hypothesis about hue vs. pattern.
# e.g.: safe_pgls(Jc ~ sexual_system, df = matched$data, tree = matched$tree)







A note for students using terminal-phase images only



If your image set is drawn primarily from terminal-phase (TP) male photographs — which is common in museum and online databases for wrasses and parrotfishes — then your m values already describe the complex, sexually-selected phenotype. In that case, this recipe tests whether the degree of TP complexity differs between species that achieve that TP status via sex change versus species where males are male from birth. That is still a scientifically interesting question, but it is subtly different from comparing sexes within a species. State clearly in your poster which phenotype your images represent.

title: Recipe 13: Sexual System and Color Complexity
text:
From the Literature

Hodge, J. R., Santini, F., & Wainwright, P. C. (2020) — Phylogenetic comparative analysis across 1,187 labrid species showing that colour dimorphism is most pronounced in coral-reef species, and that habitat-specific factors (water clarity, structural refuge) rather than sexual selection per se best explain the pattern. A key reference for any labrid group asking why sex-changers are so colorful. Proceedings of the Royal Society B, 287(1923), 20200167. DOI: 10.1098/rspb.2020.0167


Pla, S., Benvenuto, C., Capellini, I., & Piferrer, F. (2022) — The most comprehensive phylogenetic analysis of sexual system evolution in fishes to date (4,614 species, 50+ orders). Shows that gonochorism is ancestral and that protogyny is the most evolutionarily stable form of hermaphroditism. Essential background for framing why protogynous species are so disproportionately represented on reefs. Nature Communications, 13, 3029. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-022-30419-z


Marshall, N. J., Cortesi, F., de Busserolles, F., Siebeck, U. E., & Cheney, K. L. (2019) — Review of color and color vision in reef fishes covering how the clear-water reef environment shapes both signal production (color patterns) and signal detection (photoreceptors). Places the male display colors of wrasses and parrotfishes in the context of their visual ecology and what receivers actually perceive. Journal of Fish Biology, 95(1), 5–38. DOI: 10.1111/jfb.13849

title: Recipe 9: Vulnerability and Crypsis
text: Do species with higher ecological vulnerability display less conspicuous color patterns, suggesting selection for crypsis as a defense against predation?

title: Recipe 9: Vulnerability and Crypsis
text: Do species with higher ecological vulnerability display less conspicuous color patterns, suggesting selection for crypsis as a defense against predation?

title: Recipe 9: Vulnerability and Crypsis
text:
This Is an Instance Of…






Predation risk and anti-predator phenotype



This recipe tests a central prediction of visual ecology: species that are more vulnerable to predation should evolve less conspicuous (more cryptic) color patterns. Crypsis — matching the background to avoid detection — is one of the oldest and most widespread anti-predator strategies. If vulnerability imposes selection for crypsis, we should see a negative relationship between vulnerability and chromatic contrast across species.

title: Recipe 9: Vulnerability and Crypsis
section: Why This Matters for Your Clade
text:
Why This Matters for Your Clade
The FishBase Vulnerability index is a composite score (0–100) that integrates body size, growth rate, age at maturity, reproductive strategy, and natural mortality into a single estimate of intrinsic susceptibility to population decline. Species with high vulnerability are, in essence, “easy to drive to extinction” — they grow slowly, mature late, and reproduce sparingly. Such species may face strong selection to reduce conspicuousness because they cannot afford the mortality costs of being visually detectable to predators.
However, this prediction is not guaranteed. Vulnerability correlates strongly with body size (large fish score higher), and large fish may have different color strategies for reasons unrelated to predation risk (see Recipe 7). Testing vulnerability after size correction (Recipe 7b) is therefore highly recommended.






Clade-specific tips




Scarinae (parrotfishes): Bolbometopon muricatum (bumphead parrotfish) has one of the highest vulnerability scores on the reef and relatively subdued coloration as adults. Contrast with the smaller, lower-vulnerability Scarus species that show vivid terminal-phase colors.
Pomacanthidae (angelfishes): Many angelfish species have moderate vulnerability but are strikingly conspicuous. If the predicted negative relationship breaks down here, it may reflect strong sexual selection overriding predation-driven crypsis.
Any clade: Run this recipe AFTER Recipe 7b. Comparing the raw-vulnerability result with the size-corrected result will tell you whether vulnerability predicts color independently of the body-size component baked into the index.

title: Recipe 9: Vulnerability and Crypsis
text:
The Method
We use PGLS to regress chromatic contrast (m_dS) against the Vulnerability index from the FishBase estimate() table. No log transform is applied to Vulnerability because it is already a scaled composite index (0–100) with a roughly uniform distribution. PGLS controls for phylogeny, ensuring that the result is not driven by a single clade of large, dull-colored species inflating the correlation.
The key caveat: Vulnerability is not a direct measure of predation risk. It is a composite index that includes body size, growth rate, and reproductive parameters. This means a significant result could reflect the influence of any of these underlying components, not predation risk specifically. The strongest inference comes from comparing this result with Recipe 7 (body size alone) and Recipe 7b (size-corrected residuals). If vulnerability predicts color even after removing the body-size effect, the non-size components (growth, maturity, reproduction) are contributing something additional.

title: Recipe 9: Vulnerability and Crypsis
text:
How to Interpret Results








Result
Interpretation
What to say on your poster




Negative slope, p < 0.05
More vulnerable species are less conspicuous
“More vulnerable species in [family] have significantly lower chromatic contrast, consistent with selection for crypsis in species with limited capacity to compensate for predation mortality.”


Positive slope, p < 0.05
More vulnerable species are more conspicuous
“Surprisingly, more vulnerable species are more chromatically conspicuous. This could reflect aposematic signaling, or the confounding effect of body size on both vulnerability and color.”


p > 0.05
No significant relationship
“Vulnerability does not predict chromatic contrast in [family] after controlling for phylogeny, suggesting that predation-related life history does not strongly constrain color evolution in this clade.”









Common pitfalls




Vulnerability is not predation pressure. It measures intrinsic susceptibility, not actual predation rate. A species can have high vulnerability but low predation if it lives in a refuge habitat.
Collinearity with body size is the primary concern. Because Vulnerability is partly derived from body size, any correlation with color could simply reflect the size–color relationship from Recipe 7. Always compare with size-corrected results.
Direction of causation is ambiguous. Even if the correlation is real, we cannot determine whether vulnerability drives color evolution or whether color (and its ecological correlates) drives vulnerability.

title: Recipe 9: Vulnerability and Crypsis
text:
The Code

# ── Recipe 9: Vulnerability and Crypsis ───────────────────────
source("https://michaelalfaro.github.io/eeb187-demos/recipes/code/helpers.R")

# ── 1. Load your data ────────────────────────────────────────
traits <- read.csv("path/to/your/pavo_metrics.csv",
                    stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
bundle <- load_bundle("path/to/your-family-mini-bundle")

# ── 2. Pull vulnerability from FishBase ──────────────────────
fb <- pull_fishbase(traits$species,
                    fields = list(estimate = c("Vulnerability")))

# ── 3. Merge ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
merged <- merge(traits, fb, by = "species")
merged <- merged[!is.na(merged$Vulnerability), ]

cat("Species with vulnerability data:", nrow(merged), "\n")
cat("Vulnerability range:", round(range(merged$Vulnerability), 1), "\n")

# ── 4. Match to tree ────────────────────────────────────────
matched <- match_tree_data(bundle$tree, merged, species_col = "species")

# ── 5. PGLS: chromatic contrast vs vulnerability ─────────────
model <- safe_pgls(m_dS ~ Vulnerability, df = matched$data,
                    tree = matched$tree)

# ── 6. Scatter plot ─────────────────────────────────────────
library(ggplot2)

p <- ggplot(matched$data, aes(x = Vulnerability, y = m_dS)) +
  geom_point(size = 4, alpha = 0.7, color = "#264653") +
  { if (!is.null(model))
    geom_abline(intercept = coef(model)[1], slope = coef(model)[2],
                color = "#e76f51", linewidth = 1.2) } +
  labs(x = "FishBase Vulnerability Index",
       y = "Mean Chromatic Contrast (m_dS)",
       title = "Does vulnerability predict crypsis?",
       subtitle = "PGLS controlling for phylogeny") +
  theme_poster

print(p)
ggsave("results/recipe9-vulnerability-vs-crypsis.pdf", p,
       width = 10, height = 8)
cat("Saved: results/recipe9-vulnerability-vs-crypsis.pdf\n")

# ── 7. Optional: compare with size-corrected residuals ───────
# If you have already run Recipe 7b and have m_dS_resid:
# model_resid <- safe_pgls(m_dS_resid ~ Vulnerability,
#                            df = matched$data, tree = matched$tree)
# Compare the two p-values to assess whether the vulnerability
# signal survives size correction.

title: Recipe 9: Vulnerability and Crypsis
text:
From the Literature

Stevens, M. & Merilaita, S. (2009) — A comprehensive review of animal camouflage research, defining the major mechanisms (background matching, disruptive coloration, countershading) and the perceptual processes that make them effective. Provides the theoretical framework for predicting crypsis in vulnerable species. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B, 364(1516), 423–427. DOI


Endler, J. A. (1978) — Demonstrated that predation pressure directly shapes color pattern evolution in guppies, with populations under heavy predation evolving duller, less conspicuous patterns. The conceptual foundation for testing whether vulnerability predicts crypsis. Evolutionary Biology, 11, 319–364.

title: Recipe 12: Latitude Gradient
text: Does chromatic diversity decrease with latitude — are tropical species in my family more colorful than their temperate relatives?

title: Recipe 12: Latitude Gradient
text: Does chromatic diversity decrease with latitude — are tropical species in my family more colorful than their temperate relatives?

title: Recipe 12: Latitude Gradient
text:
This Is an Instance Of…






Latitudinal diversity gradient applied to phenotype



The latitudinal diversity gradient — the observation that species richness increases toward the tropics — is one of the most robust patterns in ecology. But does this gradient extend beyond species counts to phenotypic diversity? If tropical environments support more ecological niches, stronger sexual selection, or more diverse visual environments, tropical species might evolve more diverse color patterns. This recipe tests whether the best-documented macroecological pattern in biology applies to the visual phenotype of your clade.

title: Recipe 12: Latitude Gradient
section: Why This Matters for Your Clade
text:
Why This Matters for Your Clade
Most reef fish families have their center of diversity in the tropics, but many include species that extend into warm-temperate or even cool-temperate waters. If tropical environments promote color diversity through any of several mechanisms — more light for visual signaling, more diverse coral backgrounds, stronger biotic interactions, or greater sexual selection intensity — then species at lower latitudes should have higher chromatic diversity (Jc). The alternative is that phylogenetic history, not latitude per se, explains any geographic pattern in color: perhaps the colorful clades just happen to be tropical.
PGLS explicitly accounts for this phylogenetic alternative. A significant result after PGLS means latitude predicts color diversity beyond what shared ancestry alone can explain.






Clade-specific tips




Hypsigenyinae (tuskfishes and hogfishes): This clade includes both Indo-Pacific tropical species and warm-temperate species extending to southern Australia and the Mediterranean. The latitudinal range should be broad enough to detect a gradient if one exists.
Balistoidea (triggerfishes + filefishes): Triggerfishes are predominantly tropical, but filefishes (Monacanthidae) extend into temperate waters. The combined clade offers latitudinal spread.
Cirrhilabrini (fairy wrasses): Almost entirely tropical. If your clade has very little latitudinal variation, this recipe will lack statistical power — note this limitation rather than forcing a result.

title: Recipe 12: Latitude Gradient
text:
The Method
FishBase stores latitude data in the stocks() table as Northernmost and Southermost (note the FishBase spelling) for each species. We compute the midpoint latitude as the center of each species’ latitudinal range, then take the absolute value (because we care about distance from the equator, not hemisphere). This gives us a single continuous variable: abs_midlat, ranging from 0 (equatorial) to ~60+ (high-latitude). We then regress chromatic diversity (Jc) against abs_midlat using PGLS.






Field names in rfishbase 5.x



In older rfishbase (≤ 3.x) these columns were called NorthernLatitude / SouthernLatitude. From rfishbase 5.x onward they are Northernmost / Southermost (the “Southermost” spelling is from the upstream FishBase schema). The code below uses the 5.x names.


The prediction is a negative slope: species farther from the equator (higher abs_midlat) have lower chromatic diversity. A positive slope would be unexpected and could indicate that temperate species invest more in chromatic signaling, perhaps because the visual environment is less cluttered by coral reef backgrounds.
Note that the stocks() table may return multiple records per species (different populations or stocks). We aggregate by taking the first record, which gives the species-level range. Some species will have NA values for latitude. Check your sample size after merging.

title: Recipe 12: Latitude Gradient
text:
How to Interpret Results








Result
Interpretation
What to say on your poster




Negative slope, p < 0.05
Tropical species are more chromatically diverse
“Chromatic diversity declines significantly with latitude in [family], extending the latitudinal diversity gradient from species richness to color phenotype.”


Positive slope, p < 0.05
Temperate species are more chromatically diverse
“Unexpectedly, temperate species are more chromatically diverse. This could reflect stronger selection for species recognition in lower-diversity assemblages, or a confound with body size or habitat.”


p > 0.05
No significant relationship
“Latitude does not predict chromatic diversity in [family] after controlling for phylogeny. The latitudinal diversity gradient in species richness may not extend to color phenotype in this clade.”









Common pitfalls




Latitude is a proxy, not a mechanism. A significant result tells you that color varies with latitude, but not why. Latitude correlates with temperature, light intensity, UV flux, species richness, habitat complexity, and dozens of other variables. Be cautious about causal claims.
Midpoint latitude is a coarse measure. It assumes the species’ range is centered around its midpoint, which may not be true for species with skewed distributions (e.g., ranges extending far south from an equatorial core).
Sample bias: If most species in your clade are tropical (many reef fish families are), you will have many data points near the equator and few at high latitudes. This can inflate leverage for the few temperate species, making the result sensitive to individual outliers. Check for influential points.
Missing data: Not all species have latitude records in the stocks() table. Check your sample size after merging and filtering NAs.

title: Recipe 12: Latitude Gradient
text:
The Code

# ── Recipe 12: Latitude Gradient ──────────────────────────────
source("https://michaelalfaro.github.io/eeb187-demos/recipes/code/helpers.R")

# ── 1. Load your data ────────────────────────────────────────
traits <- read.csv("path/to/your/pavo_metrics.csv",
                    stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
bundle <- load_bundle("path/to/your-family-mini-bundle")

# ── 2. Pull latitude data from FishBase ──────────────────────
# In rfishbase 5.x these columns are `Northernmost` / `Southermost`
# (older rfishbase used `NorthernLatitude` / `SouthernLatitude`).
fb <- pull_fishbase(traits$species,
                    fields = list(stocks = c("Northernmost",
                                             "Southermost")))

# ── 3. Compute midpoint latitude ─────────────────────────────
merged <- merge(traits, fb, by = "species")
merged <- merged[!is.na(merged$Northernmost) &
                  !is.na(merged$Southermost), ]
merged$abs_midlat <- abs((merged$Northernmost +
                           merged$Southermost) / 2)

cat("Species with latitude data:", nrow(merged), "\n")
cat("Midpoint latitude range:",
    round(range(merged$abs_midlat), 1), "\n")

# ── 4. Match to tree ────────────────────────────────────────
matched <- match_tree_data(bundle$tree, merged, species_col = "species")

# ── 5. PGLS: chromatic diversity vs latitude ─────────────────
model <- safe_pgls(Jc ~ abs_midlat, df = matched$data,
                    tree = matched$tree)

# ── 6. Scatter plot ─────────────────────────────────────────
library(ggplot2)

p <- ggplot(matched$data, aes(x = abs_midlat, y = Jc)) +
  geom_point(size = 4, alpha = 0.7, color = "#264653") +
  { if (!is.null(model))
    geom_abline(intercept = coef(model)[1], slope = coef(model)[2],
                color = "#e76f51", linewidth = 1.2) } +
  labs(x = "Absolute Midpoint Latitude (degrees from equator)",
       y = "Chromatic Diversity (Jc)",
       title = "Does latitude predict chromatic diversity?",
       subtitle = "PGLS controlling for phylogeny") +
  theme_poster

print(p)
ggsave("results/recipe12-latitude-vs-Jc.pdf", p, width = 10, height = 8)

title: Recipe 6: Depth and Color
text: Does the light environment at different depths constrain the chromatic diversity and saturation of color patterns in my family?

title: Recipe 6: Depth and Color
text: Does the light environment at different depths constrain the chromatic diversity and saturation of color patterns in my family?

title: Recipe 6: Depth and Color
text:
This Is an Instance Of…






Environmental filtering of phenotype



This recipe asks whether an abiotic environmental variable — depth, which determines the spectral composition of available light — predicts a phenotypic trait (color diversity). Water rapidly absorbs long-wavelength (red/orange) light, so the visual palette available for signaling, camouflage, and species recognition shrinks with depth. This is a classic “environmental filter” hypothesis: the physical environment imposes a ceiling on the phenotypic variation that natural selection can maintain.

title: Recipe 6: Depth and Color
section: Why This Matters for Your Clade
text:
Why This Matters for Your Clade
Reef fish colors are not arbitrary; they exist in a world where the physics of light transmission sets hard boundaries on what colors can be produced, perceived, and maintained. Below about 10 meters, red wavelengths are effectively absent from ambient light. Species that live at depth should therefore have reduced chromatic diversity (fewer distinct hues) and potentially lower saturation, because the visual channel for long-wavelength signaling is physically unavailable. Testing this prediction against your clade’s actual color data tells you whether physics or biology dominates the color palette.






Clade-specific tips




Hypsigenyinae (tuskfishes and hogfishes): This clade spans the broadest depth range in many labrid datasets, from shallow rubble flats to 50+ meter slopes. Expect the best statistical power here, with some species occupying mesophotic zones where the light spectrum is extremely narrow.
Cirrhilabrini (fairy wrasses): Many species in this clade are mesophotic specialists (30–80 m). Their intense male nuptial colors evolved in a blue-shifted light field — an apparent paradox worth discussing. Do their reds and oranges rely on fluorescence or short-range signaling?
Balistoidea (triggerfishes + filefishes): Includes both shallow lagoon specialists and deeper fore-reef dwellers. The contrast between shallow-water triggerfishes with bold patterns and deep-water filefishes with subdued coloration may be striking.

title: Recipe 6: Depth and Color
text:
The Method
PGLS (phylogenetic generalized least squares) tests whether depth predicts color metrics while controlling for the fact that closely related species share evolutionary history and therefore cannot be treated as statistically independent data points. The dependent variable is a pavo color metric — either Jc (chromatic diversity, measuring how many distinct hues are present) or m_dS (mean chromatic contrast, measuring how saturated the colors are). The predictor is the log of maximum depth (DepthRangeDeep from FishBase).
We log-transform depth because the spectral attenuation of light is approximately exponential: the first 10 meters remove most red light, so the biological difference between 5 m and 15 m is much larger than the difference between 55 m and 65 m. Taking the log puts depth on a scale that better matches its biological effect. The PGLS model accounts for phylogeny by using the tree’s branch lengths to define the expected correlation structure among species — close relatives are expected to have more similar residuals than distant relatives.
We run two models: one for Jc (chromatic diversity) and one for m_dS (chromatic contrast). Both should decline with depth if the light-environment hypothesis holds.

title: Recipe 6: Depth and Color
text:
How to Interpret Results








Result
Interpretation
What to say on your poster




Negative slope, p < 0.05
Deeper species have less chromatic diversity/saturation
“The underwater light environment constrains color diversity — deeper species in [family] have significantly reduced chromatic range, consistent with spectral attenuation filtering long wavelengths.”


Positive slope, p < 0.05
Deeper species have more chromatic diversity
“Unexpectedly, deeper species are more chromatically diverse. This could reflect fluorescence, UV signaling, or a confound such as body size covarying with depth.”


p > 0.05
No significant relationship detected
“We found no significant relationship between depth and chromatic diversity after controlling for phylogeny. The light environment may not be the primary constraint on color in [family], or our depth data may be too coarse to capture the relevant variation.”









Common pitfalls




DepthRangeDeep is a species maximum, not a typical habitat depth. A species recorded once at 80 m but usually found at 15 m will have DepthRangeDeep = 80. This adds noise. Acknowledge this limitation in your poster.
Missing data: Not all species have depth records in FishBase. Check how many species you lose after merging. If you drop below ~15 species, your statistical power is very limited.
Fluorescence confound: Some deep-dwelling species produce red fluorescence that compensates for the loss of red ambient light. If your pavo metrics were measured from photos taken under white light, you are measuring the potential color, not the in situ appearance.

title: Recipe 6: Depth and Color
text:
The Code

# ── Recipe 6: Depth and Color ─────────────────────────────────
source("https://michaelalfaro.github.io/eeb187-demos/recipes/code/helpers.R")

# ── 1. Load your data ────────────────────────────────────────
traits <- read.csv("path/to/your/pavo_metrics.csv",
                    stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
bundle <- load_bundle("path/to/your-family-mini-bundle")

# ── 2. Pull depth data from FishBase ─────────────────────────
fb <- pull_fishbase(traits$species,
                    fields = list(species = c("DepthRangeDeep")))

# ── 3. Merge and transform ──────────────────────────────────
merged <- merge(traits, fb, by = "species")
merged <- merged[!is.na(merged$DepthRangeDeep) &
                  merged$DepthRangeDeep > 0, ]
merged$log_depth <- log(merged$DepthRangeDeep)

cat("Species with depth data:", nrow(merged), "\n")

# ── 4. Match to tree ────────────────────────────────────────
matched <- match_tree_data(bundle$tree, merged, species_col = "species")

# ── 5a. PGLS: chromatic diversity vs depth ───────────────────
model_Jc <- safe_pgls(Jc ~ log_depth, df = matched$data, tree = matched$tree)

# ── 5b. PGLS: chromatic contrast vs depth ───────────────────
model_dS <- safe_pgls(m_dS ~ log_depth, df = matched$data, tree = matched$tree)

# ── 6a. Scatter plot: Jc vs log depth ───────────────────────
library(ggplot2)

p1 <- ggplot(matched$data, aes(x = log_depth, y = Jc)) +
  geom_point(size = 4, alpha = 0.7, color = "#264653") +
  { if (!is.null(model_Jc))
    geom_abline(intercept = coef(model_Jc)[1], slope = coef(model_Jc)[2],
                color = "#e76f51", linewidth = 1.2) } +
  labs(x = "log(Maximum Depth, m)",
       y = "Chromatic Diversity (Jc)",
       title = "Does depth constrain chromatic diversity?",
       subtitle = "PGLS controlling for phylogeny") +
  theme_poster

print(p1)
ggsave("results/recipe6-depth-vs-Jc.pdf", p1, width = 10, height = 8)

# ── 6b. Scatter plot: m_dS vs log depth ─────────────────────
p2 <- ggplot(matched$data, aes(x = log_depth, y = m_dS)) +
  geom_point(size = 4, alpha = 0.7, color = "#264653") +
  { if (!is.null(model_dS))
    geom_abline(intercept = coef(model_dS)[1], slope = coef(model_dS)[2],
                color = "#e76f51", linewidth = 1.2) } +
  labs(x = "log(Maximum Depth, m)",
       y = "Mean Chromatic Contrast (m_dS)",
       title = "Does depth constrain chromatic contrast?",
       subtitle = "PGLS controlling for phylogeny") +
  theme_poster

print(p2)
ggsave("results/recipe6-depth-vs-dS.pdf", p2, width = 10, height = 8)

cat("Saved: results/recipe6-depth-vs-Jc.pdf\n")
cat("Saved: results/recipe6-depth-vs-dS.pdf\n")

title: Recipe 7: Body Size and Pattern Complexity
text: Do larger fish display more complex color patterns, and does the relationship match the threshold predictions of reaction-diffusion theory?

title: Recipe 7: Body Size and Pattern Complexity
text: Do larger fish display more complex color patterns, and does the relationship match the threshold predictions of reaction-diffusion theory?
crumbs: Recipe 7: Body Size and Pattern Complexity

title: Recipe 7: Body Size and Pattern Complexity
text:
This Is an Instance Of…






Allometric scaling of phenotype



This recipe tests whether a physical constraint — body size — predicts a phenotypic trait (pattern complexity). Reaction-diffusion models (Turing patterns) predict that the absolute size of the body surface determines the number and type of pattern elements that can form: small bodies may be too small to support pattern instabilities, while very large bodies can sustain complex multi-scale patterns. This is not merely a statistical correlation; it is a prediction from mathematical biology about how biochemistry and geometry interact during development.
crumbs: Recipe 7: Body Size and Pattern Complexity

title: Recipe 7: Body Size and Pattern Complexity
section: Why This Matters for Your Clade
text:
Why This Matters for Your Clade
Body size is one of the most fundamental traits in ecology — it correlates with metabolic rate, trophic level, home range, predation risk, and lifespan. If body size also predicts color pattern complexity, then many of the ecological patterns you might test in other recipes could be confounded by size. Murray’s 1981 reaction-diffusion model makes a specific prediction: pattern complexity should increase with body size, but not linearly. Instead, there are threshold zones where qualitative changes in pattern type occur. This recipe lets you test that prediction with your clade’s actual data, and it sets the stage for Recipe 7b (size-corrected residuals).






Clade-specific tips




Scarinae (parrotfishes): This clade offers an extraordinary size range, from Cryptotomus roseus at ~12 cm to Bolbometopon muricatum at ~130 cm. If Murray’s rule holds, you should see a dramatic shift in pattern complexity across this gradient.
Balistoidea (triggerfishes + filefishes): Another clade with substantial size variation. Triggerfishes tend to be medium-bodied with bold geometric patterns; filefishes range from tiny to large with variable patterning. The size–pattern relationship may differ between the two families.
Cirrhilabrini (fairy wrasses): Relatively uniform in size (mostly 6–12 cm), which means less statistical power for detecting a size effect, but also means size is unlikely to be a major confound in other analyses.
crumbs: Recipe 7: Body Size and Pattern Complexity

title: Recipe 7: Body Size and Pattern Complexity
text:
The Method
This recipe uses two complementary visualizations that address different aspects of the size–complexity question. Understanding when to use log-transformed vs. raw body size is important.
For the PGLS model, we use log(MaxLengthTL) as the predictor. This is standard statistical practice: body size distributions are typically right-skewed, and the log transform stabilizes variance and linearizes the relationship. The PGLS model tests whether there is a statistically significant monotonic relationship between body size and pattern complexity (m) after controlling for phylogeny.
For Murray’s diagnostic plot, we use raw (untransformed) MaxLengthTL on the x-axis. This is because Murray’s theoretical prediction is about absolute body size thresholds — the physical dimensions at which reaction-diffusion dynamics change qualitatively. The theory predicts transitions at specific size scales (roughly ~10 cm and ~50 cm), and these thresholds only make sense on the raw scale. You cannot see threshold zones on a log axis.
Both views are informative, and presenting them together shows scientific sophistication on your poster.
crumbs: Recipe 7: Body Size and Pattern Complexity

title: Recipe 7: Body Size and Pattern Complexity
text:
How to Interpret Results








Result
Interpretation
What to say on your poster




Positive slope, p < 0.05
Larger species have higher pattern complexity
“Pattern complexity increases significantly with body size in [family], consistent with reaction-diffusion scaling predictions.”


Negative slope, p < 0.05
Larger species have simpler patterns
“Larger species in [family] have simpler patterns, possibly reflecting a shift toward uniform disruptive or cryptic coloration at large body sizes.”


p > 0.05
No significant monotonic relationship
“No significant linear relationship between body size and pattern complexity. The relationship may be nonlinear (consistent with Murray’s threshold model) or absent in this clade.”


Murray plot shows threshold zones
Qualitative pattern shifts at size boundaries
“Visual inspection suggests threshold-like transitions in pattern complexity at body sizes of approximately X cm, consistent with Murray’s (1981) reaction-diffusion predictions.”









Common pitfalls




MaxLengthTL is a species maximum, not a mean. It reflects the largest reliably recorded individual. Actual adults in your photo sample may be smaller.
Log vs. raw confusion: Use log body size for the PGLS (it is a statistical requirement for well-behaved residuals). Use raw body size for the Murray diagnostic (it is a theoretical requirement for interpreting threshold predictions). Label your axes clearly to show you understand the difference.
Size range matters: If your clade has a narrow size range (e.g., all species between 8 and 15 cm), you have little power to detect a size effect and the Murray thresholds will not be testable. Note this on your poster.

title: Recipe 17: Stripe Orientation and Ecology
text: Do vertical versus horizontal stripe patterns correlate with habitat or behavior — and does that relationship hold after controlling for phylogeny?

title: Recipe 17: Stripe Orientation and Ecology
text: Do vertical versus horizontal stripe patterns correlate with habitat or behavior — and does that relationship hold after controlling for phylogeny?

title: Recipe 17: Stripe Orientation and Ecology
text:
This Is an Instance Of…






Testing a Pattern-Function Hypothesis



You are testing whether stripe orientation — one of the most salient and ecologically interpreted features of reef fish color — predicts where a species lives or how it behaves. The pavo metric A (aspect ratio of color patches) is your quantitative proxy: values above 1 indicate patches taller than wide (vertical bars); values below 1 indicate patches wider than tall (horizontal stripes).
The ecological predictor can be categorical (FishBase DemersPelag habitat codes: reef-associated, demersal, pelagic, etc.) or continuous (FishBase DepthRangeDeep, the maximum recorded depth). The analysis is a PGLS regression that asks whether habitat type predicts stripe orientation after accounting for shared ancestry.
This recipe connects visual ecology theory — the prediction that vertical bars disrupt outline against vertical reef structure while horizontal stripes aid schooling in open water — to a macroevolutionary test across your entire clade.

title: Recipe 17: Stripe Orientation and Ecology
section: Why This Matters for Your Clade
text:
Why This Matters for Your Clade
The orientation of stripes is not arbitrary. Behavioral and visual ecology studies suggest two main functional predictions:

Vertical bars create disruptive coloration against the complex vertical geometry of coral reefs (coral branches, sea fans, crevices). They also disrupt the perception of body outline for edge-detecting predators.
Horizontal stripes facilitate schooling: a horizontal stripe makes it easier for conspecifics to track each other’s movements, and in open-water schools they contribute to the “dazzle” effect that confuses predators trying to track a single fish.







Natural fits for this recipe



Acanthuridae (Surgeonfishes) — The genus Naso is largely pelagic and plain or horizontally striped; the reef-associated surgeonfishes (Acanthurus, Ctenochaetus, Zebrasoma) are more variable. Does habitat type predict stripe orientation across the family?
Pomacanthidae (Angelfishes) — Many angelfishes have dramatic vertical banding. Are the most vertically banded species also the most tightly reef-associated (shallower, less pelagic)?
Halichoerine wrasses — This large clade spans habitats from exposed reef crests to rubble zones and even deeper water. With 50–70 species, you have the sample size to detect a depth–orientation signal.
Balistoidea — Triggerfishes that form midwater schools (Melichthys) show more horizontal color elements than the solitary reef-dwelling species. Does DemersPelag or depth predict this in the broader family?
Any clade — Even if the prediction does not pan out, the absence of a habitat–orientation correlation is ecologically informative. It might mean that stripe orientation in your group is primarily driven by species recognition or sexual selection rather than habitat-mediated crypsis.

title: Recipe 17: Stripe Orientation and Ecology
text:
The Method
Step 1 — Identify your predictor. Choose one of two options: - Categorical: FishBase DemersPelag codes (reef-associated, demersal, benthopelagic, pelagic). Collapse to two groups if needed (reef-associated vs. not-reef-associated), since small sample sizes in each category will limit your analysis. - Continuous: FishBase DepthRangeDeep (maximum depth recorded for the species). Log-transform before analysis.
If you are not sure which to use, start with DepthRangeDeep — it tends to have fewer missing values and gives a continuous gradient to work with.
Step 2 — Pull the predictor from FishBase. Use pull_fishbase() with fields = list(species = c("DemersPelag", "DepthRangeDeep")).
Step 3 — Check your response variable. Your response is A (aspect ratio) from your pavo metrics. Print a histogram. Values near 1 are square patches; values above 1.5 are meaningfully vertically elongated; values below 0.7 are meaningfully horizontal. If most of your species cluster near 1, the signal may be weak regardless of the predictor.
Step 4 — Match to tree and run PGLS. The formula is A ~ DemersPelag (categorical) or log(A) ~ log(DepthRangeDeep) (continuous). Note: if you use log(A), values greater than 0 are vertical (A > 1) and values less than 0 are horizontal (A < 1). This symmetric scale can make interpretation easier.
Step 5 — Visualize. For the categorical predictor: a boxplot of A by habitat category, colored by the two groups. For the continuous predictor: a scatter plot of A versus depth with a PGLS regression line overlaid.

title: Recipe 17: Stripe Orientation and Ecology
text:
How to Interpret Results







Result
Interpretation




Reef-associated species have higher A
Consistent with disruptive coloration hypothesis: reef habitat selects for vertical bars


Open-water / pelagic species have lower A
Consistent with schooling / dazzle hypothesis: open water selects for horizontal stripes


A increases with maximum depth
Deeper species are more vertically barred — could reflect different reef light environments at depth


A decreases with maximum depth
Deeper species are more horizontally striped — consider that deeper = more open, less structured reef


No significant relationship
Stripe orientation in this clade is not predicted by habitat type; other forces (species recognition, sexual selection) may dominate



Pitfalls to avoid:

A near 1 for most species. If your pavo metrics show A clustering around 1 with low variance, the signal will be weak regardless of method. Report the range and variance of A in your sample before interpreting any regression.
Reef-associated is not the same as “vertical bar habitat.” Many reef fish hide in sand or rubble, where vertical bars would not help. Refine your habitat categories if FishBase allows it (some species have DepthRange comments that clarify habitat microstructure).
Do not log-transform DepthRangeDeep if many species have 0 or very shallow records. Add 1 before logging (log(DepthRangeDeep + 1)) and note this in your methods.
Sexual dichromatism confounds the analysis. If you mixed male and female images, and males and females have different orientations (as in many wrasses and parrotfishes), your A values will be noisy. Use the same sex across all species or explicitly note which phase/sex you measured.
Small samples in pelagic or open-water categories. Most reef fish families have few true pelagic members. A categorical test with n < 5 in one category will have low power. If that is your situation, switch to the continuous depth predictor.

title: Recipe 17: Stripe Orientation and Ecology
text:
The Code

library(ape)
library(ggplot2)

source("https://michaelalfaro.github.io/eeb187-demos/recipes/code/helpers.R")

# ── Load your pavo metrics and tree ──────────────────────────────
bundle <- load_bundle("path/to/your/bundle")
tree   <- bundle$tree
traits <- read.csv("my_pavo_metrics.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
# Required columns: species, A (aspect ratio from pavo)

# ── Pull habitat data from FishBase ──────────────────────────────
fb <- pull_fishbase(traits$species,
                    fields = list(species = c("DemersPelag", "DepthRangeDeep")))

cat("DemersPelag categories found:\n")
print(table(fb$DemersPelag, useNA = "always"))

cat("\nDepthRangeDeep summary:\n")
print(summary(fb$DepthRangeDeep))

# ── Merge pavo metrics with FishBase data ─────────────────────────
merged <- merge(traits, fb, by = "species")

# ── Check the distribution of A ───────────────────────────────────
hist(merged$A, breaks = 20,
     main = "Distribution of aspect ratio (A)",
     xlab = "A (> 1 = vertical bars, < 1 = horizontal stripes)",
     col  = "#2a9d8f")
abline(v = 1, col = "#e76f51", lwd = 2, lty = 2)

# ── Option A: Categorical predictor (DemersPelag) ─────────────────
# Collapse to two groups; adjust categories for your clade
merged$habitat <- ifelse(
  merged$DemersPelag %in% c("reef-associated"),
  "reef", "other")
merged_cat <- merged[!is.na(merged$habitat) & !is.na(merged$A), ]

cat("\nHabitat category counts:\n")
print(table(merged_cat$habitat))

matched_cat <- match_tree_data(tree, merged_cat, species_col = "species")

# PGLS: A ~ habitat (categorical)
model_cat <- safe_pgls(A ~ habitat, df = matched_cat$data, tree = matched_cat$tree)

# Boxplot: A by habitat category
p_cat <- ggplot(matched_cat$data, aes(x = habitat, y = A, fill = habitat)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, outlier.shape = NA, width = 0.45) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, size = 3, alpha = 0.6, color = "gray20") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "#e76f51", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.6, y = 1.05, label = "A = 1\n(square patches)",
           size = 4, color = "#e76f51", hjust = 0) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("reef" = "#2a9d8f", "other" = "#264653")) +
  labs(title    = "Stripe orientation by habitat",
       subtitle = "Reef-associated vs. other habitat (PGLS-corrected)",
       x        = "",
       y        = "Aspect ratio A\n(↑ vertical bars  |  ↓ horizontal stripes)") +
  theme_poster +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

ggsave("fig-stripe-habitat.png",
       plot  = p_cat, width = 8, height = 7, dpi = 300, bg = "white")
print(p_cat)

# ── Option B: Continuous predictor (DepthRangeDeep) ───────────────
merged_dep <- merged[!is.na(merged$DepthRangeDeep) & merged$DepthRangeDeep > 0
                     & !is.na(merged$A), ]
merged_dep$log_depth <- log(merged_dep$DepthRangeDeep)

matched_dep <- match_tree_data(tree, merged_dep, species_col = "species")

# PGLS: A ~ log(depth)
model_dep <- safe_pgls(A ~ log_depth, df = matched_dep$data, tree = matched_dep$tree)

# Scatter plot: A vs. log(max depth)
p_dep <- ggplot(matched_dep$data, aes(x = log_depth, y = A)) +
  geom_point(size = 3.5, alpha = 0.7, color = "#2a9d8f") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE,
              color = "#e76f51", fill = "#e76f51", alpha = 0.15,
              linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "gray50", linewidth = 0.7) +
  labs(title    = "Stripe orientation vs. maximum depth",
       subtitle = "Does depth predict vertical vs. horizontal patterning? (PGLS-corrected)",
       x        = "log(Maximum depth, m)",
       y        = "Aspect ratio A\n(↑ vertical bars  |  ↓ horizontal stripes)") +
  theme_poster

ggsave("fig-stripe-depth.png",
       plot  = p_dep, width = 9, height = 7, dpi = 300, bg = "white")
print(p_dep)

What to report on your poster:

Your chosen visualization (boxplot for categorical, scatter for continuous)
PGLS coefficient, t-value, and p-value
Mean A by group (if categorical), or the slope and direction (if continuous)
A plain-language interpretation: “Species in [habitat] / at [shallower/deeper] depths tend to have [higher/lower] aspect ratios, [consistent/inconsistent] with the prediction that [vertical bars / horizontal stripes] are favored in [reef / open-water] habitats (PGLS: β = , p = ).”

title: Recipe 17: Stripe Orientation and Ecology
text:
From the Literature
Stevens, M., & Merilaita, S. (2009). Animal camouflage: current issues and new perspectives. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B, 364, 423–427. A brief review that frames the main hypotheses for stripe function — background matching, disruptive coloration, and motion dazzle — in a comparative context. Useful for framing your prediction in the Introduction section of the poster.
How, M. J., & Zanker, J. M. (2014). Motion camouflage induced by zebra stripes. Zoology, 117, 163–170. Tests the motion dazzle hypothesis directly: stripe orientation affects how hard it is for a predator to track a moving target. The logic extends to fish: horizontal stripes in schooling fish may make it harder for predators to lock onto individual targets moving horizontally through the water.
Marshall, N. J. (2000). Communication and camouflage with the same “bright” colours in reef fishes. Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B, 355, 1243–1248. A classic paper showing that conspicuous colors in reef fish can serve simultaneously as camouflage (broken outline against reef background) and conspecific communication. Directly relevant to the interpretation of vertical bars: what looks conspicuous to us may be disruptive against coral.
